LO! A DREAM..

I laid me down and slept, and In ! a dream Stole soft into my slumber, and the life 'Which bad been dying out of me did seem Regenerate; till every sense was rife • With a new power, and I myself began A state of being worthy of a man. Friends called it "death ; " said they. The end is come," ' And all around a tearful silence fell; 80, then, I knew that I was going home. And the kind thought came o'er me like'a spell That childhood had returned to me again, Bounding the key-note of my life's Amen. I slept, and dreamt, and woke to find it true— All dreams are true that land us into heaven— I was a child, with power to think and do, Born of the second life my God had given. And growing stronger with each ray of light, For le'was cradled in the Infinite. Then, as I opened first my wondering eyes • There smiled on re a vision of the past, Her face, who once had made a paradise About my childhood, and this seemed to last, While that had faded; and I felt a kiss - Upon my soul, which sealed me into bliss. That mother's face had been my boyhood's heaven, Too brief, alas! yet beautifully dear; And, now the bounds of time and space were riven That mother's face was still my heaven here; So brightly did it shine, it seemed to be The face revealed of hidden Deity. It gave me welcome to my Father's home, And smiled divinely on me ; then I knew That not my mother, but My God had come . .
To greet me, for the gracious vision grew Each moment fairer, till I prostrate fell • Before my mother-like EmmanueL S'anday Magazine.
GENEVIEVE IRON.

The highest point to which things can bring one is contentment of the mind, with which no estate is, miser- able. "It is the little things that tell," says an old adage. " Yes—especially the little brothers," says an experi- enced sister. • The perfect athlete is he who, surmounting his sinful inclinations and teenptations, exercises a perfect control over his mind. IN STATII QUO.—Mother : "Now, Emma, wh'at is the tenth commandment ?" Emma, aged five: "The same as it was last Sunday." Some years ago Miss Kellogg, the operatic singer, was questioned about her Continued spinsterhood; she made the witty reply that "she could not afford to keep a hus- band." Ax ANTICtUF. Coars-raust.—The following conundrum is sent to Messrs. Pears daily as "something new." It probably, however, dates from the establishment of their . arm 100 years ago :—What is the difference between Pears' Soap and an Arab horse ? Answer: One washes ' the beautiful and the other scours the plain. A good talker should be a ready listener, a skilful cross eieaminer, eager to discover his companion's interests and 'clever in drawing him out, while ready when needed to draw on his own resources. A bad talker invariably either wants to be a monopolist or creates a sense of unreality by too-ready acquiescence when a little opposition would fan the flame, or else perhaps falls into that most stupid of errors, a morbid striving after accuracy. ALWAYS FINDING Fetaas—Let us take care to include in our petitions an urgent entreaty that the good Lord ,in His mercy will keep us from finding fault with each other. This habit, allowed to grow and grow, becomes a very Upas tree in Many a household, killing all peace and breaking down the unity: and comfort of home. It is so easy to point out what is wrong and forget that the action criticised WAS perhaps done with the best ability of the doer. • Even if we are really sure of being able to do it better, there is no excuse for discouraging the ' attempt made by another. THE OTHER PEOPLE.—What a world—what a wonder- ful and beautiful world—could we create in a year or two but for the "other people." All the wars, all the injuet ices, all the blunders, and all the crimes are due to the other people. But for them we shouldiunite, com- bine, agree, concert, devise, and execute such things as • the world has never yet seen. It is for this long-eared race that statesmen make pledges, promises, and assur- ances; they have eyes which see not and ears which hear not: they are idolaters, and worship one man, one formula, one idea; and for stiff-neckedness, for continual lusting after things which they ought not to desire. they are worse than the Israelites in their most palmy days. —Wafter Resent. HIDDEN SOURCES.—IL is curious to notice how diffe- rently men reason when they deal with material things. , If machinery is out 'of order, if crops fail, if business languishes, they naturally and rightly seek for the cause, and, if possible, remove it. If bodily health declines, no pains are spared to discover what is at fault; the :ood, the rest, the domicile, the habits are carefully examined, and all the conditions and circum- stances so controlled as to afford the best possible chance of recevery. But when men and women go astray and commit wrong and foolish actions, neither they themselves nor others look very deep or carefully for the hidden cause. Society is content to blame the offender, and the offender who blames himself for the act itself is supposed to have gone to the root of the matter. ENTIRELY OISINTEIIESTED.—" Bub!" he called at the market yesterday morning after he had disposed of his potatoes, " is there any toy store near here ?" "Yes, sir." "Just show me the way, will you I've got to buy a few things for Christmas." "Got children ?" "Yes." "Got a boy as big as me?" "Just about your age." "What are you goin,.% to buy him for Saqta Claus ?" "1 dunno yet. I was thinking I'd git some sort of toy." "Say, lemme give you a bit of advice," said the lad as they walked along together. "Let toys alone. Steam ineines are dangerous,, toy mules won't kick for shucks, and Christmas jack-knives fall all to pieces in a week. If yon'ye got a boy, and you want to tickle him most to aeath, I'll sell you my roller. skates for half-price, cause we hain't got no place for skating this winter, and 'Want to sell 'em and; buy it all in cocoanut candy." Lesa Hist ears REV.—Some one has told the story of Haigh who died in Durham forty years ago. He was a determined man, and very penurious. He died at an advanced age. On his death bed he kept his right hand closely clutched. As he drew his last breath he tightened his hold. Everybody there knew what he held. It was the key to the chest in which he kept his gold. As his nerveless hand unclosed, the key dropped from it and clattered against the bedside. As if to hold it even after his soul had passed away, the miser had . tied the key about his wrist by a stroag cord, and had grasped it as long as life remained. He had wanted to take his gold with him. They buried him just as he was, with the key to his money chest dangling about his wrist, and to-day the key is in his grave, turned to • rust probably. And what became of the gold? Oh, the heirs took care ef that just the same. They split open the chest With ffln axe and divided the gold, and let the miser sleep on with the key about his wrist.. INVESTMENT.—WhiIe on the sub- ject we may mention the ase of Mrs. Mary Ann Halls, of Wardley, Uppingham' whose husband has been a resi- dent of Rutland County for over forty years. His is that of a shepherd, and it is safe to say that no one iTbetter known in all the country about %Yardley than John Halls. He is universally respected as an in- dustrious and honest man. In reciting" the particulars of the case, we can do no better than use Mr. Hall's own, statement =dens our reporter. He says "For- over eighteen years my wife was an intense sufferer from rheumatism. Much of the time her hands, elbows, knees and feet were swollen to two or three times their usual size, so that she was unable to walk or dress herself. She was in fact absolutely helpless. Her joints became so stiff at times that she could .not move them. During these periods she suffered the most intense agony, and in all these long years she was never entirely free from pain, either day or night. Different remedies were re- commended toles, all of which she used, but got no re- lief. Our family doctor said there was no help for her and that her case was incurable. She and I had given up all hope of her ever recovering her health or being again free from pain. She had suffered so long that she had become thoroughly disheartened. Just before last Christmas we read in a newspaper an article copied from the Loodon Magazine of Chemistry and Medicine, • which gave particulars of the wonderful cure, by St. Jacobs Oil, of Edward Evans, whose mse was similar to my wife's. As we had for years tried everything we had heard of, she concluded to try this remedy also, and I sent tothe proprietors, the Charles A. Vogeler Company, 45, Farringdon Road, London, for a bottle of it. The Oil was first applied to her hands, which had for many years been so fearfully deformed as to be almost without shape. Before she had used the contents of one bottle to our amazement and joy the swelling disappeared;" and her crippled halide once more assumed their natural s shape. You may well look astonished at what I say, but lam relating facts to you," remarked Mr. Halls. " She then applied the remedy to theNjoints of her linlbs and feet, and marvellous as it may seem, the swelling and pain, which had withstood all treatment, began to disappear, and before the coatents of this one bottle had been used, the swelling, stiffness, and pain with which she had been afflicted for nearly twenty years, vanished as if by magic. She recovered the full use of her limbs, hands, and feet. She. can walk as well as •ever she could in her life, attends to her household duties and sleeps soundly at night, while for years she had not known what it was to have a good night's rest. she is free from pain and is completely cured, and all this was brought about by a single bottle of St. Jacobs Oil. I tell you frankly that I believe this remedy has no equal in the world. It has brought comfort and happi- ness to my home and I advise everyone suffering from pain to try it. 'The 2s. 6d. I spent for a bottle was the best investment I ever made in my life." Mrs. Halls personally confirmed everything that her husband had said, and could scarcely say enough in praise of thisre- rnarkable agency of healing which had rescued her from her scifferings.—Cheansford News.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 4,1888.
A.GIRL IN A THOUSAND.
• BY JEAN MIDDLEMASS. Author of "Lady Muriel's Secret," "The Spider and the Fly," "Poisoned Arrows," "Wild Georgie," &c., &c.
CHAPTER 111. LADY FEDORA'S PERPLEXITIES.

Lady Fedora Stanhope is sitting in the morning room, which looks on to a terrace garden at the back of the Eaton-square house. There is the shadow of a great perplexity upon her comely face, which usually beams with kindly smiles. Lady Fedora is one of those women to whom high birth, greatness of position, and wealth, come...naturally. She has never been acquainted With adverse circumstances and has but little anxiety ; thus no wrinkles have prematurely markedl her brow. , _

---• • At fifty, which is about her present age, she looks scarcely more than five-and-thirty,and thatsheshould have a son who has left Oxford seems to those who see ' her for the first time almost , an impossibility. Yet she did notmarry vefy young, but waited patiently for a good offer. Nor ,was she exactly disappointed. Henry Stanhope,of Warleigh Hall, was the most cour- teous of gentletnen, the most affectionate of husbands, and the kindest of men, but money has never been as • plentiful with him as people believe; and if his wife, his beloved Fedora, has known no care, he has scarcelybeen exempt from itin his constant endeavour to keep her supplied with comforts rad luxuries. Of late his cares have so much increased that he can keep the knowledge of them from her no longer, and on learning naturally' she shares them. Henry Stanhope had struggled hard to give hi§ two sons—Geoffrey and Ferdinand—expensive educations, even against the crushing disadvantage of some nnlet farms; whilst those that were occupied were, by a heavy percentage, far lass in value than they had formerly- been. At the time of his marriage he was a so-called rich man; now he is, by comparison, a poor one, and this Lady Fedora feels as She slts conning over their affairs in the welkappointed boudoir in Eaton-square. But, alas, it is not solely Henry , Stanhope's . diminished fortunes that trouble her. Retrenchment is a word before which Lady Fedora would not have quailed. It is another and more terrible fact that lies heavily on her heart, weighing far more than nnlet farms or unpunctual tenants would ever

weigh. Ferdinand, her second son, by far the -manlier,, handsomer, and more daring of her two boys, is de- veloping ataste for expensive habits and a reckless disregard for the source whence money comes,which, if they are not stopped, will not only bring Mr. Stan- hope's grey hairs to a sorrowful grave, but will in- evitably and irretrievably injure his brptheiGeoffrey. "But it cannot. be possible—Ferdinand, her der- /ing, her pet; the son, though the second, to whom she has looked since babyhood as likely to prove the mainstay of the Stanhopes as long as he • shall live I It is all a mistake—his father must be deceived—he had always liked Geoffrey best. Impossible that Fer- dinand should so disregard his own positipn as to get into difficulties." And the unhappy, Awakening mother, usually so placid and easy-going, got up and walked agitatedly about the room; forshe could not help acknowledging that Henry Stanhope was too just and honourable in all his' dealings to dream of accusing his on son unless he had good cause, 'especially when he knew that the accusation would well-nigh break the mother's heart. Mr. Stanhope had delayed a long time before he told Lady Fedora of Ferdinand's peccadilloes. It was not till he himself had reasoned with him, threatened him, and stormed at him all in vain, that it oc- curred to him that perchance- a strong influenee brought to bear by this good loving mother mighl! succeed when he could net. He accordingly judged it expedient to lay bare some of these delinquencies of Ferdinand's, which he would so gladly have with- • held, and begged Lady Fedora to tell the young man that, in justice to Geoffrey and the rest of the family, his father would not go on paying his debts; and that either some radical change would have to be brought about or Ferdinand would have to thiow up a commission in the Army he had now held for about a year, and go abroad to the Colonies. Never before had Lady Fedora heard her husband. speak so severely or give his sentiments on business matters with so reach point. Now that at last he had determined to enlighten Lady Fedora, he re- solved to do it, as he did everything else in life, thoroughly. Henry Stanhope was a Man who never seemed to • flinch from duty, either for himself or others. Lady Fedora was the only being he had ever taken the trouble to spare, and, except by her, he would probably be judged as a monstrously severe man who.had, indeed, an iron hand ler a velvet glove. V• His children loved him, but their love was mixed with awe a feeling for which Lady Fedora frequently puzzled herself to account. Since that interview with Mr. Stanhope, in which he told her some truths about Ferdinand, perhaps she had discovered that the younger generation had good reason for standing in awe of their father, if their own march . through life was -not alkether along straight roads. l• She decided at length that she would not, however, make herself unhappy. -Bhe*was sure Ferdinand would listen to her; he did not wish to give her pain. Probably his father had been severe with him; he spoke as if he might have been. She tiad written to the dear boy, who was quartered at Horn'- slow, begging him to come and see her, and after that it would be all right. • And thus she tried to persuade herself; only anxiety would not be quieted so easily, nor the lines which since last night had come into her face, be stamped out all on a sudden. She' had stopped in her walk, and was ab- stractedly pulling the leaves off a geranium that stood by the window, when the door opened, and one of those visions of light which rejoice a mother's heart flooded the room.. Golden-haired Irene's arms were around her mother's neck, and as though. she knew of the ex- istence of those lines, she seemed to be trying to kiss them away. Lady Fedora was accustomed to Irene's effusive caresses, and though she really delighted in them, stillshe gently tried to check the girl's ardour, Now she took her by both hands, and, holding her at arms' length, looked in her face. No one delighted more in Irene's beauty than did Lady Fedora • and well she might, for the girl was a very sunbeam, and truly she lodked one now with her curling golden hair, sweet delicate face, and radiant laughing eyes. Not for a moment could you associate sorrow or trouble with Irene Stanhope, and yet, doubtless, she will be scarcely Mortal with- out her share—ay, is it not even now being garnered up for her, although -she knows it not? She reads its reflection at once in her mother's face. ' "What is it, darling mother?" she asks. is amiss ?"

another kiss. "I am not glum, child, only laughing. Tell me, why does your with Ferdinand?' "Oh, because it is a sort of fashion to think that Ferdinard is a better boy than dear old Geoff, and papa wants to keep him up to the mark, I suppose." "Who says Ferdinand is a be..ter boy than Geoff?" "Well, you do, and Purvis does, and papa used to. I took to Geoff because ha was snubbed." "Irene, it is not right of you to say, that. We all love Geoff quite as much as we love Ferdinand." "Only in a different way;' I suppose," Irene went on, laughing.. "Ferdinand is grand and manly, and .tiresome, while Geoff is a sweet old dear. He never teased me in his life, and I am quite happy if I can sit for hours and watch him painting or listen to him playing—quite happy listening to and looking at Geoff with Phyllis Knight to help me. "Is Phyllis as fond of listening to and lookiag at Geoff as you are ? " and Lady Fedora smiled. "Why, of course; isn't he her brother too, since she is my foster sister 1" " According to that rule, so is Ferdinand." "Oh, Ferdinand—he never notices her beyond a 'Good morning, Phyllis.' I don't believe he knows whether she is pretty or ugly." "Just as well, j , ust as well, muttered Lady Fedora; then, aloud, "Do you know, my pet, it is getting very nearly time that you gave up this play- mating with Phyllis Knight. You know you are to come out this season. lam going to take you to your first ball next week." As she spoke Lady Fedora s cheek grew pale and a sharp pain came at her heart, for she suddenly remembered the conversation
reason

about ways and means she had recently had her husband, and she wondered, with his other ex- penses, whether he would be able to afford tiii season for Irene. The little revolt in her mind against Ferdinand fin the injustice his behaviour was bringing to his sister was speedily crushed by Irene herself,who cried out— "Go to a first ball and have no more play- mating with Phyllis. Oh, mamma, I don't want to go to balls. I don't want to know any new people, only to lie with Phyllis—Phyllis and Geoff." Phyllis and Geoff I, There was something that jarred nnmusically on Lady Fedora's ear in the coupling of these two names. _

Were the revelations and hints about her children all to be disagreeable this day? She kissed her daughter's white brow and toyed with the golden fringe that caressed it, as she said very gently— . "You have already noticed, my: Irene, that some- thing is worrying me. You are right—something of no little importance. You surely would not wish to add to my worries by trying to set up your will against mine. 'You are a Stanhope, my child, the daughter, of a ,great house; you must go into the society that befitti your position, and—" "0)1, mother dear, don't look so grave. Of Course I will go to balls, fetes, anywhere you please to take me—only don't ask me,to give up t would break my heart. Have you folgotten how Phyllis,le nursed me when I was ill two years ago—what devotion, what love! Do.you think I should be alive now if it were not for Phyllis!" , - Lady Fedora smilsd. , "Yes, deaf, I scarcely think that Phyllis saved your life, though you are quite right to be ,o-ratefill and thankful for all the kindly care both she and Mrs. Knight bestowed upon you; still, Irene, it is time you should remember that there is a vast gulf, as far as position goes, between you and this good, bright little Phyllis. You will have to go out into the great world where I hope you will marry some good, kind-man, and be the mistress of a large house, while Phyllis will, in all probabilit,y, become the wife of some well-to-do tradesman." Irene shook her head. "I do not think that Phyllis will ever marry a tradesman," she said,' rather knowingly; " andas for my Prince Charming, well, I haven't found him yet, darling mother—let me be happy tur I do." But Lady Fedora totally disregarded the latter part of her daughter's. sentence, arid repeated— " Not mar?), a tcadesman ?Phyllis! Why not ?" Her mother's earnestness seemed to bring Irene back to a sense that she had said more than she intended, so now she only laughed and answered: "Well, I don't know. How can I know what Phyllis will do in the future? Only she is far too good and sweet to marry benegth her." "Beneath her, my dear Irene. Your love 'fat Phyllis bewitches you. Why, her mother was you nurse,her father has always been a working man,and Phyllis actually has to cook and sweep and da, servant's work, when she is at home. "And a great shame it is. I mean to speak to crusty old Simon Knight about it the first time I have an opportunity. Geoff agrees With me, and is quite indignant. He says if Phyllis has to earn her living, she ought sto have a•profession like painting or music." "Good gracious!" and Lady Fedora's breath seemed to b:almbst taken away. "What has Geoff to do with Phyllis's affairs? Is he, too, infatuated with herby chance! Irene out very red at this direct question, but she answered it by saying, "Didn't we settle just now that he is her brother? so of course he is interested in what beConies of her." _ _ _

But Lady Fedora was by no means satisfied. The lines that had been on her face when Irene came into the room had considerably deepened, and she had a sort of pr&entiment that the troubles which had been averted from her all her life were now beginning to crowd thickly upon her. . . Phyllis and Geoff! These names would clang ominously in her ears,and she determined that the mischief, if mischief there were, that had come about throirgh her children's intimacy with Phyllis Knight, , should be stopped forthwith. _

For once in her life she would be prompt and active. Lady Fedota had over borne a character for pro- crastination and indolence, and she knew her faults well ; this time, however, she would act without say- ing one word to her husband.—poor dear He had enough to torment him, and had spared her all their married ; she would spare him now. Besides, she had only a vague suspicion that all was not right, she would watch and be certain before she did anything rash. Poor little Phyllis, it would be too unkind to banish her altogether from those who loved her well, unless she were certain that such a step were absolgtely necessary. Exactly, Before Lady Fedora had well-nigh finished her meditation, the resolution to act at once with which she had begun it had faded into hesita- tion, and an idea that it was best to wait and see what it were wisest to do. So it was ever with good kindly Lady Fedora; she was utterly incapable of clutching opportunity by the for/ Ica. She had finished her conversation with Irene by biddine, her run away and practise, and not let thoughts about the fature dim the fair horizon of to-dity. Not that light-hearted Irene was in the N;ery least (Lanz& of -doing anything (if the kind. She had been all her young life far too spoiled a child not to feel very certain of getting her own way in the end, and as to imagining that her mother was likely to insist on a final and absolute rupture in her friendship with Phyllis Knight, so little did she believe such a thing to be pr'obable,that before she began to practise she wrote a note' and told her to expect her at Wands. worth that very afternoon about four, dnd to meet her in the lane at the back of the station, when they ' would have a nice walk, for Geoff had promised to accompany her. Meantime, no sooner had Irene left Lady Fedoit. alone than the mother Kit down in an arm-chair, feel- ing _very heavily weighted, to think. Not only hid she to go through a very trying in- terview with Ferdinand, but she felt she must take upon herself to have one with Geoff, and she was not sure she did not dread talking to her elder 'son even more than to the younger his reasoning powers werE so much more developed and he always had a theory for .everything he did, while Ferdinand was entirely the victim of impulse. ' "One boy was all head, and the other all heart," Lady Fedora was wont to say. If then by any chance it could possibly be true that Geoff—the unimpeach- able Geoff—was in lore with Phyllis Knight, why it was the very strangesttlii rig flint had ever happened. If it had beeriFerdinand,she Would not have been so sur- prised ; .but Irene told her Ferdinand rarely spoke to Phyllis. Altogether she was utterly bewildered, and if some one did not come to help her mad the labyrinth into which her ideas had entangled themselves the-chances were she would entirely Joao her mental wan Whether that somebody .would be Ferdinand was doubtful ; but about • half-an-hour afterwards he noisily entered the room, and a great,dashing,soldier- like; bronzed fellow he Was. Could it be possible that this fine young fellow was the scapegrace of the Staub, :es ? (7',,

The least thing has play in it, the slightest word wit, when your hands are busy and your heart is free. But, if you make the aim of your life amusement, the day will come when all the agonies of a pantomime will not bring you an 'honest laugh." BY POVERTY NOOK INTO FURTHER
STRAITS, A MIGRATION OF THE WOODCOCK. BY 'JOHN PEERS.

In Baugor harbour, as one among the many clus- tering boats, we found the natives" very, sociable. They came rowing round us.discoursing pleas- antly in Cambrian English; recounting wondrous exploits on the mountains and the seas. One old gentleman in particular, displayed great interest in the build and qualities of our floating home. Being the owner of one or more sea-going traders, he was able to appreciate the peculiarities of the craft; which he displayed by free and running commen- taries as he sculled his boat round and round us.

Saturday morning found us bound to the neigh- bourhood of Beaumaris. as we expected one, and hoped for the rest of our ship's complement, to join us here in the afternoon. In this our expectation was fulfilled and our hopes disappointed; for the "Skipper" and our old mate —he of the Love deri- ded profession-had found their duties would not per- mit them to be with us. The time was spenti plea- santly enough in rambling overthe sands n full en- joyment of the glorious weather, so essential as an element in man's out-door happiness, the sea, the scenery, and the balmy air. Now, behold! it was the hour when man's thoughts naturally tend in- wards, and their steps follow the bent of those of Old Mother Hubbard, as given in the veracious story, wherein she is said to have sought for the osseous remains of former feasts in an empty cup- board I But our pre-prandial investigation had a happier result than that of the kindly old dame of the story. The locker—our poor substitute for the ,cupboard—did furnish forth what constituted a frugal but sufficing meal, eaten in the open air with appetizing surroundings; health, congenial com- panionship, and contentment. Our position was opposite the oyster strewn beds of Gallows Point, close to the edge of the Levan sands, now bare for a great extent, and we bad a good view of the stage at Beaumaris where we expected 9ur friends to ap- pear. The steamer "Alexandria" had just been to the stage and discharged her passengers, and we had brought the mid-day meal to a satisfactory conclu- sion and were about to weigh and drop down to the stage when we saw a figure on the shore waving to attract our attention. Now this sight was produc- tive of mixt feelings; pleasure to see the one, and sorrow there were no more to give an added zest to our enjoyments by sharing them. But this was not to be; Simon camq and told us the "Skipper" and the Locksmith had found circumstances too strong for them, and were 'compelled to relinquish all idea of the trip. Our newly found mate told us he inquired of the people on the stage if such a boat as ours had been seen about, and was told that a queer looking craft "with a kind of fire place on her counter" had been seen in the harbour once or twice.

After bathing and dining Simon, we ran up to Bangor and lay there until tlei tide served for the Bridges. Whilst here we were entertained by one individual who wanted the job of piloting us through the Swellies with some lugubrious accounts of the dangers incurred by inexperienced navigators, and strongly advised us not to attempt without a pilot, especially as he was there, and his services so easily and cheaply accessible. So far he. What we thought was that, as we had already suc- cessfully braved the dangers of this intricate channel, and that after an absence frOm them Of nineteen years, we might manage the achievement again with the ex- perience of the last four-and-twenty hours still fresh upon our minds. We declined with thanks, and lived not to regret nor died lamenting it. So we gotup theanchor. and threaded the now familiar windings of the turbulent Swellies. Opposite the mansion before mentioned, with its dock and steamer, we came to a new, and to us interesting, feature in the flue barque-rigged yacht " Pandora," looking very large in these narrow waters. Shortly after this we found the grey shades of evening had given place to the sombre garb of night, and the need of some restiag place for us became evident, as the birds had long since sought theirs. This we found at the mouth of the crowded rock cleft they call a harbour at Port Dinorwic. Here we tied up to a buoy, and made things comfortable for the night, ourselves among the rest. .

Port Dmorwic iii just a deep gully in the rocks, gradu- ally narrowing upwards, the mouth, I presume, of some small river. In this crack in the land the natives have succeeded in solving a problem in packing more vessels than .seems possible to outsiders. Early on Sunday morning we found ourselves in close proximity to a large Scotch steamer that was trying to warp and screw her- self into this already well-packed harbour, which seems to be like the proverbial carpet bag—never so full that a little more may not be squeezed in. Whilst here we were privileged to see the good folks crossing the straits in boats to their morning devotions. Now this is indeed a pleasant way of doing this thing, and must be a pleasing interlude and an alleviation of the miseries of being ser- ' mOnized ; of sitting and hearing a man tell the most awful " crammers, as judged by the science of the present day, without the chance of reply. Surely these pleasant trips are some compensation for' these trials. How the dwellers in towns—who have to plod through weary uninteresting streets to this sacrifice—how they manage to sustain it is wonderful. But the power of Mrs. Grundy is still great in the world. Now one of these church-going voyagers-was observed to be atten- tively examining our " sit" upon the water. At last his pent up thoughts found vent in the exclamation, "There is something the 'matter with your fore2oot." This alarming intelligence caused me to look over the bow down into the clear water. where I could see the front terminal of our keel—the " forefoot "—in its normal, but to the Welshman, unusual shape. When the tide served, we wended our way down to Cirnarvon, where we found the " Ada ' still a her berth, while we sought and found one along .side a "slip" beneatll the grey walls " •

of tire old castle. As we were to itay here some time, my two shipmates took the oppprtunity of examining the many points of interest in this Princeiferous city. They returned to me with glowing accounts of military Welshmen marching to church, headed by the goat; the heat of the streets, autiquity of the place, its linguistic pe- culiarities,with other little details incidental to travellers in " farrin parts." Having a little time to make away before flood, we turned off from the " slip" and rowed across to the sand bank opposite to bathe and refect. Now the crockery in a small boat such as ours is apt to loose its distinguishing patterns as a consequence of the proximity of the coal pox and the locker, and the contents of the one getting mixed with the other. It being desirable that each man should know his own, we proceeded to relieve thaw from their mask el overlieing grime. A pleutiful supply of clean sand and water soon brought to light the hidden beauties of the broad-based jugs—chief o Woodcock's crockery, I ween—familiarly known as the "Cherries," "Bit o' mischief" or "High- land Rebel," "Posies," and the "Clock." One of these came to grief, and was left a derelict upon those pleasant sands. Its owner is often told where it is, or was, that he may fetch it if so minded. But he—the love derided laments but not retrieves his loss.

..... Whilst thus engaged we noticed an open pleasure boat, such as are used to carry pleasure parties up and down the Straits, turn off and head away for Beauntaris. Here then was a nice opportunity of doing a bit of racing and going about •our businessi at the same time. We soon found, with our centre board Clown,wecOuld "best" our friend the pilot, and.just hold our own with him when it was'up, his being A much longer boat than ours. When we got back to the "Pandora" again, we hung back talking to a gentleman on board that yacht, who seemed to take great interest in the history, build, and sailing qualities of our little ship. Now, there should be au assignable reason for every action of our lives. Well the reason we hung back just here was to allow our, com- petitor, the manager of which was a pilot, with local knowledge of the Swellies, to precede us in the naviga- tion of the narrow rapids. For though we had already threaded them three times in as ma,ny days, still it was as well to "make assurance doubly sure." So our friend the pilot came up, and in passing asked the stereotype question—" Are you acquainted ?" The answer seemed to convince him that we might make the attempt with-

out rendering us liable to receive unwelcome attentions from the• Commissioners of Lunacy. Nevertheless, he offered some valuable advice as to the navigation of i difficult places, which was accepted in the spirit n which it was given. We both emerged intact, but warm exceedingly with rowing, for the light air was not sufficiently strong to depend upon to clear the rocks and entangling whirl- pools we had passed. In company we slowly beat against the light wind to Gallows Point, some half-mile west of Bea.umaris, whore the two tides meet, the one running through the Straits and the ether round Angle. sea by Holyhead, Point Lynes, Puffin Island, and so into the eastern mouth of the Straits. When we reached this interesting meeting place of the waters,we naturally lost the current which had been mainly instrumental in banging us thus far, and we had again to resort gnomniously to the oars to reach Beaumaris, where we snuggfd tip and turned, in,

OVMonaay morning We found a decided change in the weather. A brisk wind from the east with a rising sea made the boat cut some lively capers as she lay at anchor. This became, as the tide rose, more lively than agreeable, so it was decided to withdraw to some quieter place. Before the little gale we ran, and into Bangor basin, about which we boxed in company with.a local pleasure boat similar to our friend the• pilot's. Now the sea wall was 'high and the wind came over it in very partial puffs, sometimes too much, and at others not , enough to ,give steerage way. This rendered the naviga- tion very tackle, among the craft in the basin, taking ad- vantage of the flaws and puffs to waltz in and among the 1 various obstructions. Our companion, in one of his tacks, misstays and sidled with hi.s mainsail against the jib-boom of a schooner, which made therein a goodly rent. However, he seemed to be provided for such con- tingencies, and was soon busy with needle and palm in repairing damages. When we found this amusement to pall upon us we went to the mouth of the basin and made fast abreast of some steps up which we could go taget to the top of the sea wall. • And the top of this wall was certainly a great contrast to the place where the boat lay so snug. The wind was rushing across it in a way that 'made standing rather difficult ; where the flattened grass i lay quivering n green sheets and the broken water swept across in sheets of spray. At dinner time our stove requiring a draught, we took it to the top of the pier-head, and there, if over; it certainly got one. Merrily danced the cinders on the bars! and fiercely the much urged tongues of flame played upon the kettle- bottom and very soon the simmering' contents issued in a boil. And what a change when we left this howling, screaming pier-head for the blissful, peaceful calm below ! Here we stayed until morning when we found the wind gone down into a nice little sailing breeze Which we took advantage of to get back to our old anchorage Beaumaris. Here we found two Warrington vesspls, the ooasting flat "Duke of York," of Sankey Bridge, 'lnd the flat "Celestial," both coal-laden, to discharge here. This latter kindly lent her punt to take the keg ashore to re- plenish and get something for the bread-locker, as we in- tended to go to sea that day. There was still a nide . . .
little breeze and just sea enough to make sailing a pleasure, so we determined to go out and see, at least, how things lo•ked.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETIER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETIER.
LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT.

The visit of Mr. Morley and Lord Ripon to Dub- lin will, I venture to think, prove an epoch in the history not only of Ireland lilt of the Empire. The arrival of these two Liberal chiefs and their popular reception, extending from the landing quay at Kingston to the classic Avenue of Sackville-street, is, an outward :and visible sign of the real union which the 'Liberal party are now heartily and triumphantly forging. It is a Curious and striking reflection that Mr. Bright was the last English statesman who met with in Iretand a popular re- ception anything like that which has greeted Mr. Gladstone's colleagues. A great deal has happened since then, including they miracle of John Bright's conversion to the axiom that force is a remedy, and his joyous reception in the ranks of the Conserva- tive party. But happily, Liberalism lives on, even if some of its whilome most active supporters turikaside, and it is from Liberal lips, in January 18:ff., that Ireland hears words of encouragement and hope such as were spoken from Liberal lips in Limerick in July 1868. When Mr. Bright spoke the burden of the Established Church was still imposed upon Ireland. Rack-renting was as yet unchecked by any effort of the Legislature. Mr. Bright denounced these iniquities in burning language, and since then the Liberal party, led by Mr. Gladstone, has absolutely done away with the alien church and has made a series of determined and honest efforts to grapple with the Land Question. The message of peace which Mr. Morley 'and Lord Ripon carry to Iroland on the specific question of Home Rule is as certain to be followed up by, ac- complished acts of justice as was Mr. Bright's mes- sage of twenty years ago. Members of the Government have been remark- ably communicative as to the programme of the session which opens next Thursday. In ordinary times, considerable mystery broods around the pur- poses of a Government on the eve of a session, and newspaper columns are filled with contradictory guesses at their scope. But everybody knows ten days in advance what will be the principal items in the ministerial bill of fare. First and foremost conies the reform of Procedure. kt the autumn ses- sion of 1882 Mr. W. H. Smith, his colleagues in the present ministry, and his supporters on the Conser- vative benches, fought tooth and nail ,against the proposal made by Mr. Gladstone to introduce an effective form of Closure. United at the tithe with the Parnellites, they met the proposal with every form of obstruction. When the force of numbers prevailed, and the modified, and, as it has turned out, practically inefficacious form of Closure was about to be agreed to, they indulged in funereal pro- phecies of the consequent decay and final ruin of the House of Commons. Next week we shall ace a marvellous change. The Conservatives being in office, have discovered that the Liberals were right in 1882, that in order to secure freedom of debate Closure is necessary, and that to be of •any value it must be effective. Sir William Harcourt is under- stood to be making a study of the debates in the autumn session of 1882, and we may look forward to the resurrection of some striking passages from Conservative speeches then delivered. After Proeedure will come the Local Government Bill, which Mr. Ritchie has promised to introduce before Easter. That he should do *36. is simply a necessity, if the bill is to pass this session. It is enough of itself to engross the attention of the House through a full session. The interests con- cerned are as complicated as they are extensive., The mass of ordinarily intelligent people are ,pro- foundly ignorant of the intricacies of the chaos we call Local Government. The House of Commons itself, as a body, will have to be carefully educated before it is in a position to legislate on the subject. Once comprehended, it is full of fascination, having a direct personal interest for every ratepayer in the kingdom. If only Mr. Ritchie is permitted to bring in a bill honestly and boldly grappling with the question, tha Government will succeed in their prime endeavour to postpone dealing with the Irish problem. Local Government is not a mattey of politics. It is a purely business question of adminis- tration, offering a tempting,fleld to men like Mr. Chamberlain, Sir Charles Die, and above all, Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Ritchie has a great opportunity, and Libeials may sincerely hope be will be left un- fettered to deal with it. I hear a whisper that this will not prove to be the case, and that a momentous decision has been taken on a crucial point, which makes the Bill a sham. Of this we shall hear more before Parliament meets. . Some snob visiting Naples has sent home to a society papers sneering noticevof what he calls the rigid' economy practised by Princess• Louise and Lord Lorne when passing through that city. It seems that the Princess and her husband travelled quite privately, walked to the hotel from the rail- way station, and dined at the table d'hôtel This paragraph is likely to have an impression exactly the reverse of that intended. The British taxpayer contributes £6,000 a year for the maintenance of

the Princess Louise, her husband, and her house- hold. But, unlike other royal alliances that is practically the sole means of income, and Princess Louise will be liked more than ever when it is known .that • she and her husband are honestly endeavouring to live within their income. The Duke of Edinburgh, it is well known, has similar tendencies, which arc foraetinies gratified to the disadvantage of County hospitals. But he has no such excuse. In addition to his annual allowance of £25,000, his wife has a princely jointure, and the Duke has saved money all his life. It is pro- bable that he manages to live pretty well on the pay he draws from the Admiralty. The Marquis of Lorne has nothing but the portion of an, elder son of the Duct House of Argyle, which, judging from the allowance to Lord Colin Campbell, cannot be munificent. But it may be safely taken for granted that the daughter of the wealthiest monarch in the world has enough to live upon without disadvan- tageously practising the economy of the table d'hOte. She and her husband probably dined in public because they like it better. I hear an account of a young English potter who has been astonishing the UnitelStates by an exhi- bition of his prpwess. He untrertook the feat of making an entire tea set of forty-four pieces in the short space of seven minutes and a half. Few be- lieved it could be done, and many wagers were laid op the event. A large number of people were pre- sent in the works when .the signal was given to commence. The pliable clay was manipulated with deft and skilful fingers, and twelve cups and saucers adorned the board in short order. Then twelve plates were piled upon each other, and then four large plates, a teapot, sugar bowl, and two other vessels prang up as if by magic, all shapely and almost terfectly formed. When the last piece was finished the hands on the majority of watches indicated the lapse of eight minutes from the time of starting, and the remarkably quick wc.rkman rested beaten by a half minute. But he can make the set in seven and one half minutes under, more favourable cir- cumstances. The whole work, including moulding, is accomplished by the fingers, and the only tools used are a thin brass wire for cutting the clay, and a small revolving wheel. What do they think of ' this in the Potteries? The workman's name is Harry Flaxman, and he is said to come from Wedg- ' wood's establishment. Is anything known of him at Burslem or Hanley? At the studio of Felix Moscheles, this week, a curious assemblage met for an interesting discus- sion. At one side 6f the platform, on an easel, was the portrait of Henry Richard, M.P., the President of the International Arbitration and Peace Associa- tion, and on the platform, and looking uncommonly like the portrait, was Mr. Richard himself. Some gentlemen and many ladies were equally conspicu- ous, and the room was crammed with people who came to listen. The host spoke first. He hoped the discussion would be Confined to the subjeet of church edueatiou, had indeed it was the best wish he could express, for the room held many faddists—' all keen to get the public ear and vent their special , views. Mrs. Ormiston Chant had a great deal to 'say, and said some of it.very well. It seems we teach our children war from the time they are babes. Mrs. Chant would not allow her boys to play at sol- diers, or to have guns or pistols in their toy boxes. History, too, was emasculated to suit the timidest dis- positions, and the Wars of the Rosesqwere left out. Many you people must have envied Mrs. Chatit's children. Next followed Mrs. Elizabeth Cady Stan- ton, a very picturesque and charming old lady full of gentleness and distinction, and really most per- suasive. ,4Llniversal peace was the easiest thing to achieve if only mothers thought so. They had but' to teach, and the children would do as they were taught. She herself belonged to that lucky country America; which had no army. And as it bad no army it could have no war. It was really quite de- lightful to find that human nature could so easily be made perfect, and that we need not care what be- came of our navy. Then Miss Burstell, a teacher of history, thought 'time was lost on stupid facts and questions of which the answers could be crammed, dates, and the like. Children should be taught con- stitutional and social history. Miss Burstell chal- lenged anyone to tell when wheat was introduced into England. No one could. •Soon afterwarfis thT guests had refreshments. There is something very sad in the report of &sale of autographs which has just taken place. Amongst the letters disposed of was one from Henry Field- ing'• complaining of money disappointments"; one from De Foe "complaining of his treatment"; one from Goldsmith "giving a doleful account of his travels on the continent "; one from Sterne request- ing a loan of £5O; and one from Swift setting forth that such was his poverty that "if I come to More Park it must be on foot." It would be impos- .sible to name Hie men who stand higher in the ranks of English classical literature than those here mentioned. And yet, when by chance, odd letters from them turn up at a sale by auction a century or so after their death, we find them with one ac- cord bewailing the straits in which loverty has landed them. Nine guineas Swift's letter brought; a sum that would have taken him to More Park in a post chaise ha& it been forthcoming in the moment of need, I wonder how much will be paid at atic- tion in-1988 for a letter from Charles Dickens in which "the distinguished novelist mentions that he earned in three years xpo,coo by the reading of chapters from books for Nthich he had already been paid a princely price.'

div.head: LOVE AND LEARNING.
div.p: LOVE AND LEARNING.

A well-known, elderly nobleman, of large wealth, wooed and wonp a few years ago, a young and very beautiful girl. Their life has been as happy as it is pos- sible for married life to be, when December is united to May. His lordship is distinguished in scientific circles and possesses high literary attainments. Some time after his marriage he was foolish enough to think that his lovely wife was not sufficiently educated, add laid out a course of reading for her. A month later he inquired about heoprogress, a book. He set up his eye. and found that she had hot opened brows after the manner of old husbands when their young wives have displeased them. Whereupon she looked up at him with a bewitching smile, and said: "I was made to be loved, not to be learned." She won the day, of course. What Is learning compared to the light of a sunny blue eye? Would sot a husband rather be met with a smile and a kiss, than by a wife who assured him that she " knew her lesson ?" Wisddin Is all very well, hut winning ways go further. Laughing eyes beat, Greek roots all to nothing. A woman's lovely tresses, waving on the outside of her shapely head, are More precious in a husband's eyes than ever so much learning in- side of it. Therefore, all women should endeavour to preserve their attractions, and welcome their liege lords with loving looks, pleasant smiles, and flowing silken tresses, for after all a beautiful head of hair is the crowning charm of a woman, a charm which all may possess by using Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will keep the hair healthy and strong, restore gray or faded hair to its original c6lor, and make it soft, silky, wavy and luxuriant. It may be h;td of any chemist or perfumer. •

Assetrra ON A CoNsTABLE.—Luke Duffey, farm labou- rer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Preston Brook, on the 28th Janttary, and together with Martin Rogers, was charged with assaulting P.C. Jack- son whilst in the execution of his duty at the same time and place. Defendants pleaded guilty, and their em- ployer, Mr. Percival, spoke to their previous good char; acter. Duffey was fined ss, and costs for being drunk. and a like sum, with costs for assaulting the officer; and Rogers was fined 10s, and costs. ALLEGED LICENSING OFFENCE.—Thomas Bowers land- lord of the Bridge Inn, Acton Bridge, was summoned for permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises on De- eelnber 25th ; and Samuel Goulding was charged with being drunk at the same time and place.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defendants.—F,S. Neale and P.C. Barte gave evidenca for the prosecution, but after a number of witnesses had been heard for the defence, tho Bench dismissed the case against both•defendants. AssAtlLT.—James Cliff was summoned for an assault 'upon Emma Jameson on the sth January.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Arthur Browne for the defendant.—The evidence went to show that on the night in question, the complainant, who was a domestic servant in the employ, of Mr. James Owen, farmer, Higher Whitley, went in company with her mis- tress on business to the house of a Mr. Plant, who lived next door tcrthe defendant. When they came out again for the purpose of returning home, the defendant, it was alleged, suddenly made his appearance and assaulted the complainant by knocking her to the ground twice, , and tearing her dress and bonnet. The only reasoncom- plainant could assign for aft assault vas that up to De- cember last the defendant had been in the same employ as herself, and that she had been kept en when Le was discharged. The defendant was bound over in hie own recogrnsances of £5 to keep the peace for six months. GAME TriEspess.—Joseph Miller, a young man, waS charged with having unlawfully committed a trepass on land at Grappenhari in the occupation of William Derby- shire in search of game on the 14th January.—PC. MU- lington stated that at four p.m. on the date named, in consequence of a complaint made to him, he went down a lane which led off the Thelwall-road and saw the defen- dant, who was carrying a -gun, in company with th4ee other men, and they had with them two dogs. Two of the men were on their knees by a hedge at the bottom of a field in the occupation of Mr. Darbyshire. . Witness got over the hedge and went towards them, and when they saw him they moved into the next field. He went to Miller and asked him if he had a license.for his gun, and he replied in the affirmative, at the same time hand:; lug the license to witness. He asked the defendant wile' business he had there, and he said none. Witness the . took defendant's name, and upon asking him for his ad- , dress, defendant replied " I live at 42, Church-street, Warrington." Witness afterwards went to the address, and found that defendant did not live there. All the other men gave wrong addresses. He afterwards found defendant at Fleming's tanvard, As he was coming away witness saw in the field a ferret, which they had I left behind them.—Mr: William Derbyshire, farmer, Grappenhall, affirmed that the field spoken of by the constable was one in his occupation. On the day in guestion shots not only came in through the windows of his house, but struck one of his children. He had never- given the defendant, or any other person, permission to • shoot over his land.—ln defence it was contended that the defendant was not on Mr. Derbyshire's land at all, but on, that of a neighbouring farmer; Mr. Rowson, over , whose land defendant had permission to shoot.—The : Bench, however, imposed a fine of lOs and costs. : EMBEZZLEMENT BY A FRIENDLY SOCIETY'S TRIISTEE.— William Millington, bootrnaket late of Antrobus, was charged that on the 19th October, 1887, being a trustee of the Wheat Sheaf Lodge of the Ancient Order of Shep- , herds, he did unlawfully misapply the sum of £5 belong- ing to the lodge .—Defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. Percy Davies, who prosecuted, stated that the defendant had , been a trustee of the lodge fronNits formation until the • time of his discharge in October, 1887. It seemed that on-Decenaber 13th, 1886, defendant drew from Parr's Bank the sum of £l5, and of that amount he had only accounted to the society for £lO, and the balance of 25 • he had never paid, although repeated applications had been made to him, and he had,over and over again, writ- ten promising payment.—The Bench inflicted a fine of • £l. and £1 18s 6d costs, and a further order was made ; that the £5 be paid over to the lodge officers within one month.

He justified the discussion of the acts of the •ltagistrates and police, and even judicial ,act, when they caused great popular discontent. He ,denied that :be or. Mr. Balfour was a nimble political and platform giaaja,.. 'tor, and as he di a not always avoid inaccaraciesund ve- hemence of language he was bound to receive hard blows from opponents. He denied that the Government I Pelicy.badloeen successful. 11r. Goscben only claimed ' that they had held their own, and before long they‘will not hold their own. If there was less crime in Ireland it Vas owing to Mr. Gladstone's policy a conciliation. The Govtrnment had not diminished the power of the -National League, and before long the scale must fall -from the eyes of the Govermnent, and lead them tol .adc.pt, a policy of conciliation.

Mr. W. H. Smith; M.P., responding, on Monday, to.the toast.of the Houses of Parliament, at a banquet inau-, Mating the new premises of the Chelsea Conservative (31n13, stated that it was the firm intention of the 'Government, in the approaching session; to enforce rules which would prevent the obstruction .of business -and render-it no longer possible for a certain body of men to regartlthe House of Commons as an arena within which they could carry on warfare against the Constitution of ;the •countrv. Referring generally to the question Of ProtectioniMr. Smith said he did not believe himself in Protection as a measure by which the industries of -this country .could be brought back, for in those oeuntrieis whereittimd been carried to its fullest extent, the do- . prestion.bad been at last as great as in this country, and, •even maier. 'LOCAL GOVERNMENT. Mr. Riteble.trresident of the Local Government Board, oPeaking at a•Conservative meeting at Sheffield on Mon- day said that rst in the programme for next session wowld he reform of procedure. The Government would introduce me/twins also Mating to railway rates, employers' liability, limited liability, technical education. and local government. He denied Sir Charles Mike's assertion that tbeGoVernmentthad not made up their minds and woulld 4tot introduee a Local Government Hill WI late in the session. The bill was practically , settled last autumn, and it was the deliberate intention of the GoVernmen't to introduce it before the House separated for Easter. There hadsbeen no division in the Cabinet, and he behaved the bill would prove absolutely acceptable to the 11tionists. He was not at liberty to describe the provisions of the bill. It would confer full powers on the local authorities at once, and would knock • on the head the pundhs of the quarter sessions, as Sir William Harcourt desired. He "hoped there would be as little interference with the present boundaries as • nossible', and no propoaals would be made for extending borough areas. The measure could net be extended to , Ireland under present ,circumstances when disloyal +persons administered lcettl affairs to tit& disadvantage of i . the loyal subjects.

A Tarr -no JAPAN .—The word Japan has such afar off sound, and has been for so many years associated with the idea of an infinite distance, that a trip to that °win- try is considered a very remarkable circumstance, and a person who has been there is looked upon as having done something worthy of more than passing notice. -While the trip may not be "as easy as rolling off a log," still it is not a difficult one, and it is a wonder to me that I never went before, and it will be a greater wonder.to me if Ido not go again in the near future. •This is the sum and substance of it: You go to San Francisco—six days. Then you take a White Star steamer, and in six- tee% days more you are in Japan. That's ally ,The steamers on the Pacific are regular White Star boats ; the same line which runs the Atlantic ocean service. The steamers are elegant and not in the }east inferior to the floating palaces on the Atlantic.—Colonol George P. Ma- ul', in tbe Hanford (Con.) CourFat.

Nine farmers, for a similar offence, were sentenced to one month's imprisonment; the bench refusing to increase the penalty with a view to an appeal.

Intelligence reached Belfast onllonday that the people in county Leitrim who were attacked 'by hydrophobia, after eating the carcase of a pig whidh died front the bite . of a mad dog, have almost completely recovered under the treatment of a Cavan farmer, named WGovern, who is credited with the possession of a certain -crure for the disease. The voung girl Stewart, described a' 'few days ago by the Rev. Robert Leech, rector if Drumlane, county Fermanagh, as being in a fearfal cOndition from the ravages of the disease, is now in n' fair way, towards complete restoration to heard'.

An extraordinary case of 'murder was 'investigated on -Monday by the magistrates at 'Killarney. The in- quiry was held at the lunatic .aspum. A family named Doyle lived at Beaufort, near Killarney. A son, aged 13, was an idiot, and,kis mother, Mary Doyle, had seine hallucination that' 4s long as the boy lived the family would be subject-to evil influences. She had confessed to having on this account killed her son with three strokes of a hatchet. She imagined she had been to heaven and seen several Pf its ."'accepted citizens." The father, Michael Doyle. is amian, rif low intelligence, but not insane. The son. 22, howed the methert mono- mania, and a daughter, Julia, also had superstitions about evil spirits.- Since Saturday night the members -of the family had ill-treated each °the/Ir.—The father was remanded for inquiry, and all 'the otherswere committed to a lunatic asylum. COLD-BLOODED 'MURDER. A terrible murder tool' place on Tuesday, at Lixnaw, a place on the North Kerry Railway, a few miles from Tralee. A man named Edward Fitzmaurice had been under police protection for some time past, because of his having taken a farm at Aliabee, friim which. his brother was evicted. It ;appears that Fitztnaurica set out for Trate° fair on Tuesday morning, :witlos some pigs. He was accompanied 'by his daugh- ter and a police escort. The escort left him, as usual, when they had taken him . a/ little distance from the village, and he proceeded onward. Before he reached the fair, however, two own crossed the fence by the road side, and shook hands with if to make sureof his identity. As he turned away, they discharged several revolver shots into the lower portion ef his body, and then decamped. Fitzmaurice died soon afterwards.

FOREIGN NEWS..

THE PROSPECTS OF WAR—CONTINUED PREPARATIONS FOR A GREAT CON- FLICT. VIENNA, MONRAY.—It IS reported from Constantinople that the Sultan has become very uneasy at the movement Of Russian troops in Asia Minor, and representations ou this subject have been made to the Ambassadors of Great Britain and Austrialllungary. • There is no cessation at • the armaments in Poland and Bessarabia Eight large magazines are being built at Kremenetz. Trenches are being opened round Huhu*, and huts for 40,000 men 'have been erected there. The commissariat in pessarabia has been ordered to supply provisions and fodder for an army of 20,000 men. ODESSA, MONDAY.—Privateletters received here from Bulgaria state that the Prince, army, and people maintain the same 'firm resolution to resist, at no matter what sacrifice of 'blood, any attempt of Russia to foist her own candidate upon the, principality. These letters also mention a rumour current in official circles Of an intention of Prince Ferdinand to send a special Ministerial Embassy to the Courts of certain of the Powers which Signed the Berlin Treaty. CoNsturrixorzr„ SUNDAY.—The Porte's financial dii • ficulties are crowding thick upon it. Throughout the 'Provintes all officials are unpaid, only three mouths' • salary out of the present financial year, beginning in Itarcb, having been paid. Near Broussa the soldiers attacked the local director of the Treasury and beat him. The Ottoman Bank has refused an advance of £lOO,OOO, on the ground that other advances have not been paid. Krupp has given notice that unless the . amount due to him be paid within a few days he -will consider himself free from all engagements. FIGHTING IN BURMATI. TifAXDALAY, SATURDAY.—A successful engagement be- tween a British force and a band of rebels, believed to he Potoks, took place last evening about 20 miles from Ifyingyan. The rebels lost 10 killed and manyavounded. /t is reported that the people are adverse to tile further advance of the Shan column, and the Woonthoo Tsawbwa Is doing his utmost to retard the success of the mission into his country. RANGOON, SUNDAT.—The local Government has re- "solved that the whale of Burmah shall be disarmed, sod that as a rule firearms shall be possessed only by Govern- ment officials not below the rank of the Thug,a,is,aoho •ore the officials employed in collecting revenue. This -regulation will not apply to Europeans or Eurasians in 'certain outlying playas, and where adequate police pro- tection cannot be offered. 'GALLANT CAPTURE OF A 'SLAVE DHOW. Her Majesty's ship Garnet, stationed ott the East India station, has lately been cruising dff the east coast of Africa, above Zanzibar, for the prevention of the-slavo trade, with her beats detached, on the look out for dhows. About midnight on the 22nd December, the 'crew of the cutter saw an Arab dhow under easy sail near the coast, and immediately gave chase. The Arabs a Crowded all sail, but were pursued Ipy the cutter,,which "Was just able to keep pace with her. After a.close chase of some four hours the Arabs ran their craft agoore to save their human cargo if possible, bathe blue jackets :wen too smart for them' and came op in time to pre- -vent the removal of all but three. These were afterwards -recovered, but the Arabs escaped. Twenty-oneslaves in All were rescued, and the dhow wastowed off in triumph 'as a lawful nri7.e. THE GERMAN CROWN PRINCE. BERLIN, THIIRSDAY.—The " VOSSISChe Zeittillg " pub- lishes a, telegram from San Remo stating that Sir Morell 'Mackenzie has received a letter from Professor Virchow, -in which the latter, declares that, in spite, of the most aminute investigation, and the care taken by him that t any unfavourable indications should not escape his no- • tice, he has discovered nothing of a serious character in :the particles from the Crown Prince's throat examined by him.

At Ennis, on Saturday, the 'trial of 'Mr: Cox, M.P., for speaking in a proclaimed district, last. October, was re- sumed, before Messrs. Bolderand Roche. resident magis- trates, sitting is a court of summaryjurisdiction, under the Crimes Act. .Thepolice-evidence, in reference to the posting of notices proclaiming the county of Clare at the police barracks and courthouses in various towns and villages in the district, was continued. At the conclusion of this class of evidence, Mr. Murphy, having argued that the meeting at which Mr. Cox spoke was proved to be unlawful, referred to portion of Mr. Cox's speech, in which allusion was made to Mr. Conybeare, and expressed surprise that that gentleman had not come forward to stand by his. friend. If the case was reversed, Mr- Cox would have gone to the assistance of Mr. Conybeare. The defence contended that .the prosecution had failed to substantiate the case because no proof had been put in that proclamations torJaidding the meeting had been posted on the police stations. The-court decided, how- ever, that notices had been posted bra perfectly legal manner', and bearing in mind.the responsible position of Mr. Cox, which increased his culpability, passed a sentence of four montbsr imprisonment without bard labour. Notice of appeal was given,.and bail was granted in two sureties of £250 each. Qn leaving the Court-house Mr. Cox was at oncore-arrested on a warant issued against him at Kildysart, and was taken back to gaol in the custody of the police to await trial on the new charge. Mr. J. Cox, M.P., was on Tuesday charged before Mr. Hodder and Mr. Cecil Roche, R.M., at Kildvsfirt, County Clare. at a court under the Crimes Act, with taking part in an unlawful assembly, namely, 4 meeting qf the Irish National League, in the proclaimed district of Kildysart, on the 24th October last. There was.a second charge of ineting others to take part • in the :mime assembly, and advising people not to pay vent. THE PROSECUTION OF FATHER .34c.FADDEN.

_ Father James McFadden, and Mr. Alt Ox. Mane, M.F. reached Letterkenny on Saturday, under a strong escort of the King's Revel Rifles, and were enthusiastically greeted by a crowd of country peopleimost of whom had been up all night, awaiting their,arrivaL The prisoners were allowed to breakfast at the barracks, and to speak to the local priest, and were then conveyed to Dun- fanagby, under* an escort of Rifles, 'Dragoons, and ,Engineers, under command of Mr. Cullen, R.M. The hearing of the charge against the Rev. Father Mc.Vadden, of Gweedore, of deliverinv e, speech inciting tenants not to pay rent, was veaumea at 'Doufanaghy • Court-house, on Monday, before Mr. Thomas Hamilton ,and Mr. Garrett Nagle, resident magistrates. Counsel for the defendant announced that he would call no evidence, but would claim the disoharge of his , client. On the conclusion of the address of the. defendant's counsel the magistrates decided to hear • the second 'charge of taking part in an illegal conspiracy, before de- ciding on the charge of inciting to conspiracy. . The Court on Tuesday gave its decision, on the applica- tion of Fr. Mc.Fadden's counsel, that he -should be treated as a first-class misdemeanant. The magistrates Alsid they had no power to grant theapplication, but the appeal judge might do so. The trial of Mr. Alexander Bien% Ml'., for inciting to , conspiracy, was then proceeded with,,and a sentence of four months' imprisonment was passed. Notice of ap- peal was given.. , ;Father McFadden has received a telegraefrom the Catholic Bishop of Derry, bidding him be of good cheer, as no matter:how the trial goes victory mill still be his.

• THE CORK SCANDAL. • - At the Ct.n.k Police Court, on Tuesday, thecilarge against Major Roberts, governor of Cork Gaol, of assaulting Tnung „olds, was proceeded with. The Major withdrew when the case was called.—Mr. Wright, Crown solicitor, in stating the case, said if one of the charges was sus- tained it would amount to a felony, as it was alleged the defendant had criminally assaulted a girl under 13 years of age. Mr. Wright complained that the police iwere harassed by •Canon O'Mahoney. The aathorities. 'continued Mr. Wright, were thwarted 'by Canon O'Mahoney, and were denied access to the principal wit- nesses, the r*. gentleman claiming that Major Roberts shotild bring an action for libel. As Mulch of the evi- dence to he produce& would only be admissible under such tire stances, the Government had nothing to do with the civil actions. The depositicns of one witness stated she sew the defendant commit immoral sets with young girls several timer. • deposed that he first called attention to Ile never charged Major Roberts with Ctahneon charges. Ol lahon having misoonducted himself with a girl under 13. lie spoke generally of children of tender years, but he did not specify their years. Re referred to children under 16 years. Abundant evidence would be produced that defendant committed immoral acts with children over 13 years. In cross-examination, witness said the meeting at which he first alluded to this matter was one of sym- pathy with Alderman Hooper, when he said the detec- tives were neglecting the real criminals. The fact that Alderman Hooper had been compelled to wear prison dress did nbt weigh with him in bringing the case for- ward. • The magistrates refused A conviction on the first sum- mons, charging the defendant with immoral acts with a girl under 13. A second summons was then gone into, charging Major Roberts with criminal acts with a girl over 13 years. ' • The second charge fell through, as more than three months had elapsed since the last offence. In addressing the Court for the defendant, Mr. Camp- bell said the case against him was brought for purely political spite. He blamed the authorities for sacrificing a trusted official to the political jackals of Cork.

RAID ON A CLUB: OVER SIXTY 'PRISONERS VN COURT.— At the Marlborough-street Police Court, London, On Menday, Louis'Lud in, Robt. Mextin, Fredk. Myer, Francis Hildebrand, steward, secretary. barman, and waiter respectively, of the Whitfield Club, situated in Whit- field-street, Tottenham Court-road, were charged with keeping and using their club, as a common gaming twine. Fifty-nine other persons were also charged with f usi iv the premises as a gaming house. The,eaurt had to be cleared to make room for the prisoners. Supt. Dra- per -deposed that he went to the premises at one o'clock on Sunday morning, with a warrant for arrests. Evidence as to card playing being carried en was given, and bremand was asked for. Joseph Blackstone, one of the prisoners, asked to have the case settled at once. The prisonees were all working maym, and might lose situations if remanded. The prisoners were re- leased do sureties of £5 each, except Ludin, £lOO, Martin,ltlyere, and Hildebrand, £2O each. lINPOSCANT PROSECUTION OF A TOBACCO MANUFAC. Tx:num.—at Bury, on Saturday, Frederick Smith, tobacco manufacturer, York-street, Bury, was summoned by the Inland Revenue Depaxtment for having on the ,I,st Becember used an excevive amount of moisture in the manufactxre of tobacco.—Mr. H. E. Squire, 'solicitor, Somerset souse, prosecuted, and Mr. S. F. Butcher, ap- peared for the defendant.—Mr. Squire stated that Mr. Thos. Burgess, Apervisor, visited the defendant's works and took -Eve samples of tobacco two being rolled tobacco. Those. were sent to the Laboratory at Somer- ?let House, and the thick twist was,found to contain 351 per cent, of moisture, and the pigtail 38.8 of moisture. —ln cross-examination Mr. John Holmes, one of the analysts at the Laboratory, 'Somerset House. stated that he had found some tobaccos contain 17 peralcent of natural moisture. If it contained less than 10 per cent a higher duty had to be paid, upon it—Mr. Butcher, for the defendant, said that in the way of practical trading it was difficult to comply exactly with the la*. In Lancashire manufacturers were obliged to manu- facture tobacco to retail at 3d. per ounce. The tobacco had to bear duty 3s. 2d. per lb., the cost of the leaf was Bd. per lb., and there would be 3d. par lb. for -the manu- facture, so that with interest on capital, &c., it would make the cost 4s. 2d. to 4s. sd. per lb. As the manufac- turers had to sell it at from 3s. 3d. to .3s. Bd. per lb., without the limit' of water allowed by the Act of l'arlia-. ment, manufacturers ould not expect to have a* profit. He contended that the samples were not fairly taken, and suggested that if the centre of-the roll contained an ex- cessive quantity of moisture, the outside would be drier, so that on the average the roll would have contained less than the quantity allowed.—The magistrates inflicted a fine of 40s. and costa. ,
