Not low ago, a. aaother and daughter called at ih6 office of a prominent London physician. The young lady was fair of face,graceful of form,with , plexion indicating health, and yet her .mother there was every indication to her that she was tl% prey otsome mysterious disorder. At her request , the physician rrnade a searching examination. No- thing was discovered. At the importunities of the mother, another physician was called in and another examination made, with the same result. In less than three months the young lady was deacl. In the same city another prominent • physician was visited recently by .a young lady of attractive address, refitted manners, and winsome appearance_ She had scarcely stated her case when her lips quivered, her face, paled, her arms drolokretto her side, and she was dead! She had dild alone with her medical man, and gossips ,rnade high scandal; hut a post-mortem examination showed that her death was caused by a convulsion, and the voice of slander was hushed. Medical science does not tell us all we ought to know. It is small satisfaction that death must lay our friends low before we can find out the nature of their disease. Life is a great mystery, and it is a sad commentary on present human attainments .that death is the only'key which, in many cases, can unlock the depths of this ,isiystary. There is something more to be dreaded than cholera, more to be feared than consumption which is preying upon the health Id our young people, • because, mlike them, its approadh is insalious, and we 'know of its pre- segue only by the death it brings. MT. J. S. Green- 'smith, of 4, Walker's Mount, Warwick-read, Batley, had lau i experience somewhat similar to the motherwhose case is above related. His daughter, when but five years of age, seemed suddenly to droop. She was exceedingly languid, and was ftequently prostrated with 'headache and nervous depnksion. The medical man who was called in said she was suffering from ferver. He attended her for sometime, but she steadily grew worse. At this time Mr. Greensmith read a treatise on Bright's disease of the kidneys, and made up his mind'that his daughter was suffering from this complaint. At the suggestion of Mr. E. Fisher, chemist, of Roshcliffe, . Huddersfield, he made use of a well-known remedy, and he tells in the following interesting manner, what the result was "I called at the chemists on Sunday, after coming from church, and procured the medicine. I gave the first dose to my daughter that evening with the result that she slept better than she had for months. I gave the remedy regularly for nearly two weeks, and my child was soon running argund as well as ever she was in her life. lam certain that I owe her life to the 'remedy used." In the first case mentioned, death 'was caused by what is called Bright's disease of the kidneys; in the second, ft was found that urenic blood poisoning, caused by the same disease, produced the fatal convulsion; and in the thircl case, death was threatened by the same dis- order, but was averted, when every other means failed, by Warner's SAFE Cure, the only known specific for such complaints. "I am not surprised," said a candid phy- sician to the writer the other day,, "when I know the ignorance and incapacity of the ',profession concerning such disorders, that Warner's SAFE Cure is doing such effective work. If it can accomplish What we .can- not, people are very foolish if they •do not resort to its use.'
—This great remedy, which is working such wonders, can be had of all chemists, at 4s. 6d. per bottle, or of H. H. WAVER AND Co., 86, Clerkenwell-road, Lon- don, E.C'

div.head: ECLIPSE OF THE MOON.
div.p: THE ECLIPSE OF THE MOON.

'At about half-past eight on Satmillay flight attentive Observers of the moon's face began to detect a slight obscurity on the eastern side of the 'orb, and in the course of the following hour this dimness increased and spread gradually over the entire disc. The eclipse, in fact, had commenced, but the early stage consisted merely of the passing across of what is called the penumbra or partie} shadow of our earth. The exist- ence of such a dim outline may readily be proved by any one who will take the trouble to interpose a ball between a candle or gas light and the wall. It will then be seen that the shadow of the ball— fairly distinct in itself—is surrounded by a dim burr or halo of partial obscurity, and in astronomi- cal language this burr is called the penumbra. At half-past nine the true shadow of our planet began to show itself on the moon's face, anti in the course of another hour this also gradually Stale across the disc until the whole light was blotted out. Whether the moon was at airy time altogether invisible is very doubt- ful. As a rule, the light of the sun breaks through and around the atmosphere which envelops our earth, and is refracted upon the moon, but is its passage is accom- panied by,an abstraction of the blue rays, the only ap- pearance presented by the moon is that of a dull, coppery-red ball. In other eases the disc has been said to partake of an ashen gray hue, and in some i instances it has been entirely nvisible. The muse of these variations has not been accurately deter- Mined, but in all probabilitye exact degree to which the moon is blottedth from view de- pends upon , the condition of our atmosphere at the time, and its capacity for decomposing the light which steals in round the earth's circumference. The middle of the eclipse, or the time at which the moon occupied a central positien in the earth's shadow. PM at half-past eleven p.m.. and at ten minutes past twelve on Sunday morning a faint streak of light began to appear on the eastern side of the orb. As time went on this also gradually increased, but the penumbra did not alto- gether leave the surface of the moon until ten minutes -past two. The total duration of the eclipse sesta. there- fore, rather more than five hours and a half, but the pas- sing across of the true shadow only occupied three hours and a half, while the total eclipse lasted only a little more than one hour end a half. To astronomers tile event was one of great interest and importance in Connection with the occultation of stars. The occultation of a star means its disappearance owing to the interposition of another body, and in the course of Saturday night's eclipse no fewer than 60 stars, 'many of them, it is true, of small magnitude, were hid- den from sightby the moon's face. Such an occurrence is of course common enough, but at ordinary times, when our satellite is shining brightly, it is difficult for an astronomleal observer to calculate the exact titrri, of the disappearance and reappearance of the star, especi- ally when, as often happens, the star is of tiny propor- tions. During an eclipse the smallest constellation can be seen as it vanishes and reappears behind the moon's, body, and by noting the time which elapses between the two movemenla very valuable results are obtained with irgard to the diameter and parallax of our satellite. Instructions were, therefore, issued to all official and unofficial astronomers to note caretntly the time at which these occurrences took place; and while ordinary 'lay individuals were Merely watching with curiosity the varying aspects of the eclipse, scores of scientific observers were' gathering materials for what may ultimately prove a source of valuable 'astronomical discovery. As it will be nearly four years before another total eclipse of the moon is visible in England, and that at a far less convenient hour for observation, everybody appeared desirous of grasping the opportunity which presented itself on Saturday night of 'Witnessing so beautifuts, phenomenon.

div.p: 'PRE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.

Four fresh cases of smallpox havo occurred at Tod— mordert, and there are now 13 cases in the hospital at Sourhall, belonging to the Local Board. All .the cases 870 repelled 70 be mild ones, and the patients are doing welL

Preaching at'WesleyFollege, Sheffield, on Sunday, Dr Dallinger said that having regard to the laws of nature the smallpox epidemic was bound to spread, and con- sidering the circumstances by which they were sur- rounded he could not and would not pray for the re- moval of the scourge. To do so would be a mockery of God. They had not heipcd themselves, and how dare they ask the Almighty to Help them? .0n Saturday, at the meeting of the Chesterfield Rural Sanitary Authority, Di. Mackintosh, the Medical Officer of *Health, repOrted that since the last meeting there had been five fresh cases of smallpox—two at F,ckington, ene,at Whalley Thorns, one at Brimington, and one at New Tupton and that there had been two deaths. There had now been in the anthority's district 24 cases, and four deaths—about an average proportion.

Byrequest of the Archbishop of York prayers were said in the churches of Sheffield, on Monday, for the de- liverance of the town from the plague , of smallpox. Archdeacon Blakeney, preaching in the parish church, spoke of the difficulty in the way of dealing with the epidemic presented by people with little or no common sense. The Archdeacon condemned the sensational and exaggerated account of the visitation which has been publishedin London, and said it had done great harm to the trade of Sheffield, and he concluded by giving the congregation some practical advice on the s9bject. • At the Kendal Board of Guardians, on Saturday, Mr. John Bohm in the chair, a letter was read Irons the Settle Board of Guardians recommending that vagrants p,ecommodateit at the vagrant wards at Kendal, Miln- Thorpe, and Kirkby Lonsdale should be provided with a certificate showing "from whence they came and whither they were going," itt view of the prevalence of smallpox in the West Biding. After some discussion it was decided to provide the certificate.--The Chairman said that in some unions the officers had been re-vacci- .nated. They could not compel the officers to be re- vaccinated, but he thought it was desirable.

At the High ,Court of Justiciary, Edinburgh, on Peon- . Alex. Maclean, Donald Mackenzie, and John Mackay, Ittee of the 13 crofters charged with riotous conduct and assault on the police at Aiguish, were found guilty. Sentence was deferred. '( '

div.head: 'TITHE QUESTION.
div.p: THE 'TITHE QUESTION.

Amongst the accounts that were placed before the Board wits one for tithe, and Mr. PRBYSHIRE asked if it was for the land atl Padgate School.—The Ci.aa: Yes. —Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that he understood farmers haA got a reducelon of tithes, and he wished to know if there .had been any reduction in this eage.—The CLEK : I have not heard of ony in the Warrington district. —Mr. DAR- RESUME : Oh, yes, 10 or 20 per cent.---Mr. BLACKHURST They will not look upon us as farmers.—Mr.D.ApsTontau said they had the interests of the public to look after.— Mr. BLACK:HURST : You may depend upon it you will have to pay.—Mr. DARBTSRIRE : More than we have the right to pay P—Mr. RLACKHURST : I don't know about that.—Mr. RATCLIFFE The church will have all it can eL—Mr. W. HouoirroN said he did not think that 'Board pined in the petition of the farmers. He thought Mr. Darbyshire was n bit remiss in pot seeing that that Board took its share. (Laughter.)—Mr. JOLLEY said he was sorry for the farmers and for the poor clergy as well. He thought they ,ought to have their sympathy as a Board. —Mr. RATCLIFFE : It is money easy got is the clergy's money. (Laughter.)—The matter then• dropped. I • THE pADGATE SCHOOLS: ALLEGED UNSANITARY CONDITION OF. THE SUPERINTENDENT'S ROUSH.

The Padgate Schools Committee stated in their report that letters had been read from Dr. Joseph and Dr. Pea- cock, which -wore left over for the consideration of the Board, as there was only a small Committee meeting. The CLERK read the letter from Dr.: Joseph which had been addressed to the superinten- dent (Mr. Mines) and stated as follows : "The serious, and -regret to say, fatal outbreak of diptheria in your house, together' with the results of your own inspection; inmy opinion, urgently tall for immediate, thorough, and systematic examination of the sanitary conditions of the dwelling, as well as such structural arrangements as bear upon the kanitation of the building."—ylr. Isurawooo said it appeared that Mr. Mines had lost two children from diptheria, of his own family and in his Bwn house. Mrs. Mines was also ill and confined to her bed. Ile (Mr. Isherwood) thought that a thorough.ex- amination was required. A few of them had gone round, and there were a few downspouts wanted altera- tion, and he thought that would meet the case, though :they did not go into the house.—The CLERK said it should be remembered that this had 'reference to Mr. Mines' house and not to the institution in any way. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Tomagy suggested that Dr. Sephton and Mr. W. Owen (the medical officer and surveyor Of the Rural Sanitary Authority) should be asked to make an examination of the place. They were the two pro- per and official persons to put the Hung right.—Mr. RAT- CLIFFE said that a fortnight ago a drain was stopped up, and he did not doubt that was the cause of thdlillness. He suggested that the drains should be properly trapped. —Mr. DARBYSKIRE pointed out that the Padgate Schools are situated in the Rural Sanitary Authority's district, and as the Authority met on the following Friday the matter was sure to be brought before it.—The CLERIC then read the report of Dr. Peacock, medical officer of the schools, in which it was stated that the general health of the children was very good. Referring to the illness of Mr. Mines' family, Dr. Peacock recommended that the house should be thoroughly overhauled from the sanitary point ,of view by some competent person.--1 The matter then dropped,. it being understood that Dr, Sephton and Mr. Owen would make an.examination of -the building.

div.head: SCARLATINA.
div.p: SCARLATINA.
The Workhouse Master reported that three or four .children in thew/orkhouse had been infected with scarla- tina. Proper precautions had been taken with regard to the cases.
SCHOOL FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 66 old and 31 new cases. The minutes were confirmed, it being remarked by Mr. Jolley that the num- ber of fees allowed had been steadily growing. THE HOUSE COMMITTEE.-PROPOSED EXTENSION OF WORE:-

div.head: HOUSE.
div.p: HOUSE.

The minutes of a largely-attended meeting of the House Committee, held on the 27th January, were read. The question of accommodation in the Workhouse had been considered, and the committee reported as follows: " That the maximum accommodation fixed being 407, inclusive of house, hospitals, and fever wards, and, the number of inmates this month having reached 427, the present meeting is specially convened to consider the question of accommodation for inmates. Mr. Voisey was appointed to preside. The Master reported that the fever or infectious diseases hospital was fitted for 24 beds, but it had been used for 36 non-infectious cases; and, by removal of such ordinary cases, it is now ready for us dif the necessity should arise. Two children from the -workhouse schobtis suffering from scarlatina occupy two beds. It is resolved that, if it should be found necessary that by any further outbreak in the house or tramp wards, of zymotic disease, the Master be author- ised to employ one or more persons to act as assistant or temporary nurse or nurses at the infectious dis- eases hospital, and that in view of the growing necessity for increased general hopital accommodation and enlargement of the house, the Board be advised to instruct Mr. W. Owen to report upon the best triode of meeting snch necessities, and on the probable cost thereel."—Mr. Volsci', in moving the confirmation of the minutes, having referred to the pressure upon the accommodation of the Workhouse, said the question for them to consider was not one of rushing into expendi- ture, but whether the spending of money was not abso- lutely netesgary, and he thought it was clearly. shown that there should be an extension somewhere. The number of inmates was increasing, and in view of the Ship Canal he had no doubt there would be a great in- flux into the town of a class of people who were likely to seek help at the workhouse either in the casual wards or the general portion of the house. . Re moved that the minutes be confirmed, and that the whole matter be han- ded over to Mr. Owen to investigate and to report to the Board at an early date.—Mr. JOLLEY seconded the adop- tion of the minutes and remarked that he thought they were bound to make an extension of the house. It had been thought that provision should be made for 100 ex- tra beds.—Mr. RarcupTc said it had been advertised for and near that the Ship Canal was to provide employ- ment, andthis had brought a lot of people together. The Canal might benefit Warrington but it would be a serious loss to the out townships, as they should have to bear their share in supporting the increased number of pau- pers. He had known more people to be in the house than- at present—as many as 450. —Mr. BLscxnunst asked if the Local Govern- ment goard inspector had made any complaint Mr. Veiny said he had not heard of any, but it seemed to him that the Local Government Board would. not allow them to run so close to the wind as they were do- ing.. If it came to 'their3mowledge that their rules were being broken they would insist upon an extension.—Mr. BrAcitiatrusr said they had had that question before the Board before, and the inspector had been down when they had more than their proper number of inmates in the house, yet he had passed it over. He (Mr, Black- hurst) thought, however, that the time had come when they should make some little extension of the Workhouse. The part that required notice most was the hospital. Ile thought if they got accommodation for 30 or 40 more the matter would stan4 over for a few years.—Mr. DERBYSHIRE thought it might, probably, not cost a great deal more to provide accommodation for 100 beds than for 50. If the pauper population continued to increase as it had done in the past he was sure that 100 beds would soon be occupied.—Mr. HAMMON said there could be no doubt that additional aceommodatiem was needed, and he suggested that the question of giving up the present Board-room, country guardians board-room, and other offices might be considered in order to provide more accommodation. The Board could then meet at some place in the town.—Mr. VOIBEY thought this sug- gestion a very good one.—The CLERK then read a report made some time ako by the medical officer (Dr. Spiuks) as to the hospital, in which he complained of the want of proper provision especially for zymotic cases. He (the clerk) also read a report which showed that both population and pauperism had steadily grown in the Union during the past 20 or. 30 years.—The minutes of the House Committee were then adopted.

RUNAWAY. Mr. IsttEn*oon asked the clerk as to punishment they had the power to inflict upon lads who misbehaved them- selves at Padgate Industrial Schools. They formerly had "Jack Warrington," who was always running away, but now that he had been sent away, they had another one, as bad or worse. This one had run away several • times, and once-he was brought back by a policeman at two o'clock in the morning. When he ran away from the school he was in the habit of sleeping on cinder heaps and other places, and on one occasion he was brought back with his clothes allinost burned off. When questioned, the lad said he was determined to follow Jack Warrington to the "Clio."—The CLEAN having specified the punishments that could be inflicted in such a case as that mentioned, the subject dropped.

SCARLATINA AT THE wanknoutii. In answer to a question the Workhouse Master Mid the only way in which he could account for the outbreak of scarlatina at the workhouse was that the child first affected had caught the disease from its mother, who, he was told, had another child ill of the disease, and who had spoken to the child in the street.—lt was agreed, on the motion of Mr. BIACHHIIRST9 that in consequence of the illness in the workhouse the master should have dis- cretionary powers as to allowifg persons to leave-and eater the house.

' A terrible murder, followed by the suicide of the murderer, was committed at half-past one o'clock Lon Wednesday afternoon at 147, Back Church Lane, Whitechapel, a poor thoroughfare running out of the Commercial Road, London, and inhabited mostly by a low, type of foreigners and small shop- -keepers. The house before mentioned had _atuongits occupants a boot finisher name 4 Louis Cohen, and living with him as his wife was a young Russian Jewess whose name, as far as can be ascertained, was Potstami. It is stated that the woman came to England from Russia about five months ago in company with her husband, whom it is alleged had married her froiiii a house of ill repute. Two months since she left her husband and went to live with Cohen, and the husband, though much distressed, kept himself at a distapce, not even disrlosing his address. On Wednesday morning, however 7 a man who called at Cohen's for as. owing to him, -remarked that he had seen the woman's husband in the street. particular notice was taken of this, and at about one ' o'clock the woman went out to buy some provisions. Soon afterwards Cohen heard the woman screaming, and on rushing down the stairs saw her lying in the middle of the road with her throat cut from ear to ear. She was just able to point in the direction of Commercial Road, and then became unconscious. Meanwhile some neigh- bours saw the husband running away and pursued him, but in passing along Greenfield-street, after crossing Commercial Road, he noticed a constable coming towards him, and turning his back upon the policeman he cut his own throat with a shoemaker's knife. The constable procured a cab and took him to the London Hospital, but he expired on the way. Whilst this was taking place, thg woman had been removed to the same hospital, but she also died before arrival at the gate. Althoughno one actually saw the murder committed it is evident that the man attacked his wife and cut her throat at the foot of the stairs as she , re-entered the house, and that she ran out and fell down in the road, the floor at the foot of the stairs had a quantity of blood upon it, and the provisions which the woman was carrying were strewn in all direc- tions. The murderer was in the same trade asCohen, and the knife with which he committed the deed is now in, the possession of the, police. It fs 'an ordinary boot finisher's knife, and was secured by the constable at the time the man committed suicide. The police are en- deavouring to ascertain where the murderer had been living recently.

div.head: TERRIBLE SUICIDE AT WINWICK:
div.p: TERRIBLE SUICIDE AT WINWICK:

A painful sensation was caused in Winwick and the surrounding country districts on Wednegday morning by the announeement that Mr. William Blackledge, farmer, of Warrington-road, Winwick, had committed suicide by blowing out his brains at about five o'clock wittra gun. •The deceased, who. was a large farmer and evidently in prosperous cir- cumstances, bad suffered somewhat from a hurt to his foot occasioned by a cart a couple of years ago, and had been under the care of Dr. White. of War- rington. He went to bed in fairly good health on Tuesday night, but it is stated that his mind has been unhinged of late, and while in a fit of despon- dency the rash act was no doubt committed. He was fifty-six years of age, and leaves a wife in rather delicate health and a large family, all of whom, however, are grown up. The deceased had been strange in his manner since Sunday last, when he refused to go to bed as usual. He remarked on I Monday evening to the charwoman (a person‘named Porter) that she might not see him again, but little importance was attached to the obseri ation at the time. On Tuesday night, as he refused again to re- tire, he was left in the kitchen, and his wife ap- peared to have some misgivings as she got up once or twice during the night and listened, but heard nothing of her husband's movements. At five o'clock in the morning, however, she and her family were awakened by a loud report, and rushing down stalls she found her husband in his armchair by the fire, his head being completely shattered. His right hand was resting on a table, on which lay a double barrelled gun, One of the chambers was loaded! 'and the other showed signs of having been recently discharged. The firearm was loaded with small shot for shooting birds, and had been so, it is stated, fol. some time. Information of the sad occurrence was at once sent to the police authorities, and P.C: Parker (Winwick) and Police-sergeant Commins (Newton) quickly attended. Dr. Patterson, of Earlestown, was also called in to examine the body. Near the right ear the skin was found to be burnt and the hair singed, and it is supposed that the de- ceased placed the barrels of the gun at that spot while he pulled the trigger.

div.head: WORKPEOPLpS TREAT AT WAR-.
div.p: WORKPEOPLpS TREAT AT WAR-.

RINGTON. • On Saturday afternoon nearly 1,500 of the work- people employed 'at Cockhedge Mills were gener- ously treated to a tea by their employers, Messrs. Armitage and Rigby. The repast was served up in the Drill Hall, and, in consequence of the large number who bad to be attended to, these in charge of the arrangements were very fully engaged. How- ,eier, by dint of perseverance they succeeded in meeting the demands made upon them, and the operatives had a very pleasant tea together. After tea the tables were cleared, told the hall made ready for a short but enjoyable entertainment. These sub- sequent proceedings were presided over by Mr. Ziba Armitage, J.P., who was supported on the platform by Alderman Davies. J.P., Mr. and Mrs,. P. Davies, Mrs. Ziba Armitage, Mr. W M. Armitage, junr.. Mr. and Mrs. Wiliam Rigby, Mr. and Mrs. S. R. Armitage, Miss Smithies, Mr. W. F. Fielden (manager of the weaving department); and Mr. W. T. Smithies (manager of the spinning department.) Letters had been received from Mr. W. Armitage, T.P., and Mr. S. Rigby, "J.P., expressing' regret at their inability to attend the gathering. In opening the proceedings the Chairman said that the present was rather an unustial occasion. Many of them were in the habit of meeting every day, but not exactly in that kind of way'. He thought that they had so far enjoyed themselves, and it would be their endea- vour to make the evening a pleasant one. Ther were a good mans- friendswith them that evening, and the pre- sence of Alderman Davies was asure Aga that the interest was not going to flag. He thought they would be dis- posed before they had closed that part of the programme lo say that it had been very pleasant. (Cheers.) A programme of songs and Inunourous recitations was then gone through by the following ladies and gentle- men :—Mrs. Rigby Armitage, Miss Smithies, Miss Wil- cox, and Miss A. Warburton; Messrs. 'Smithies, W. Rigby, Alderman Davies, and Percy Davies, the latter of whom gave two songs in character.—On the conclusion of the programme Mr. S. R. Armitage briefly proposed that a vote of thanks be passed to Alderman Davies; Mr. P. Davies, and the other friends who had contributed to the evening's programme. He also proposed a vote of thanks to Colonel Greenall for having given the use of the Drill Hall. (Cheers.)—After the motion had been heartily carried, Mr. W. F.. Fielden said that he had the honour that evening to be selected to propose a vote of thanks to Messrs. Armitage and Rigby for the very generous manner, in which they had en- tertained the " hands " in their employ (Cheers.) He was sure that the action of the firm was deserving of commendation. He was afraid that his remarks would be quite inadequate to the occa- sion, but he could say that since he came to work for the firm, six years ago, he had known the members of it pretty well, and he had always found them honourable and upright in their dealings—(cheers)—and assiduous and attentive to business. They were, too, what might be called silent givers. It was not known what they had given. He knew from demonstrative faets since he came to the employ of the firm that they had enlarged their works in order to find work for the unemployed. He was sure that such actions as these deserved the greatest commendation, and he thought that they should all be thankful that they had such employers—(cheers) —who had given them such a generous treat. (Cheers.) In making the proposition that a vote of thanks be passed to Messrs. Armitage and Rigby; Mr: Heiden wished' " Sutcess to Cockhedge Mills."' (Cheers.)—Mr. Smithies seconded the proposition. He felt, he said, al great pleasure in doing so, and in reciprocating all that Mr. Fielden had said. It was not everyone who had the pleasure of working under such employers as Messrs. Armitage and Rigby. (Cheers.) Wherever the name of the firm was mentioned it commanded respect, and was always spoken of in the highest esteem. It washonoured on the Manchester Exchange, and the firm stood one of the foremost in Manchester. He hoped that the work- people would do their best to promote the welfare of the concern, which depended more upon their individual efforts than perhaps they might imagine. They all had a duty to perform, and he hoped thAl they— 'would" perform that duty to the best of their ability. (Applause.)—After the vote of thanks had been accorded with loud cheers, Mr. William Armitage, jun., in response, said that he was sorry that his father was not able to be present that evening. Ile wrote-that morning asking him (the speaker) to say how sorry he was that he could not be present, but he was net very strong, and was not able to come out that night. He, however, hoped that they would all have a pleasant evening. They were much obliged for the man- ner in which the vote of thanks had been passed. Manu- facturers and their workpeople must work together if they want to do any good. (Cheers.)—The remainder of the evening was spent in dancing and other amui:e- merits, the younger employes being sent home.' Prior to going, however, they were each presen,tol witla .an ' orange. •

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
- - SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 4, 1888.

Colonel EYRE, M.P. for Gainsborough, seems to have been talking at large on the land question 'to a number of Conservativi assembled at Run- corn, on Monday evening. He had a thin audi- ence, and we dare say some of those present con- cluded that the address was likewise thin. ‘• But we must be thankful for- small mercies in the way of instruction from Tory orators; and it is some- thing to find one of them venturing to touch the land question at all. Colonel Ems is either him- self in happy ignorance of the need of reform, or he assumed that that was the condition of his hearers, and determined to leave them as he found -them. So far from recognising the need of great 'llanges, the burden of his song was that "Eng- land is a happy land," and that "Whatever 'is, is tight." Referring to' the demand for reductions Of rent, he asks—who will be the richer for re- (llictions ? and he directs attention to the state- llient that the spending power of the landlords has -been reduced by something like forty millions. We question the accuracy of the assertion that the landlord class have been affected to this extent. whatever may be the reduction in their case, lt is as nothing compared to the losses of the ten- ritS• It is estimated that farmers losses from 1875 to 1883 are no less than £150,000,000. It is undeniable that the reductions in rent are a mere • e compared with this vast sum. As to Colonel -"nes question—who will be the richer for rent reductions? we have toanswer—the farming class, and, through them, the whole community—that is, if by means of reductlions farmers are enabled to remain on the land and keep it in cultivation with a fair prospect of making both ends meet. Surely the member for Gainsborough is not so audacious as to contend that the primary use of land is for the preservation and propogation of aristocra- tic landlords? There is a story told of a haughty lord who threatened a deputation of his tenants that, if they did not cease to trouble him about ' reductions, he would leave the country and never 'see them more. "Well, but yo'll not take th' land With yo, will yo? " said one f the farmers; and this question brings. the issue home. Landlords caunq exist without land; but land can exist With out landlords. The men who toil not, neither 6:1. they spin, may be of some consequence to them- e° yes, but they are of no consequence to the 4nnunity • and the fewer there are of them the • better. Colonel Ems said he should like to know ihe direction in which land laws ought to be ltered ; and he. proceeded to refer to the Productiveness of the soil, and to the fineness our flocks and hezds by way of enforc- uV the conclusion that there was no .need for a change. What delightful reasoning !. Honey is a Illveet thing in the way of food; and it might be that the very best honey was produced; but if it • 'll went to the support of a few drones, whilst the working bees were left to starve, it Would be °b- e 'ions that there was something wrong in the sys- tem of distribution. Again, if through the Stupidity, selfishness, or muddle-headed interfer- ence of the drones not more than half the honey 'was produced that might be produced, it would be Clear to those who have eyes to see that there was Pressing need for a change. And this is precisely the state of affairs with regard tO the land ques- tion. The idlers whb have got ,possession of the land—fraudulently. in many cases—exact in the first place too much of the produce of the 'workers for simple leave to toil; and in the second Place, in their foolish pride arid unpardonable ignorance, they block the way to alterations in the.law which Would result, in due time, in the produce of the country being more than doubled. According to Sir JAMES CAIRD, land in this country in 1770 averaged 13s. per acre, and in 1850-1-that is 80 years later—it was 275. an acre, and to-day the average is higher still. Is it the landlords who have more than doubled the value of the land— the curled darlings of society who flit, butterfly- like, from flower to flower, and make merry over the clownishness of their dependants? Not a bit of it. It is the sturdy incessant toilers who have `l"cle England as wealthy .as she is to-day; and "what is needed is that just laws shall be made Whereby the producers shall have a better chance of reaping where they have sown. As to changes, we require to get rid in the first Place of the laws of primogeniture and entail—to :weer) away, in fact, the rubbish heaps bf our feudal system. As Professor BLACKIE shrewdly ob- -BerveE--" We have made Laws enough to preserve the Landlords and the Game, and it might seem w,ise now to make a few laws, to preserve the reople." The exaMple has been set us on the Continent; in France, Switzerland, Gereany, Ana: atria, Rolland, and Belgium they have got,rid to a I,arge extent of the old bad system, and the result la that instead of land getting into fewer hands, as in Great Britain, the owners on the continent are • steadily increasing. Peasant proprietors in this "liltry ate almost unknown; in France there are five millions of people whose holdings average seven and a half acres each; and when Colonel lihrßE challenges any man to name a single system of land tenure which has had more prosperous re- sults than those obtained in England/ we point to France by way of response to his challenge. It Was from these millions of peasant proprietors that the bulk of the money balm • which was sent to Germany to pay off the -war indemnity, after the Franco-German war. Was that not a sign of Prosperity Our poor, miserable agricultural labourers, always on the verge of starvation, and Often ending their lives in the workhouse, couldint have raised a tithe of tht sum ; it would be a mockery under similar circumstances to ask them. Let us ewe our labourers a chance of becoming owners of

and by breaking down the barriers which prevent and c ming into the market. Nay, if need be, let us say to the millionaires who are driving away men and sheep in order to create deer forests—" You shill not starve inen in order that deer may thrive; you shall cultivate the bulk of the land you hold, or we will take it froni ion, and put it into the hands of those who will make it fruitful and replenish the earth." It is no use men like Col. Eyre'going about the country preaching peace o'n the land question when there is no peace. There is a spirit of inquiry astir in the country; the wor- kers have long seen that they were the chief suf- ferers in the terrible social inequality which exists; and they are now beginning to see that there is a remedy for sOme of their wrongs. They perceive that the land is the great source of wealth; and they,' are determined to better their own condition and the condition of those who come after them, by a radical reform of the land laws.

LORD DERBY cut the first sod, at St. Helens, on Saturday, of the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway, under auspices of ja most favourable kind. There was a large company, the weather, winter though it is, was beautifully fine, and his lordthip set an example to the directors and everybody else by taking his coat off to the work. leis significant that he said he never knew a railway which started with fairer prospects of success. Speaking at the banquet later on, Lord DERBY said he had served on many railway committees during the last thirty-five years, and he had heard so many astounding statements made in perfect good faith that a kindiofj involuntary scepticism as to all such statements had become part of his nature. Under these circumstances, his expras- sion of opinion as to the prospects of the new venture becomes all the more valuable, and we do not doubt that it will hate a favourable influence upon intending investors. There is a special claim upon employers in the district to furnish as much of the capital as possible. They stand to gain in any case; if the London and North-Western Railway Company in the eagerness of competition should reduce the present rates, the manufacturers would profit by it, p.nd could afford to wait for a sub- stantial return for the money laid out with the new company. Not that we think there is. much risk of having to wait. It is obvious that a railway is needed for ,passenger traffic when, as at present situated, a person who desires to run over to a place so near as Southport is required to change twice. It is noteworthy that the route about to be taken is that which was originally suggested for the first railway between Liverpool and Manchester. The landed gentry were at that time strongly opposed to railways; but they, like other people, can live and learn ; and it thus hap- pens that in this case the whirligig of Time brings in his revenge by having Lord DERBY and Lord GERARD at the cutting of the sod of the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway. It is idle, perhaps, to speculate as to what would have happened if the line had been carried through as at first pro- posed, but it is pertinent to remark that, as St. Helens hiss developed so rapidly—it is one of the most thriving towns in the kingdom—there is good reason to believe that its trade will receive an im- petus when sits manufactories are brought into more direct communication with Liverpool, and with the lime and coal districts. The inhabitants have coal at their doors, and yet, guch is the irony of fate, it has been taken from their doors, because the coal waggons could not conveniently go their way. There is an 'immediate coalfield of 400,000,000 of tons, with/ an output of a million and a half tons yearly; but, extraordinary as iti may seem, not more than five per cent. of this coal is used at St. Helens, although the Haydock collieries are only three miles from the town. And the anomaly becomes even more Oaring when it is stated that St. Helens consumes twice as much coal asthe total output at Haydock. It is estimated that the new line will make coal in St. Helens 2id per ton cheaper, and ,this means that the chemicals manufactured will, in consequence, be from one shilling to two shillings per ton cheaper. As to limo, the Widnes manufacturer is so situated that he gets his materi 11 from Derbyshire at sixpence per ton less than is paid at St. Helens. Then there is Warrington, which may be said to over- run with railways, and the outcome of so much Icompetition is that in the carriage of iron it has an advantage of 10s per ton over St. Helens. It ts naturally hoped that the new undertaking will re- sult in a levelling process—not by bringing War- rington and Widnes up in carriage to St. Helens, but by‘bringing St. Helens down to them. In this way the energies of manufacturers will be stimu- lated, the resources of the district •.rill be judi- ciously developed, and the whole community will thus benefit by the construction of the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway.

PENKETH WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOL —A valuable selection of plates illustrating the eye, framed and mounted, was presented by Miss Garnett to the trustees of the Wesleyan School for use of the scholars. The plates were first exhibited before the members of the Mutual Improvement Association a fortnight ago on the occasion of a lecture delivered by Miss -Garnett. MINERS' ORGANISATION IN LANCASHIRE. The annual meeting of the Ashton, Haydock, Havannah, Thatto Heath,-Whiston, Little Lever, and Radcliffe Miners' Association was held in Bolton, on Satur- day. Mr. S. Woods, miners' agent, presented a re- port on the year's operations. It stated that ninety- four lives were lost in connection with the West Lancashire coalfield during 1886, a decrease on the previous year. During 1887 wages had, been lower than ever, the average wage of thousands of col- liers being 144 to 16s per week. There bad been fifty-four local strikes, eighteen of them being sta- ted to be the result of either political or petty spite by the underground managers aPthe Park-lane Col- lieries. There had been several disputes in connec- tion with the "dirt" question, which was a very complicated matter. During increased year the member- ship of the organisation had over 100 per cent. In January, 1887, the membership stood at LW, and was now 2,300. The report said in conclusion that the financial position of the organi- sation was satisfactory, and progress had been made beyond expectation. • AMERICAN MANUFACTURES AND FREE TRADE.— Arguing that a lower tariff means lower profits and better wages. the "New York Herald" says :—lf Alexander Hamilton, the father of Protection, could come back and see some of the results of his theory, he would be astonished and chagrined. He pro- posed a crutch for our infant industries until they got strong in the legs and could stand alone. All right: but the fact is that the crutch is becoming more important than the legs. If Hamilton could look down on this condition of affairs he would say, to our manufacturers, "I wanted to protect you 7 but I didn't expect you to become helpless. If the doctor's medicine makes you bedridden, you had better change the doctor." Now, we are seeking a profitable trade. We want to drive bargains with the people of every nation. We have the geniis, the enterprise, the machinery that ensure success. Give us a larger free list, multiply the number of free raw materials, and the hum a increased busi- ness will be heard everywhere. Open the tariff dcror wide enough to let in the raw goods, and our merchants will send their manufactured goods into every foreign mart, and it will go hard with us but we will enter upon an era of national prosperity such as we have never seen before. President Cleve- land's policy of opening up a larger market for American manufacturers not only commends itstlf to the country's pocket, but also to the country's patriotism. Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton t raa Dxgtey and Wright's, which for strength is uneguall•3d.-44tve.

div.p: THE .EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 4, 1.888:
"TOUCH AND GO."

- - --- • Somebody has been lecturing at Frodsham on the "Road to Rome." The audience was small; it is probable that the inhabitanti of the district thought they knew, as Fell as the lecturer, that the road to roam was to leave the road alto- gether.

A contemporary says good story is told of a Cardiganshire local preacher. He was declaim- ing one pf Mr. Spurgeon's sermons—unknown, of course, to his hearers in a Bethel of miniature dimensions, which did not even possess a gallery. Towards the close he electrified the little congrega, tion with the sentence, "And now, I turn to you —the hundreds in the gallery."

The conduct of the Mayor of Warrington -in patronising the exponents of " thb manly art of self-defence" seems to be pretty freely criticised. But it is for "a good cause,' and "a good cause" sanctifies everything. Besides, his Worship is un- selfish as well as broad-minded--he does not want to have .all the "knocking down" to himself.

John Chinataan ha f 3 at last awoke to the fact that it is desirable to know something of other countries, and accordingly Chinese Commissioners have been sent to this country. Their mission is a wide one; it eovers "the affairs of foreign countries generally." That will keep them going for half a century; but the Chinese are not in a hurry—espvially when it is a case of !making the acquaintance of the "outer barbarians."

Messrs. Armitage andßigby, of Warrington, set an e]gtmple of kindly regard for their work-people by furnishing them with a good tea in the Drill Hall on Saturday last. It is something to be willing, as well as able, to make fourteen hundred people happy. There is a tendency at the present time towards-a separation oaclasses ; a little more social cement of -this kind would help to keep' all classes together.

Judging from the speech of Mr. Richie, Presi- dent of the Local Government Board, the Local Government Bill will be neither fish, flesh, fowl, nor good red herring. It will be devoid of any ruling principle. But the first item on the Government programme is the reform of procedure—always reform of procedure. The Irish members are being "run in," and the English members are to be gagged. This is Toryism.

The Liberal Unionists are ever ready to aver that their views are making progress in the coun- try; but it does not look like it in the Tradeston Division of Glasgow, where Mr. C. Corbett, the Liberal Unionist member, has been addressing his constituents, and has had a resolution carried over the head of his supporters, to the effect that he has forfeited the confidence of the constituency. Something like this has happened at several places, but we do not' know of a case in which the resolution has. gone against a genuine Liberal.

Cardinol Manning showed his good sense in put- ting his veto on the proposed Requiem Mass on the centenary of the death of "the last of the Stuarts." • The Young Pretender made a great stir in his time, andwas the occasion of the famous verse epigram by ,John Byrom : . God bless the King, I mean the faith's defender: God bless—no harm in blessing—the Pretender; But who pretender is, and who the king— God bless us all—that 's quite another tlaing.

"Charlie Stuart" excited the enthusiasm of the Scotch in 1745; but he is amongst the men who failed, and he died at Rome on..TaAlary 30th,1788. Mrs. Miller, who saw him in 17711 says :—" The Pretender is naturally above the middle size, but stoops excessively; he appears red and bloated in the face; his countenance heavy and sleepy, which is attributed to his being given to excess in drink- ing." And so on; but it is not the portrait of a saint.

Mr. Spurgeon has issued a formal reply to what he _calls "The Baptist Union Pensure." He likens the Union to a Noah's Ark which Affords shelter "both for the clean and unclean and he will have none of it. But if he will have Scriptural authority, why does he use the Ark comparison? Perhaps he thinks Noah was wrong in sheltering the unclean. Noah could not be in the right if he differed from Mr. Spurgeon. His ,doxy is ortho- doxy.; that of those who do not agree with him is heterodoxy.

There is a growing feeling against the death- traps known as level crossings. Oii Saturday after- noon, a man was killed on the Great Western Rail- way, aet a level crossing near Hayle, West Corn- wall. The man was driving a horse and cart over the line, and was run down by the mail train. At the inquest the jury brought in a verdict of man- slaughter against the directors of the Great Western Railway Company. This is about the best thing that could be done—next to catching a railway director in the trap.

The Widnes authorities are moving in the matter of the nuisance caused by alkali waste heaps. It has been resolved to appoint an in- spector to watch over the deposit of waste; and it is proposed that no waste shall be laid within 300 yards of a dwelling-house. At a conference, on Tuesday, the manufacturers present were given to understand that legal proceedings would be taken in case of nuisances in the future. The action of the authorities may cause a little incon- venience for a time.; but this is as nothing compared with the health and comfort of the in- habitants.

Lord Ripon and Mr. John Morley have had a splendid reception in Dublin; for, to use a Shakesperian phrase, the city cast its people out upon them. A correspondent in4t contempotary falls .foul of the Reception Committee; and chuckles over the fact that it contains "only three noblemen.". He does not seem to see that he "give himself away" when he admits that the Committee includes 85 Irish members of Parlia- ment, "and all the Mayors of Ireland except Bel- fast and Derry." When the classes are on one side lit a struggle, and the masses on the other, it is sile to prophecy how it will end.

Speaking at Sutton' the other night, Mr. Seton- Karr, M.P., denied that the Crimes Act was being used to put down their political opponents by brute force; but he said "an outbreak of crime took place immediately after the act came into operation." Exactly! It comes to the same thing; free speech is made a crime by the act; and it is thus that political Opponents are put down. Lord Salisbury Aaid that a Crimes Act would crefre ten times as much evil as it would repress, and , Mr. Seton-Karr admits the impeachment. And ' yet the Tories have the audacity to talk about wise legislation!

There were a great many people on Saturday night looking at, to quote Shelley— That orbed maiden with white lire laden, Whom mortals call the moon. The eclipse was on everybody's tongue, and by ten o'clock it had gained the attention of everybody's eye. It is stated that a Wilts fanner, having heard from a local paper that the eclipse would be seen at Devises, drove some three miles to that place, and took the wife with him. He was not going to miss the sight through staying at home. Old Giles' had evidently a taste for astronomy, but it would seem that he had not got much further in his notions than the people of three thousand years ago, who had a ten-miles radius for sun, moon, and stars. After all that he has heard since Saturday, he will not take a ride of three miles to see the next eclipse. He knows better now.

Mr. Herbert Rhodes, the defeated candidate at the general election for the High Peak Division, has explained his reasons for retiring from the constituency. He said he had never regretted the course he took at the last election, whieh cost him k 1,200, but under the present altered circum- stances he did not see any chance of a general elec- tion for at least three years. During the past twelve months, he.had received 300 begging letters —from the minister building a new chapel to the old woman wanting a new set of teeth—and, whilst he was always willing td do his utmost in the cause of dharity, he thought that was going a

little too far. And so it is. Candidates are used badly in this respect. If electors would look less to pence avid more to principles in connection with candidates Tor their suffrages, they would be much better represented in the House of Commons.

Assuming that the Irishman who was brought up at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, told a true story, it must be said that, coming to this Country as a stranger, he was "taken in" after a fashion that was surprising. He was charged with being on the premises of Captain Herbert for an unlawful purpose. This sounds formidable; but the offence resolved itself into Thomas Shea having knocked at the door of Captain Herbert's house, late at night, to make an inquiry. He had tramped from Liverpool in search of work, and was on his way to find an acquaintance in Warrington. Seeing a light, he made to it, as he would in his own country, aild as any sensible man would' under similar circumstances, in any country. The Captain, it is said, aid ,not press the charge, and Pat was let off with a caution. Really, the magnanimity of Captain Herbert and the Bench is astcarishing. It ,must be remembered that this was only a poor Irishman; if Captain Herbert had been taken to gaol fir making an Inquiry, he might have wanted to sue somebody for false imprison- ment.

FORTHCOMING CONCERT.—The members of theßuncorn: Tonic-Sal-Fa Choir announce a performance of the his- torical cantata "Magna Charta" for the 13th February. The capabilities of the choir are well known, and a treat may be anticipated. THE CATHOLIC BALL.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Anderson, c the Railway Hotel, applied* through his wife for an occasional licorice to sell at the Drill Hall, Widnes, On the occasion of the Catholic ball. The magistrates granted the application, but declined to allow the sale of spirituous liquors after two o'clock in the morning. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.—At Widnes, on Thursday, the following persons were summoned before the magis- trates on a charge of not sending their children regularly to school :—Wilham Houghton, Frances Garbett, Samuel Costley, Joseph Davies. Sohn. Fenny, Dennis Malone, E4,ward k Lightfoot, William Carter, Edward Price, Martin Holland. Henry Rimmer (two cases), Michael Mullory, Owen Rorke, Peter McLoughlin, Thomas Walsh, Thomas Fallon, and John Walsh. BREAKING INTO A SHOP.—During the night of Tuesday, the shop of Mr. F. Fairhurst, draper, Preston, formerly of Runcorn, was entered by burglars, and all the drawers searched. The private office was broken: into, the papers thrown about, and the safe tried, but not broken open. The burglars did not succeed in tinding any loose money, and made their way back again through a sky- light on the landing, by which they had entered. Up to the present Lothing has been missed. RUNCORN GAS COMPANY.—The annual meeting of the directors and shareholders of this company was held at the Gas Works yesterday morning. Mr. F. Rigby, J.P., chairman of directors, presided. The report and balance sheet was passed on the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. J. Handley, 1.P., and the usual divi- dend of 10 per cent as declared. The Chairman re- marked that the amount qf gas consumed was increas- ing, and the directors had decided to make a reduction in the price of 2d per thousand cubic feet. The present price is 3s ed per thousand feet. The proceedings, which only occupied a few minutes, were brought to a close by a vote of thanks to the chairman

WIDNES POUCH COURT.—On Monday, before Mr. F. 11 Gossage, the following persons were ach fined for drunkenness : Patrick 'McKenna, Ellis Dodd, Eliza Madden, and ThomasSmith.—Thomas Gallagher, of Flint, was bound over to keep the peace for fighting.— Herbert Woodhouse, John Clark, and John Wilson were each sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging. —On Tuesday, before Mr. Brock, Mary Tracy was sent to gaol for 14- days for being drunk, and a similar sen- tence was passed upon Catherine Hynes for committing a breach of the peace.—On Wednesday Mr. George Pil- kington fined Richard Mercer 53 and costs for being drunk, and sentenced Robert Johnson to seven days' hard labour on a charge of begging.—On Thursday, be- fore Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. G. Pilkington, the fol- lowing persons were charged with disorderly conduct and were bound over: JamesAurray, Michael Horan, James McKeown, Mary McKeown, Mary MeWilliams, John Smith, and Mary MullarkW.—William Atherton, waterman, Martin Kuntighan, labourer, and J. A. Nealon were each fined 2s 6d and costs for allowing their dogs Ito boat large unmuzzled. FasNwoarn GRAMMAR Senoor..—The results of the Christmas (1887) examination of the College of Precep- tors, held at the school, are as follows :—First-class, honours division: J. R. Bate, with special certificates in arithmetic and chemistry; F. N. Mercer, with special certificates in French and chemistry. First-class, pass division: C. A. Bate, with special certificate in arithme- tic; J. Smith, with special certificate in chemist- ry. Second-class, first division : J. A. Eatock. Second-class, second division: J. W. ClibbOrri. S. H. Tinsley. Third-class, first division: E. Franklin, W. A. Watts, with special certificates in physics and chemistry; J. L. Griffiths, A. E. Wareing; R. Showan. Third-elms, second division: A. E. Barlow. Third-class, • third divi- sion :E. E. Wigg. Twenty-four candidates were sent in, of whom 24, or 100 per cent, passed in English; 14, or 58 per cent, in history; 24 in geography; and 23, or 96 per cent, in arithmetic. In algebra, four passed out of 10, or 40 per cent; Euclid, nine out of 11, or 82 percent; book-keeping, 10, or 100 per cent; French, 15 out of 24, being 62 per cent; Latin, 16, or 66 per cent. Id physics, 7 out of 8, or 87 per cent; chemistry, 7, or 100 per cent; drawing, 19 out of 21, or 90 per cent ; and in music, 6, or 100 per Cent. • LIBERAL CLUB, WINSFORD.--4 lecture on "Ireland; its natural beauty, past history, and present misery," was delivered in the club room; W;insford, on Thursday night, by Mr. W. Handily, secretary of the Northwiel Division Liberal Association. Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., presided. There was a crowded attendance. The Chai,- man said there was an interest in 'relent, at the present day more than in any other country. Ireland, once an island of saints, culture, and civilization, had now its light almost extinguished by it,s long struggle with op- pression and suffering. Still she kept her own charac- teristics. England had used an arm of force, and al- though she held•Peland to-day by brute force and vio- lence, it was impossible to crush the spirit of nation- ality, and Ireland was to-day looking hopefully to the great democracy of England, 'Scotland, and 'Wales to redress her grievous wrongs, Mr. Ellis then formally. introduced Mr. Handley. Mr. Handley then delivered his lecture, which was illustrated by means o the oxy- hyorogen lantern. A number of photiwaphs of pro- minent men of the Liberal side were also shown, and! caused rounds of applause. At the close a vote of thanks was ac,coicied to the lecturer, on the motion of Mr. Ellis, seconded by Mr. T. Gibson. Mr. Handley, after re- sponding, proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, which Mr. Tolfree seconded.

PENKETH WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEASENT ASSOCIA.TION. On Wednesday evening, in the Wesleyan School-room, an ,instructive and interest- ing lecture on "Longevity?' was given before 'the members of the association by the Rev. E. 11. Jack- son, Wesleyan minister, Warrington. There was a good attendance. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was proposed to the lecturer by Mr. B. Hobson, seconded and supported by Mr. Garnett, and Mr. C. E. Parker. The president, Mr. J. Watson occupied the chair. —RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fort- nightly meeting of this Board was held at the Work- house, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood; Messrs. Knowles, Hadfield, Bran- dreth, Parr, Aaron, J. Stokes, Hewitt, Knowles, r. Hall, T. Forster, J. Smith, Hamilton, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Liqaker (deputy clerk.)—The Financ4 Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to .-C7 16s, and this was agreed to.—The Workhouse Master (Mr. Connell) reported that he had carefully conbidered the means of ex- tinguishing a fire at the workhouse, and he con- sidered that they were at present inadequate to cope with an outbreak.—lt was decided to refer this matter to a committee for consideration.—The rest of the business was formal. Tuurr OF CLOTHIN6.—At Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a man named Bernard Finn was brought upon remand on charges of felony. He pleaded guilty to having, on the night of the 24th of last month, stolen a coat, a vest, a pair of trousers, and a pair of boots, the pro- perty of a labourer at Brow Farm, Sankey; and to having, on the same night, stolen a coat, a vest, and a pair of trousers, the property of a labourer at another farm at Sankey. Prisoner pawned the clothing at Widnes, where he was appreheqded by P.C. Dugdale, and brought to the Bridewell at Warrington. For these offences be was committed to hard labour for a term of two months. He was also charged with stealing clothing from a farm at Cuerdley in September last, and pleaded not guilty, saying that at that time he was in Ireland. The magistrates, however, after hearing the evidence, sentenced him to a further term of a taonth's im- prisonment with hard labour. GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.—The • monthly ineeting of this Board was held at the Board Schools, Great Sankey. on Thursday afternoon. There were present Mr. Ridgway (chairman), the Rev. E. S. Yackson, and Mr. Grange, and Mr. S. Sut- ton (clerk).—Financial: The Clerk reported that the balance at the bank in favour of the Board was £l5l 3s 5d.--The Attendance: The master's report as to attendances, &t., having been read, the Chair- man remarked that the attendance seemed to be creeping up again. As far as he could hear. Sankey Bridges was now clear of measles, but he believed there were still a few cases at Penketh.—Rev. E. S. Jackson said the measles had greatly decreased. There wasno fever he was glad to say.—./feligioto Instruction: The Rev. E. S.lJackson said that at pre- sent there was no religious instruction given in the schools. He had mentioned the subject to the late chairman of the Board, but he said that as the Sun- day school was so efficient, it was not necessary to give religious teaching in the Board School. But still they had their duty to do as a Board, and re- ligious teaching was supposed to be given, three days in the week, and he thought they ought to teach what religion was lawful.—The Chairman thought that was a matter iSI which they should move carefully, but he thought no parent could ob- ject to its being taught to the extent that was al- lowed.—Mr. Clarke, the master, was then called into he room, and in answer to questions, said that no religious instruction had been given in rezular lessons folquite eighteen months. He bad spoken to Mr. Tufner, the late chairman, about it, and he said it would be sufficient to give a high tone of morality.—The Rev. E. El Jackson said he should be inclined to teach the children as they were taught in other schools.—Mr. Clarke said he always asked parents when they brought their children if they had any objections to scripture lessons, and they said they hadn't.—The Chairmin said it was a mat- ter for the Board to consider seriously, and he sug- gested that it be left over till the next meeting, and this course was agreed to.—The rest of the business was formal.

01/LOREN'S CONCERT AT APPLETON.-A very • pleasant evening's entertainment was provided on Thurlsday evening in St. Bede's School, Appleton, by several of the children attending the girls' depalk- ment of St. Bede's Day School. Despite the in- , clemency of the weather, the room was crowded. The first psistion of the programme consisted of the songs," Let us dance on the sands," "Erin. the tear and the smile,' and the vocal waltz, " Fairie voices," by the qhildren ; recitation, "The little hero," Alice Bonny; dialogue, "Dolly's mamma and the doctor," Edith Ireland and lyelhee'enning- ton ; and the dance," Keel Row," by the Misses 'Nellie Pennington, Dora Hunt, Annie Twist, Martha Callon, Lizzie _Beesley, Mary Pennington, Si,r.nnah. Busby, and Sarah Hosker. The second portion of the evening was devoted to the representation of the drama; "The Flowets of the Forest." The characters in this were portrayed by the following girls :—The Misses Mary M. kean, Mary Canavan, Mary Rooney, Lucy Beesley, Kate Canavan, Annie Grady, Emily Taylor, Alice Bonny, Lizzie Hurst, Mary. Pennington, Martha Callon; Rose Daley, Mary Maher, Martha Davenport., and May Davenport. The drama was exceedingly well represented, the scenic Arrangements being good, the dresses pleas- ing, and the acting very creditable. Miss Wright, the schoolmistress, has had the training of the chil- dren, and her pupils throughout the whole enter- tainment did her credit.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

'A gCHOONER BCNK Ar WIDNES.—On Saturday the schooner Joseph Howe, of Belfast, laden with fire brick from Glasgo* to West Bank Dock grounded on the sand bank opposite the dock gate. The position of the vessel was very awkevard, and at high tide next morn- ing she sank. The vessel was not insured. ACCIDENTS AT ,WIDNES.—Two patientsllwere admitted to Widnes Accident Hospital on Sunday. One was John Ross, aged 20, a labourer, of Ditton-road, Ditton, who had had several of his•ribs, his back, and other portions of his body severely crushed by falling through the trap of a hoist. The other was Thomas Cox, aged 35, a chemical labourer, of 20, Mary-street, Moss Bank, who had sustained a fracture of one of his legs by falling whilst walking. Both men were attended to by Dr. 011eeffe. •

'DV PROPOSED TREAT TO AGED PERSONS AT RUNCORN. —The gentlemen who have taken .upon themselves the responsibility of carrying out the annual custom of giving the old 'folks a tea party and entertainment have decided that the treat shall take place on the 10th inst. They are meeting with encouraging support, and a good sum was realised by the football match on Thursday. The Duke of Westminster has contributed £3 3s and Lord Egerton and Mr. Joseph Verdin have given b. is each.

A PM:WM SCALED AT WIDNES.—By the instructions of Dr. Hutchinson, a man named Thomas Ackers, of Cooper-street, Runcorn was admitted into the Widnes Accident Hospital, on Tuesday morning, suffering from severe scalds to the face, neck, and various other parts of the body, which he had received whilst following his employment as a plumber, at Messrs. John Hutchinson and Co.'s works. It appeared he was repairing one of the vats when the plug gave way and the caustic 'Uglier which the vat contained rushed out upon him. MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES.—A public meeting in aid of the Wesleyan Indian Mission was held on Tues- day evening, in Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel. Mrr T. Robinson presided, and on the platform were Gnanamutthu, a Hindoo manager of day schools in Madras; the Rev. G. Mackenzie Cabban, missionary from India; the Rev. R. Burdon Rev. J. Bryant; Messrs. S. Robinson, B. Brown, and B. Fogg. There was a crowded audience, and several interesting ad- ,dresses on missonary work in India,were given. MILL BROW MILITARY BAND CONCERT, RUNtOlO7. The second of the series of admirable concerts arranged by the above named Band was given in Runcorn Public Hall, on Fednesday evening. The concert was a success both as regards attendance and music. The artistes, who acquitted themselves in a manner that won univer- sal approval, were Madam Emilie Young, of Liverpool; Mr. W. E. Williams, the celebrated baritone, Mr. Wilson Blackledge' the Lancashire humourist, of St Helens, and Mr. Wm. Goode, of Liverpool. The Band also gave much pleasure by their performances. . FIRE AT RUNCORN.—On Saturday evening, between eight and nine o'clock, the flue of the chimney of a log- mg-house, in Mersey-street, was discovered to be on fire by P.C. Dale. Information was at once given to the Fire Brigade, and the flames were extinguised in a very short time. About eleven o'clock a woman observed smoke issning from a passage in the Mersey Vaults, and the landlord, Mr. Thomas Blease, upon being informed, found that the wall adjoining the flue of the lodging- house was on fire. With the aid of k hose the fire was quickly subdued, but not before the Fire Brigade was on the spot under Mr. Superintendent Wright. The damage done was very slight. DEATH OF A RUNCORN FLATMAN.—Mr. Clarke Aspin- all, coroner for Liverpool, on-Monday held an inquest on the body of William Davies, aged 51, the keeper of the Camden Hotel, Surrey-street, Runcorn, and also master of the flat Ellen, of Widnes. belonging to Messrs. Goss- age and Sons. On Friday last the deceased came down the river in his flat, and while in the act of lowering the mast preparatory to entering the Sandon basin, a span- ner, weighing about seven pounds, fell from aloft, and striking deceased on the head rendered him insensible. He was afterwards removed to the Northern Hospital in the horse ambulance, but died there early on Saturday moraing from the effects of his injuries. Verdict, "Accidental death." RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AT Wonc—At the instance of the Runcorn School Board the following persons were summoned before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday on a charge of net sending their children regularly to school :—Abraham Hampson, Jacksonalane ; Reuben Pickering, Fryer-street; John Neil, •Handley-strt ; Thomas Brown' Mason-street; John Newall, Waterffio- road ; Samuel Abrams, Lock-street; Thomas Lawton, Speakman-street; Fred Dunbavand, Percivals-lane; George Lvdiate, Surrey-street; Owen Roberts, Surrey- street; Richard Done, Cooper-street; James Robinson, Surrey-street: and Thomas Neild, Bridgewater-street. Attendance officer Bowyer proved the cases, and a fine of 5s was imposed upon each defendant. TROTTING MATCH NEAR WIDNES.--011 Tuesday after- noon, despite the inclement state of the weather, a crowd of persons assembled on Bold-road to witness a trotting match between Mr. James Smart's Silence and Mr. George Neil's Jessie, both of Widnes. The distance was two miles, Jessie to receive 200 yards start, and the stake £5 a-side. The horses were set to a good start by Mr. H. Singleton. It was at once evident that Silence, who was going in grand style, had the race in hand, as she over- took Jessie just as she pleased, and proved an easy winner hy ten yards. Silence was steered by her owner, and Jessie by Mr. W. Houghton. Mr. Thomas Edward- son and Mr. Thomks Fyldes acted as umpires, and Mr. W. Halligan, of Liverpool, a well-known man in trot- ting circles, made a good referee. The batting was 25 to 20 on Silstice. FOUNDERING OF A WIDNES STEAMER.—On Monday night, a strong gale was blowing off Liverpool, and re- sulted in the founderiflg of the coasting steamer, the Evarsfield, bound to the Mersey with a cargo of lime- stone. The disaster occurred near the northwest light- ship at four o'clock on Tuesday morning. The crew abandoned their vessels leaving in one of their own boats. They were only just in time, for the steamer foundered toon afteithey left going down in 10 fathoms of water. The heavy nature of her cargo aided her in going down very quickly. The men in their tiny craft made for the Mersey, and although the weather was heavy they succeeded in getting to the George's Land- ing-stage, whete they landed on Tuesday. The Eversfield WEE only a small steamer of 123 tons. She was Bringing the limestone from Llandulas, and had been for some time engaged in that capacity. She belonged to Mr. L. Kilcross, of Widnes. WIDNES LIBERAL CLUE.—On Monday evening the second smoking concert in connection with the above club was held. Major J. W. Wareing presided, and there was a large attendance. The first item was a violin solo by Mr. Gordon. Mr. T. Williams then gave a song with great taste. A song by Mr. T. Singleton was given with good effect, and an encore was demanded. Mr. J. G. Kiddie then sang "the heart bowed down." On being recalled a humorous song was given, which created much amusement. Mr. W. Jones sang "Thou tart so near and yet so far;" Mr. Gordon gave "Mr. Riley," and on being encored gave "Mr. Malchahery." Mr. Morrison sang Let me like a soldier fall" and "Ballyhoolev." Messrs. Gordon and Kiddie gave a violin duet item "Ii Trovatore," and, being encored, "The cockoo " duet. Mr. W. Williams sang " The Trallala Brigade," with good effect. Mr. Morrison moved a vote of thanks to My Wareing for presidbag ; this was seconded by Mr. F. Clve. Mr. Wareing having responded, a very pleasant evening was brought to a close.
