A RUNAWAY APPRENTICE AT RIINCORN.—At Runcorn Petty sessions on Monday, Frederick Ellison, blacksMith, Norm* summoned his apprentice John Platt, aged 17, for w ongfully absenting himself from his eniplovment and otherwise misbehaving himself, and he asked that the deed of apprenticeship should be rescinded. Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, said the apprentice was a pauper, and he appeared to watch the case on behalf of the Guar- dians. Ellison said the youth had been with him for two years and eight months, and was apprenticed to him until he was 21 years of age. He received £2 10s with the boy, and there was another £2 lOs due now. The boy left his work on the 10th January' and had since lived at a farm. He would never make a smith, and he (complainant) thought it was a pitx to keep him at it. Mr. Linaker pointed out that the boy had been entitled to sixpence per week since the first of October, and Mr. Brundrit asked the complainant if he had paid those wages. Ellison replied that he had not as he thought the defendant did not need them, and that it would be bettor to give the money in a lump. 4r. Lin- aker said the Guardians thought it would be in the in- terests of the boy if the indentures were cancelled. The Magistrates cancelled tho indentures on the complainant, undertaking to repay the premium of £2 10s, and to pay the wages due.

div.head: 'RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS,
div.p: 'RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS,

The monthly meeting was held at the Town •Hail, on Thursday. Mr. J. Dobson presided, and there were presentOfessrs. Once, Hankinson, Meadow- croft, Wiswall,Speakman. Timmins, Smith, White, Lake, Pritchard, Mellor, Taylor, and Fishtr, with Lake (law clerk), Marshall (secretary), and Barker (surveyor).

_ HEALTH OF THE TOWN. • The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month , amount to 37.. Of these two were inquest cases, and of the remaining 35 deaths 13 were due to bronchitis, 7 to nat iral decay, 3 to measles, 2 to apoplexy, 2 to misen- teric disease:2 to congestion of the lungs, 2 to inflame,- tion of the lungs, 3to diarrhcea, and 1 to convulsions. The 37 deaths show an average death rate for the fwelve months of a portion over 26 per 1,000 of the estimated population, and, exclusive of the inquest cases, of a little over 24 per 1,000. •
-HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS _oolemn-ricx.

The minutesof the Highways and Buildings Committee, which were approved on the motion of Mr. Taylor, se- condedby Mr. Fisher, contained the recommendation thatthe tender of Messrs. Kirkham and Co. for re-flag- ging the footpath on the west side of Wellington-street be accepted, and that the plan of Mr. John Thomason for the erection of three cottages in Thoma.s-street and four cottages in Stanley-street be `aTproved.

FINANCE.-THE LIBRARY RENT INCREASED. The Finance Committee reported that during the past month the treasurer had received £633 2s 6d, and had recommended for payment accounts amounting to £BlB Os Bd. It was recommended that cheques be drawn on the treasurer for the following expenses incurred in con- nection with the I,iverpool Waterworks and Improve- ment Bill, viz sc Mr. I'. Speakman £lO 3s, Messrs. , Mackie and Co. £6 15s, Mr. G. Bellamy £4 10: 6d, &Leers. of C. Gerrard 9s, managers of Bethesda School, 1.56. That the rent of the Library Committee be increased from £25 to £36 per annum, such increase being for the extra ac- commodation, cleaning, heating, lighting, and mainten- ance provided in connection with the library premises. That the assessment of Mr. T. P. Parkes. Bridge- street, be reduced from £B7 lOs to £52 10s. That additional ventilators be fixed in the reading room and in the secretary's office.—Mr. Fisher moved, and Mr. Grice seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Lake asked on what basis the in- crease in the library rent was made.—Mr. Fisher replied that the increase was on account of the extension of the library premises. The Board had to borrow something like £l7O, and they had to pay back each year principal and interest amounting to £lO Be 9d. They had added 11s3d forrextra fire, attention, kc, so that the committee had not been very heavy in the matter.—ln reply to Mr. Lake, the Secretary Stated that £6 103 was interest, and the remainder of the amount principal.—Mr. Lake pro- posed an amendment that the rent of the library be £32 instead of £36. He said when the question was under discussion before the plans were passed, it was objected to the Library Committe making. the altera- tions, because of the mconveniente that would arise in the committee being owner of one half of the room and the Board the owner of the other half. It was therefore, decided that the ißoard should borrow the money on the general district rate and charge the library an increased rent, which should be a fair return on their outlay. Now the Finance Committee wished to charge the library an increased rent of more than the full amount of the Commissioners' yearly payments, and at the end of 30 years the library woald have paid for all the alterations that had been made, and yet the owner- ship would not be vested in the library, but in the Commissioners. For :the two rooms the library occupied the committee proposed to charge £36, pith heating and clea,ning. The rooms were in a back Oosi- tion, in a back street, and approached through a back entry (he referred to Egerton-st.' not Waterloo-rd.) and they werenot worth more than £lO a year. He submitted that the charge was a monstrous charge; and it was not as if they were obliged to de it. He knew the argument that they had conscientious scruples against allowing more than the penny rate to be expended on the library, but the law said they should give the library reasonable terms as landlords. The Commissioners could if they chose let the library have premises for next door to nothing, so that they were not tied down in any way. It came to this, would they by friendly desire help forward an institution which had done more for the education, for the amusement, and for the improvement of the tovSn than almost any other institution in it, or would they by taking a hard and fast and rather grudging view of the matter, give them as little as they possibly could. He submitted that £32 was a very ample rent for those two rooms and for the little cleaning they required.—Mr. Mellor seconded the amendment.—Mr. Meadowcroft said the members must look at the question .from a practical point of view, and eliminate from their minds altogether the feeling etf sentiment which Mr. Lake had brought forward fqr their consideration. If it was to be a ques- tion of sentiment and education, the Board would not be entitled to charge scarcely any rent to the School Board for the occupation of their offices. They must deal with the matter in a spirit which would be rust to the rate- ' payers at large. The committee, in asking the library to repay the principal and Interest which the Commissioners were coenpelled to pay out of pocket were only asking for a fair and reasonable return, and for no more than the obligation the Commissioners had taken on their behalf. The relit included cleaning, heating, lighting, and maintenance, phial he thought were items of considerable importance. The premises were of a creditable character, and being adjacent to the Town Hall was an advantage to them rather than otherwise, and ;they were free from rates and taxes. There was no desire to extort anything from the Library Committee. Mr. Fisher said if they. were only to charge the Library Committee the interest on the money then they would be giving them over £4 a year, and he was confident that if more than the penny in the £ was spent that a surcharge would be made. He questioned whether the Commissioners could allow the Library the premises rent free even if therwere disposed. Ile thought the Com- mittee were acting justly both to the Library and to the ratepayers at large. For the amendment there voted Messrs Lake, Mellor and Pritchard, and nine members against.—lt was therefore lost Mr. Lake then. moved a further amendment that the minute be referred back to the Finance Committee, and was making a speech show- in/. that the Commissioners for the £l7O they had spent would have the bricks and mortar,—when the chairman ruled him out of order. The minutes were then passed.

AN IMPORTANT POINT TO PROPERTY OWNERS. The Parliamentary and Legal Committee having been requested by the Highway and Buildings Committee to considerthe question of the responsibility of the town for the sewers, drains, traps, and paving of the back passage between Shave-street and Surrey-street, with the view of obtaining counsel's opinion on the game, re- commended that the opinion of counsel be taken forth- with on the matter.—Mr. Speakman moved, and Mr. Meaclowcroft seconded, the adoption of the minutes.— Mr. Smith said he should like to know if the committee had taken into consideration thA probable cost of coun- sel's opinion. It seemed to him to be strange to take counsel's opinion about a small affair like this.—Mr. Speakman said after all the circumstances were taken into consideration it was thought the best thing to do in the interests of everybody concerned.—Mr MeadoWeroft: The opinion is not expected to cost £lo.—Mr. Smith: As a rule it is ten times ten.—Mr. Meadowcroft explained that the question was not a small one. Under the deci- sion in this ease depended the very important question of how far the Board were liable throughout the town for work of this character.—The minutes were then adopted. ASSOCIATION OF LOCAL BOARDS.-21•LETTER. FROM M. - snurame. , •

The Secretary read a letter from he Association of Local Boards, asking the Board to pass a resolution hav- ing for its object the securing of the issue of regulations authorising the payment of expenses in connection with the association. It was the unanimous opinion of the council of the association that It behoved Local Boards, in view or the projected County • Government Bill, to have their organisation in the greatest possible state of efficiency if any action they might wish to take in obtain- ing amendments to the Bill, should its provisions be de- trimental to their interests, was to have any effect. The following letter, addressed to the clerk, was also read : " Winmngton Old Hall, Northwich, January 31, 1888.— Dear sir,—Mr. Brunner desires me to ask you to press upon the members of your Board the advisability of sup- porting the action of the Association of Local Boards with reference to the Local Authorities (Expenses of Con- ference) Act, 1885. The framing of the regulations by the Local Government Board will not Involve them hi any expense, and will be a very great help to the asso- ciation, which has already done good work.—Truly yours, Tumras ELtis."—On the motion of Mr, Speak-

man, seconded by Mr. Hankinson, it was decided to knowledge Mr. Brunner's letter, and to refer the ques- tion to the consideration df the Highway and Buildings Committee, which consists of the whole Board.

FIRE AT BRIDGEWATER FOUNDRIt.& Mr. Timmins said recently he had a fire at lire foundry, which might have been serious, and he desired to know if he could arrange with the Commissioners to use the hydrant in the town's yard, in the case of another outs break.—lt was explained that the Fire Brigade could use any hydrant in case of the, and there was n 3 objection to Mr. Timmins using the one in question. • There was no other business.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Colonel Ashton (in the chair), the Rev. J. Lockwood, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs, Aaron, Brandreth. Hadfield, Parr, Stokes, Knowles. Hewitt; H. Linaker (clerk). 4and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.) WESTON PAEOCHIAL AUTHOEXTY.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board in reply to the application for urban powers, similar to those in force at Frodsham and Prodsham Lordship, for the township of Weston. The Local Government Board expressed their willingness to grant the 'powers applied for with the exception of those re- ferring to slaughter-houses, which they did not see any necessity for in Weston.—The Dtputy Clerk: The powers they gave you relate to bouses and streets.—The Clerk said he replied to the effect that he did not think the powers with regard to slaugh- ter-houses were required.—Mr. Aaron: Oh, no.—Mr. • Hadfield asked if the powers obtained 9- plied to farm eatbuildings. Would authority have to be got to put up these out- buildings. The Clerk : Yes. Mr. Stokes; Even a wooden building? The Clerk: All buildings.—Mr. Hadfield : I think it is very foolish.—Mr. Aaron explained that the Weston bye- laws would have to be prepared and afterwards sub- mitted to that Alithority, and then to the Local Government Board.—Mr. Hadfield: Some of the Frodsham bye-laws are perfectly ridiculous.—The Clerk said it was always supposed that the mem- bers of the local committees were men of common sense.—Mr. Hadfield: But they have no common sense in London.—The Clerk: • But the common sense is supposed to be in the country P—Mr. Parr: It has got to be a very scarce article. (Laughter.) —Mr. Aaron then moved that the following persons be appointed to compose the Weston Parochial Com- mittee, viz. :—Messrs. J. W. Kirkham, E. Aaron, J. Handley, T. Ford, T. Jeffs, R. Clarke, and W. Griffiths.—Mr. Stokes seconded this proposal, which was akreed to. SCARLET FEvini.—Dr. Adams (medical officer) - reported the occurrence of a sporadic case of scarlet fever at Frodsham Bridge. The Cue Was one of a youth, aged 15 years. He (the medical officer) could not trace the origin of this case, no, history of any exposure to infection being obtain- able. All the usual precautionary measures had been taken, and final disinfection would be per- formed in about a week. He recommended the abolition of a cesspool at the back of the cottage in which the fever had occurred, and also the lay- ing of a proper drainage course, laid with trapped grid, This was all the business of public interest.*
THE WASTE NUISANCE AT WIDNES. CONFERENCE WITH MANUFACTURERS.

On Tuesday afternoon a special meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held at the Town Hall for the purpose of 'conferring with the manufacturers who deposit chemical waste in the township. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., occupied the chair, and the members present Were Dr.' O'Keeffe, Messrs. D. Wright, F. Heyes, J. Taylor, H. Gaskell, junr., S. Sadler. B. Brown, E. Canty, J. Dlidwood, and T. Handley, with J. T. Allen (clerk.) • The Board at once resolved themselves into committee, and the repre- sentatives of the Press had to retire; but we learn that after half an hour's discussion in private the depUtation of manufacturers were called into the room, the follow- ing being present :—Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., and Mr. J. H. Lewis (representing Muspratt and Sons), Mr. Geo. Pilkington, J.P. (Pilkington and Son), Major Cross (Hut- chinson's trustees), Mr. R. H. , Davies (Golding and Davies), and Mr. J. Leath (Lancashire Alkali and Sul- phur Company). v„ The Chairman explained that the attendance of the deputation had been requested in consequence of the numerous complaints that had been made of nuisances arising from the laying of waste, and stated that the Board were satisfied that there were good grounds for these complaints. The Board were also of opinion that the best practicable means had not been adopted for laying the waste, and that it should not be laid so near to house property as was the custom at present. It was advisable not to lay waste near the Central Station, the- vacant land there might be filled with rubbish. Since the last meeting of the Board there had been several inspections of the waste heaps made, and on each oc- casion a considerable nuisance was found

A letter was read from Messrs. Brock and Sullivan, stating that as they did not deposit waste in Widnes they did not think it necessary to attend that meeting. Mr. Pilkingten said his firm did net lay waste in the township, but he attended the meeting out of compliment to the Board. At the same time he could assure the Board that every care was used by his firm in laying waste properly. • Major Cross and the other manufacturers present as- sured the Board that they would do their utmost to pre- vent any waste being so laid as to create a nuisance.; It was suggested, on behalf of the Board, that it*might be advisable to lay waste in layers of three or four feet deep and then baiter it well down. Mr. Leath pointed out that in St. Helens waste was laid from 30 to 60 feet high near house property, and that the Corporation had two inspectors constantly at work seeing that no nuisance was caused. On the deputation retiring, it was unanimously re- solved, on the motion of Mr. Gaskell, seconded by Mr. Taylor, that an inspector should be appointed by the Board, at a salary of £2 per week, to watch over the deposits of waste, and to report daily any nuisances that' might occur. This inspector is to be under the General Purposes Committee. Mr. Midwood. did not vote. The Board also considered that waste should not be laid within 300 yards of any dwelling house, and it was resolved to send notice to this effect to the depositors, on , the proposition of Mr. Wright, secoudsd by Mr. Sadler. , Again Mr. Midwood did not vote. It should be mentioned that during the interview the depositors of waste were given to understand that in the event of any serious nuisance being reported by the inspector there would be no other course open to the Board than to take legal action to remedy it. In the course of the discussion Mr. Muspratt called attention to the drain from Violet-street, under the Central Railvvhy. Occasionally the tide backed up thn. sewage and damage from the waste in this sewer and thus a nuisance was caused. The surveyor (Mr. Hig-- ginson) was Instructed to inspect this sewer and report to the committee.

STRANGE. DEATH OF A SCHOOL GIRL AT 'WIDNES. On Monday morning Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy county coroner, held an inquest at the Ram's Head Inn, Newtown, Widnes, on the body of Annie Hynes, aged 11, daughter of Edward Hynes, a labourer, of Catherine-street. From the evidence adduced it appeared. that the deceased, who, was subject at times tq fainting fits, went to St. Ilarfa Roman Catholic School on Thursday afternoon, ap- parently in good health. Whilst at school she was no- ticed by her teacher (Miss McMahon) to look pale, but it was thought that this was through fear of being punished for. some mistakes she had made in an exarm- nation held m the morning, as after being struck by the mistress (Miss Cullen) on the hands ana arms, like the other girls, she recovered her colour, and did not com- plain. At four o'clock, however, when school was dis- missed, she complained to her school mates of her head aching, and when she got home madeasimilar complaint to her parents. After sitting by the fire for a while she vomited, and was then put to bed, her mother and sis- ter, at her request, sleeping alongside her. She was not undressed, as she said she felt too tired. Next morn- ing she appeared to be a little better, and her clothes were taken off, but at night she became worse, still com- plaining o her head. Dr. O'Keeffs was then sent for, but he was unwell and could not come, and then Mr. Burgess, assistant to Dr. McCambri.dge, was summoned, but he did not attend, - and the grin died on Saturday morning.—At the conclusion of the evidence a juryman asked if Miss Cullen could not be called.—The Coroner said he did not think it was neceSsary, as the flogging or thrashing which had been inflicted did notappear to have been very excessive, and only such as was dealt out to other girls, one of whom they had had before them that morning in perfect health. Should they want to make a charge against Miss Cullen he should refuse to call her, as he did not consider it right to take a person's evid- ence, and then turn it against her. If the jury liked, however, he should adiourn the inquiry, in order that a. post-mortem examination might be made, and some more evidence brought forward ; but, in his opinion. t.he evidence which had been adduced was all that was requis' ite. With respect to the doctors not coming when sent for, it was their own look out. Some coroners made, a practice of blaming doctors for not attending when they were sent for, but doctors were not forced by law to attend, and he supposed they knew their business better than anyone else. From what appeared to havo been the condition of the decea.sod, he should think that, the parents ought to have sent for medical attendance before they did. It did not appear that the girl had been crammed. No doubt the caning the girl had received whilst unwell had brought on shock to the system, from which she had been unable to recover, but the mistress should have been informed of her state. A ver- dict of "Death from natural causes" was ultimately re- turned.

div.head: RUGBY,RULES.
div.p: RUGBY,RULES.

• 1 WIDNES v. Asperm.--The return match between these teams wait played at Widnes on Saturday, and resulted in a splelllid victory for the home team by two goals, three tries, and eight miners to nil.. Aspull had several of their usual players absent owing to the marriage of jCartwright, their captain, and Hughes was again unable to play for Widnes. Considering the recent frosty weather, the ground was in a very fair condition. There was a large crowd of spectators, at least 3,000 being pre- sent. A game of two thirties Was played. Smith, for Widnes, kicking off up the slope, with the shining sun with dazzling brilliancy in the face of his men at a quar- ter to four. The Widnesians at once began to press. Farrell essayed a drop at goal, missing narrowly, and. and after two minors had been addegl, J. Bingham, who received the ball from a pass by Hardman, ran to the line, where he was brought down,Within a yard of the coveted streak. Some tough 'scrimmages foamed, and Aspull were at length compelled to save. A moment later Hardman dashed over the line, and secured a try, from which Plumpton placed a splendid goal. This was followedby a brilliant run, half the length of the field, by Barker, who grounded the ball over the Aspull line, but the try was not allowed. It was not long, however, before the line was again crossed, and Kiddie secured an Indisputable try, after a fine pass by Wilkinson. Plump- ton made a good attempt at goal, but did not succeed. Half-time followed, with the score—Widnes, one goal, one try, and three minors; to nil. We should have stated above that Plimpton also had an apparently genuinetry disallowed. In the second half Widnes continued their victorious career. A magnificent run by Plumpton three parts the length of the field was rewarded by him secur- ing a try behind, the posts, from which, however, Farrell slid not add the major point. Then the Widnesians ran up a total of eight minors,without once &Aug theiroppo- ments a chance of scoring,andsubsequentlyPlumptonand Parkinson obtained tnes,the latter close behindtheposts, and Smith kicked a neat goal. Speakman got away with a splendid run from the kick off and missed to Lloyd, who was held by Andrews near the quarter flag. Whittle next put in a strong run and passed to the forwards, Littlewood missing a chance of scoring by knocking theball forward with his hand. Whittle passed to Evans, who kicked, the ball going dead. Half-time was celled, with the score—Warrington one goalstwo tries, and six minors, to -Waltbn nil. Spedding restarted on behalf of the visitors., Jolley returning well. A short run by Whittle and kick by Samson took play to near the Walton line, but the Visitors saved by touching down. Another minor point was scored immediately afterwards from a long kick by Jolley. Bate receiving a pass by Whittle, put in a grand run, and from a line-out near the visitors' goal-line, Speakman threwout quickly, Isherwood placing the ball over the line. The final match of this annual fixture was brought to a close at Barrow, on Saturday, before a moderate atten- dance of spectators. Several of the Warrington team originally chosen failed to make the journey—biles', speak's-lan, Warren, and Littlewood being absent. An early start was made, and Barrow was reached in good time. The frdst had been very severe on the previous night, but on enquiring as regards the condition of the ground it was stated to be hi capital playing order. The home team mustered their full strength, and at three o'clock both sides made their appearance in the enclb- • sure. They weiie received with cheers, and no 'arrange- raent having been come to with respect to the ground, which was totally unfit to play on, Kinnish started from 'centre, and the home team forwards invaded the War- rington 25.• 1 Barnes was the first to show up with a neat run to the • half-way flag, and it was soon apparent that the state es the ground caused several of the Warringtonians to play timidly. This, however, was not the case with the Bar- row men, for they tackled in strong fashion. Soon after Barnes' run from the kick off, the home team placed the visitors on the defensive, but pretty 'passing by Davies, Antrobus, and Barnes, placed the home team on their Jinn. Good play by Woodburn was now shown, and from a kick by the fatter, Nevins almost let in the Bar- row men, but the mistake he had previously made was soon rectified by a smart save of a rush of the home for- wards. Give-and-take play was the order, and runs by Gregory and Forshaw were negatived by the powerful kicking of Massey. Passing by the Barrow backs looked like scoring, but Barnes prevented this, and the Warring- ton skipper came again to the fore by a smart run and kick from his own line to half-way.. Exchange kicks by Nevins and Woodburn settled play In neutral territory, but from a pack here the Visiting forwards rushed the leather to the line. Smith responded to this dribble by a smart run to the half-way, but again Massey forced the North Lane-shire men back.. Antrobus passed smartly to Massey. but the slippery state of the ground prevented his taking advasstage of it, robbing Warring- ton of a certain score. Nevins "made his mark" from a kick of Harley's, and Fair. Turner's attempt almost lowered the Barrow citadel, the ball grazing the outside, only a minor resulting. Forshaw was compelled to con- cede a minor shortly afterwards, but soon after the re- commencement, Barnes lost a golden opportunity, owing to the nature of the Found. Ashton was conspicuous by a neat dribble, an a free kick to Forshaw availed his side but little. The home team were placed on the de- fensive the most of this half, atid Bell'tried hard to re- lieve the pressure, but found his way impeded by Fair. Turner. Daniels now looked like scoring, but the de- fence of the Barrow backs could' not be broken. The home team now rallied, and forced a way into warring- ton quarters. Harley shone with a neat run and pass to Forshaw, the latter being pushed into touch close to the line, half-time being called with the score—Warrington 2 minors, Barrow 1 minor. Frank Turner re-started from centre, Sinnish returning. Berries put in some tricky work, and Leak° responded by taking the leather to half way. The Barrow men now got away with a good rush to the Warrington line, scoring a second minor, and from the drop-out Dillon was the means of forcing the game in the home team's territory. Dillon and Fair. Tur- ner dribbled to the opposing line, and had hard lines in not scoring. Barnes was applauded for some sterling work, but Harley relieved his lines in grand style, punt- ing to halfway. The visitors would not be denied, for

i THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AD THE DISTRICT. NO. 3.—LOWER, WALTON AND STOCK- TON HEATH. , ' In addition to the making of the two new roads mentioned in our previous article—the one to the left from near, the Stag Inn to Warrington, and the other to the right to Stockton Heath—there are other works to be carried out at Lower Walton, which will necessitate changes of the most thorough- going description. First and foremost the canal it- self will breakthrough the centre of that part of the village which lies between the Chester and Warrington road and. the Runcorn and Latchford canal, sweeping away everything in its course. The white-walled and thatch-covered cottages, which are scattered about in picturesque irregu- larity, the gardens of the cottagers so pleasing in the summer time to the senses of sight and smell of the passersby, the roads and stream, will all have to give place to the imperious requirements of the great undertaking. In this locality the centre line of the canal is marked to run through the garden ground, pasture, and osier beds in the occupation ,oz Mrs. Elizabeth Smith, the gaidenjand in the occupation of Mr. Joseph Stringer and Mr. Samuel Stringer, and the garden and outbuilding occupied by Mr. John Robinson. Of course, from this centre line out- wards on both sides to the full width of the canal the houses and buildings of every kind will be , pulled down, and their very fotpulations displaced 1 by tio spades of the navvies. . STOPPING OF ROADS, &c. At the present times there are tero lanes branch- ing off from the Chester and Warrington-road at Lower Walton. which, after merging into each other some distance away, lead down to the banks of the Runcorn and Latchford canal, and the Mersey. One of these lanes branches off from the east side of the large pond ot water' between the northern side of the Chester-road and Walton Mill, and the other from the western side of the pond. It is evident that, as the Ship Canal is to run it course midway between the Chester-road and the Latch- ford canal, Ohese lanes will have to be inter- sected and broken ' up. As a matter of fact parts of both roads will be stopped up and all rights of way. extinguished. Of the wes- tern road, the part stopped will lie between a point about 110 yards from the Chester-roed and a point about 220 yards; and of the more easterly road, that is to say, the one nearer Warrington, the part on which the right of way will be extinguished lies between two points, one of which is about 88 yards, from the Chester-road, and the other 220 yards. In consideration of the stoppage of these roads, a new road will be made from the more westerly one, to run along near the southerly banks of the Ship Canal, and finally merge into the new road to be made frdm the Stag Inn, across Arpley fields to Warrington. The junction of these two new roads will take place about 250 yards from the Chester-road, and the pedestrian or driver of a vehicle, whether he branch off from the Chester-road at the Higher Walton side of the pond referred to, or lower down on the new road near the Stag Inn, will still cross thd canal by the same swing bridge and pursue his journey to Warrington by the same road across Arpley fields. It may be mentioned that the new road behind Walton Mill will have to be construc- ted with gradients not steeper than 1 in 95, and wilf have to be completed before the portions of the two roads of which it is to be the substitute have been stopped up. It may be safely predicted from what has been stated above, and in our previous article, that a very complete sort of transformation will be wrought in Lower Walton by the new canal. It is not difficult to imagine that a person who has known the village 1 in its pristine state, and who returns a few years I hence to find it in its changed conditions, might I find appropriate expression of his feelings in the words of Goldsmith's wanderer, . 'limes are altered; trades unfeeling train . . Usurp the land, and dispossess the swain. But, as against the hopeless desolation of the" Sweet Auburn " of the poet, it may with some degree of assurance be anticipated that Lower Walton will, 1 so to speak, rise from its ashes into a new and more vigorous life—that its present bucolic somnolence will be succeeded by an active and a prosperous future. . CENTRE LINE OF CANAL. But leaving matters of curious ' speculation aside, let us regain the Chester main road and passing down it a short distance—to a few yards on the Wilderspool side of where now stands the Stag liin—let us turn into the new road which is to lead from here to Stockton Heath. From the point where it branches off from the Chester-road till it reaches the Northwich and Warrington high- way, through Stockton Heath, this new thorough- fare will run in pretty close proximity to the southern bank of the Ship Canal. It may be noticed ' from here that the house of the late Mr. J. T. Cun- liffe, which at present stands just off the Chester- road, has disappeared, as also has the row of com- fortable - looking houses, with well-kept little . gardens in front, which now stand just on the . Walton sidtt of Tom Paine's Bridge. The place of ' this bridge, too, will then know it no more, and its • exact site may perhaps in time become as much a • matter of controversy as the last resting place of ' the bones of the famous historical personage whose • name it is known by. The centre line of the . new canal is indicated to strike through the Ches- ter-road—which, as we have before mentioned, is to - be closed for some distance on both sidesrof Tom ' Paine's Bridge—in a diagonal direction 'in front of ' where now stands Mr. CunliffeYs house, and con- tinues a straight line to Stockton Heath and beyond. Between Paine's Bridge and Twenty-step . Bridge at Stockton Heath the Runcorn and Latch- ford canal, which these bridges span, describes a 1 bold curve forming almost half a circle, and as the ' ( Ship Canal is to take a straight course its centre • line is marked to pierce through the existing canal : into the circle, a short distance on the eastern side of Paine's Bridge, and about an equal distance on i the western side of Twenty-step Bridge it again . pierces the Latchford canal out of the "circle." Considering the great width .of the Ship Canal, this • practically means that that portion of the bed of the Runcorn and Latchford canal which lies be- tween the two bridges mentioned will be absorbed by the new channel. At Stockton Heath the centre line of the new canal is marked to pass through gardens in the occupation of Mr. Joseph Monks and Mrs. M. A. . F.airhurat, and house, garden and outbuildings oc- cupied by Mr. John Wright. all of this property being just on the south side of Twenty-stop bridge. Passing along the new road to Stockton Heath, it may be noticed that it is not less that tairty feet in width. the Act requiring this width for all new roads to be made in the district of the Daresbury Highway Board (except where otherwise provided), and also that the roads be made to the reasonable satisfaction of the Highway Board. This new road will debouch into the Northwich and Warrington highway just on. the Warrington side of St.

again the Warrington forwards, headed by Ashton an Frank Turner, put the game at the Barrow quarter flag From a line out at half way, Daxison, Bell, and Smith rushed the leather down the field, and Bell overrunning the bail again joined in the issue, tlnik placing himself off-side, but the leather was taken over, Alexander com- pleting the try. LORD ItIPON AND • MR. JOHN MORLEY IN IRELAND. The Marquis of Ripon and Mr. John Morley travelled to Dublin on Wednesday, bearing, as was said by one of them, a " message of goodwill" from the Liberal party of England to the Irish people. At Chester and other places on this side the Channel the distinguished travel- lers were recognised and cheered. At Kingstown they they had a great reception, and the Town Commissioners I presented an ably written address. In reply Lord Ripon said they had come to Ireland in the hope that it might be in their power to do something to lay the foundation of that closer and more intimate union betVreen the Bri- tish and Irish peoples which was the great object of the Liberal party. The time of repression and coercion was past. Mr. Morley said the outlook in Ireland was now far less promising than when he left the country a year and a half since. The Government had no policy, and the result had been a lamentable condition of things which 53W %tit i..-ngliqh and Irish clepiorad. They had come to Ireland with a rneASage of hope te convey to the Irish people, and of the support both of the leaders and of the Liberal rank and file. 'Proceeding to Dublin, the visitors weie met and escorted by a magnificent proces- sion. On Thursday the freedoin bf the city of Dublin was presented to M. John Morley and the Marquis of Ripon, in recognition of their strenuous efforts to secure the re- Cognition by the English people of the inherent and national rights of Ireland. Ex-Lord Mayor T D. Sulli- van presided, in the absence through ill-health of Mr. Sexton, M.P., the Lord Mayor. Lord Ripon, who met with a magnificent reception, assured the vast audience that the design of the Liberal party of Great Britain was to accord to Irishmen a full recognition of their real and legitimate political aspirations. He still to the pregnant saying that "force is no ly," and would labour to found the union of the three kingdoms upon the only safe and sound basis— a real union of heart and will Of the three peoples.—Mr. John Morley, who met with a reception as warm as that accorded to Lord Ripon, remarked that he was the first member of Her Majesty's Privy Council in Ireland who had been admitted to the honour of the freedom of Dub- lin. He had not always judged rightly of Irish affairs, but he had never faltered in his conviction that the greatest triumph that an Englishman could achieve weuld be to reconcile the people of Eno.- land with the people of Ireland, and that for that reconciliation they must look in one direction i only, and that was n restoring to Irishmen a fair and ploper share—a full share—in the management of their. own country. After replying to the old ascendanay arguments used in the Leinster Hall the other night, which he said were now antediluvian politics, Mr. Morley said it :was a farce and a grievous error th extend the county franchise in Ireland two years ago if no at. tention was to be paid to the popular voice, and if the British Government and Legislature were to go on listen- ing only to the select and exclusive minoritry. A mass meeting was held in the evening ;iv the Zeins- ter Hall, which was densely packed an hohr.before the proceedings commenced. Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., presided, and M. E. D. Gray, M.P., Moved a resolution welcoming Mr. Morley and Lord Ripon to Ireland, and tendering thanks to Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party for their generous efforts to restore peace and prosperity- to Ireland, and to end the long and sad chapter of Irish misgovernment by the restoration of an Irish Parliament, which alone could create between the two countries a true union based upon the loyalty of a contented and self-governed people. The resolution having been carried with great enthutiasm, the Marquis of Ripon said the spirit and purpose of the visit of himself and Mr. Morley had been rightly interpreted as that of reconciliation. A policy of perpetualcoercion was a policy of perpetual discontent, continued unrest, and ceasless uncertainty, and the return of prosperity under such a system was altogether hopeless—Mr. Morley, in the opening of his speech, asked if the policy of coercion had succeeded in its object, and said he wished to see some of the fruits of the policy that could be tested, and to be shown that the Government had advanced an inch on the road to the grand pacification which they promised. The policy had so far been a failure, and was a pitiful and a cruel farce.. The right hon. gentleman then dealt with the attitude of the Liberal party, and proceeded to ask the landlords what they had gained by the policy of the Tories.

The road to Warrington willliere be carried over the canal by a swing bridge. With regard to these swing bridges; of which there are several to be utilised near Warrington, it may be mentioned that there area number of conditions laid down in the por- tion of the Ship'Canal Act providing ." for the pro- tection of the Corporation and traders, &c., of War- rington" It is enacted that the swing bridges to be made at or near Warrington to carry roads over the cantl shall be made of the clear width between the parapets, of na.less,than 36 feet, including on either side a crgivenient footway, • and that they shall be sufficient in all respects for the passing of carts, carriages, and other vehicles. If in consequence .of the construction of a swing bridge the level of any road is altered, the Canal Company is to wake easy approaches to the bridge on Ixith sides, and the bridges are, providing the persons having jurisdiction over the roads consent; to be constructed with a beadway.of ncit less than twelve feet 'above the waterway. so as to admit the passage under them Of all small craft wing the canal. The bridges are to be made to turn by hydraulic power in not more than, one minute and a half of time, and are not to be kept opeirat'any one time for any longer period than ten minutes under a penalty of not less than forty shillings and not more than five pounds. The Daresbury Highwayßoard have also sought provision that tke Canal Company are at all times to keep_ a proper and sufficient staff to work the bridges without unnecessary delay to traffic, and tbat the bridges are .to be available to the public free of charge. During the night time, the bridges are to be sufficiently lighted, and when they are open for the passage cd vessels danger lights are to be exposed to ensure the safety of the .(To be contiaued.) •

and at the outer end or point; between them there- fore is a Itng slot, in which swings an arm of ad- justable length, depending from a fulcrum fixed on .the upper member of the jib; and at the base.of the post is a circular platform, on which a man stands to regulate by.means of a hand-wheel the "reach" or length of radius of the arm. The scoop or bucket is fixed at the lover end of the arm, and is raised or lowered by the main chain passing over the ex- tremity °Ube jib. he whole of the movements are controlled by the "driver" and the "wheel- man." The driver raises the scoop while making its cut, swings it round into position for discharging. and. back again afterwards, and lowers it down. The wheelman regulates the 'depth of the cut, releases the scoop from the face of the bank, and opens the door or bottom for discharging its contents. Al- though apparently somewhat. complicated, the several movements of the navvy are each very simple. Three quarters of a minut3 is sufficient for scooping out from 1 to 24 tons of stuff, according to the capacity of the bucket, for dropping the stuff into the wagon, and for returning the Scoop into place ready for another cut. , After the machine has dug, out all within reach, the. jack-screws which steady it are eased; and the .propelling gear being put in action, it is moved for- wards three or four feet; the screws are then tightened down, and another series of cuts is com- menced. The cuts all radiate from the centre round which the • jib swings ; and they may to- gether 'form a hole nine or less resembling a crater, according to the plan adopted in making the exca- vation.

The engine is of the ordinary vertical type, with a cross-tube boiler carrying usually 801bs. pressure, and a pair of cylinders of 10. horse power nominal; it .runs up to 160 to 170 revolutions her minute under the control of a governor. On the crank shaft is keyed a pinion, gearing into a spur wheel four times its size on the main-drum *haft, from which all the other motion a are transmitted. The number of men required to do the work by hand that Is done by the navvy will vary'very much. For instance, in excavating 190 cubic yards per day the following men were necessary :—One ganger, ten gullet men, seventeen wingmen, two platelayers, one brakesman, two horses, and two drivers; or a total of thirty-three then and, two horaes. At the same rate to excavate by hand 600 yards per day, as the navvy does, ninety men would be required. The steam navvy may, Clete- fore, be considered equal to at least sixty or seventy men.

The navvy can also be worked for excavations under water, for which pUrposc they are mounted oil pontoons, which are about 50 feet longly 22 feet wide, and draw 2i .teet of water. When so used the machine delivers into a barge on one side of tho pontoon, a second empty barge being kept in readi- ness on the other side. As a. dredger the machine has not been extensively tried. For mud and sand it is hardly considered as a competitor of the dredgers in ordinary use; but where there is a very hard, bottom and a fair face to work at, it offers without doubt very considerable advantages.

div.head: TICE " AMERICAN" STEAM NAVVY.
div.p: TICE " AMERICAN" STEAM NAVVY.

Of the implements mid machines used. in the —cen- struction of the Manchester Ship Canal, 8.5 far as the work has proceeded, nothing hascaused greater and more widespread interest than the ysteam navvy, of which we give an illustration as it is seen in operation. The more common title is the "American steam navvy," because the Machine is claimed to be an American invention, and to have been first put to apractical test in that country, so renowned for its gigantic enterprises. There are not wanting those, holvever, who refuse to acknow- ledge this claim, and who assert that to England' belongs the credit of revolutionising the method of "nay vying." But to outsiders this question can be of little importance, and it may be dismissed with. the information that themachines employed by Mr. Walker are manufactured by Messrs. Ruston and Proctor, engineers, of Lincoln. A good idea ofthe appearance of the navvy may be "thered from the accompanying sketch; It will be seen that wbile it has much in cothmon with the ordinary steam crane, there are wide points of diver- gence, and the machinery is of a more complicated character. As in the crane, there is a boiler and'en- gine, a revolving roller, and a moveable arm or jib; but there the comparison ends. In the jib of the navvy there is a slot or opening, in which is placed a long arm that works up and down, upon what is technically known as a rack. To this ' arm is fild a huge bucket, in shape bearing mach esemblance to an ordinary coal scuttle. This bucket is supplied with four broad knives, or teeth, for cutting into the earth. The whole machine weighs about, 20 tons; and is fixed upon a solid frame with *heels. The " navvy" works best in a cutting 20 feet deep, although it has been employed in cuttings having a depth of 40 feet. When in use tips machine requirqs three men in direct attend- afice, namely, a fireman, an engine driver, and a wheelman ; while platelayers and other labourers to the number of nine are fully employed in the immediate- vicinity: The driver's position is no sinecure, as may be imagined, when he has besides attending to three levers with his hands, to work one with his foot. Supposing the bucket to be lowered to the level of the machine, the driver commences to draw it u? the face of the cutting. and the wheelman by means of a break over which he has control, sees that the teeth of the bucket press Mto)the earth with sufficient force. On either side of the machine waggons are standing on rail- way Metals, and immediately the bucket is filled it is swung round over a waggon by the jib, the wheel- man pulls a string, the bottom of the bucket drops, and out falls the earth. As the face of the cutting is worn away, of course the navvy has to be moved nearer, and this is easily accomplished, because the, mochine is upon railway metals and is self-propel- ling. Each time the bucket' scoops up the face of the cutting nearly two tons of earth *fall into its capacious mouth and it is estimated that in the course of an ordinary working day the navvy is capable of removing no less than 1,200 tons of clay. The bucket three times filled is suffi- cient to load a wagon such as is used in the Ship Canal works, and this can Naccomplished in some- thing under a minute and a half. We understand that on the entire lengih of the canal, from East- ham. to Manchester, no less. than 75 of these machines will be sat t 3 work.

The steam navvy, it maybe stated, excavates and delivers into wagons any material capable of being cut, such as sand, gravel, chalk, and clays of all kinds; digging out with equal facility the hardest and toughest, such as require blasting when worked by band. It can also deal with these materials when thickly , interspersed with stones and heavy boulders; and without being unduly strained it cuts through streams of flint, shale, slate, or even sandstone which may intersect the face of the ex- cavation it is at work upon. With the assistance of blasting, it is also used with advantage in much more difficult stuff,:such as hard Marl and has rock. Since its introduction many iniprovements have been made, increasing its power and efficiency. The framework has been considerably strengthened throughout, augmenting the total weight by severa? successive increments from 22 tons in the earliest machine to 32‘toits, which is now adopted as the standard. The scoop averages a capacity of about 25 per cent. larger than at first, and has an increased angular range. The duty has progressed in a greater ratio, nearly ok per cent. having been added to the original output. At first 180 to 190 wagon loads were considered a good day's work; now 240 to 250 are often obtained, and even more under very favourable conditions; the day consisting of ten hours, and the wagons being the size ordinarily used by contractors, holding three cubic yarns each, in which, however, the stuff is more solidly packed by the navvy than when they are loaded by hand. With extra large wagons: holding four cubic yards each, an equal number has been filled in a day, equivalent to the grand total of nearlyil,ooo cubic yards per day. The machine may be described generally as con- sisting of a strong rectangular wrought-iron frame mounted on wheels, forming a substantial base to which all the parts are secured. On the back end is placed O. engine, beside which the driver stands. At the front end rises a wrought-iron tower carry- ing the top pivot of a crane jib, the lower pivot resting on girders fixed to the main frame. The jib may be said to be of twin construction, being com- posed of two sides which are united only at the post

div.head: GERMAN STEAM NAVVY.
div.p: THE GERMAN STEAM NAVVY.

The German steam navvy that has just been erected near Bob's Bridge, about a mile distant from the village of Moore, is also a wonderful and ponder- but instead of having a oils piece of mechanism, vast • scoop like the "American," it ia worked, dredger fashion, with a series of buckets. It is, a great machiae adapted to further the carrying on of great undertakings. Thelaakers of this leviathan excavator are the r übeck Machine-Construction Company, of Lubeck, Ger- many, who make. a speciality of excavators and steam dredgers for sea and river work. These ex- cavators, in their present improved conditien, have become , almost • indispensable for the pur- puss of executing earth works, in ciattings and excavations on a large scale. The makers of the , machine claim that, in addition to the economy in using steam excavators in place of manual labour, it is a 4 important element to be considered that by such means work can be carried out with precision, independent of strikes epd other labour movements. They also claim that in this way tlie risk to contractors of having to paY large forfeits for the non-completion of works in a certain stipulated time would be obviated. The growing demands and necessity for increased speed , in the execution of large earth works also renders obligatory the, employment of the most improved steam machinery. By the use of these patent ex- , cavators as much as 2,600 cubic yards of light soil, or about 1.960 yards of tenacious ground, can be excavated per working day of ten hours. Tile ground near Bob's Bridge is of this latter 'descrip- tion, and it is estimated that the navvy there placed will excavate about 1,600 cubic yards per working day of ten hours. These machines are also used 'in coal-mining enterprises. In coal-mining, especially in open working in brown coal, the owner is under the old system obliged always to retain a number of the better class of workmen, even in slack times, in order to be preparde for a large output in case of a demand arising for it. The employer of labour in this respect also finds a way out of the inconvenience by the employment of excavators in openillg the ground and getting coal. The few men required to attend to the machinery are, if it is desirable to retain them on the works, found other .occupa- tions.

These dry ground dredgers, as they are very fittingly termed, are employed in many other works, i such as n cement manufacture, the extraction of gravel, sand, or other allied branches of industry. They are, of course, worked by steam, are self-pro- pelling, and are arranged to move on iron rails at a .4aiitable gauge. All the machines of this descrip- tion are constructed to work either in cuttings or excavations, but for each kind of work a special set of dredging buckets .is required. The machine at Bob's Bridge, is fitted for excavating below the level of the rails. Tile 'form and fittings of the buckets are modified in order to suit the scope of. a cutting. It might be thought that damage would- often result to the machinery by the contact of the buckets against boulders and other obstructions in the ground operated upon, but the mechanism con- tains the necessary safety appliances to meet such eventualities. The machine erectdd at Bob's Bridge has been laid on rails of heavy calibre, with broad footings. Inside these rails, and parallel with them, are laid the transport rails, on which the locomotives run that drag the trains of tip- waggons. The buckets, of which there is a chain of about two dozen, are made to run on a .Towerful rack depending from the top of the machine, and as each bucket strikes the ground and is filled with soil the machinery forces it up another rack and the soil is then tipped into the waggons, which run through a kind of shed that t orms the frame- work of the machine, the actual working portion of which is elevated. The apparatus fills the tip-wag- gons automatically, the rails upon which the ex- cavator woiks being so arranged that the deliver. Shute of the apparatus lies over of the centre of the transport rails. '

When the machine is at,work, an empty train of ballast waggons is brought by the locomotive be- neath the apparatus and remains stationary. The excavator, beginning at one end of the train, is made to slowly advance, tearing up the soil as it does so, and, as the contents of the, buckets are • ,

1 discharged by the delivery shute into the waggons, one after another of them becomes filled, until the whole train is fully loaded.: The locomotive then 1 puffs off with the excavated material to wherever it has to be disposed of, and another locomotive brings up another train of empty waggons, which in their turn are filled. Thus the digging progresses with a rapidity Ulla is scarcely conceivable without absolute ocular demonstration. So methodical is the working of this stupendous navvy; that; owing to the construction of the filling Antes, no material ,can be spilt between two waggons. Also, what is equally surprising, the forward movement of the excavator is so regulated that each 'waggon is equally filled. As no moving of the train is required during loading, the lqcomotive can, while that operation. is going, on, be employed in • removing another train. A train of thirty waggons, of a capacity of three cubic yards each, can be filled in about thirty minutes, and if the distance to be hauled is %correspondingly short, one locomotive will suffice for the work. The machine requires the services of three men. One is the foreman, who mtmages the reversing lever; the second is the stoker, whose business is to attend to the boiler and the steam engine; and the third is engaged at ' the loading shute. In' addition to these three, from ten to fourteen labouring men are required for laying rails, procuring water, fuel, &c., and doing ' other necessary lobs. ' For a full wor cing day the coo. consumed amoimts to from 16 to 20 cwts., and the consumption of water ranges from 1,320 to 1,760 gallons per day of ten wotking flours. The machine is made of iron and steel,‘ and is so constructed thatall movements, excepting the turning of the filling shute, are effdcted by the steam engine. All the motions have similar gear, and ate .put in and out of work by' frictional "clutches." The power necessary for keeping: in motion the chain of buckets that dig up the soil is transferred by a hydraulic frictional "clutch," which acts with great precision, and the forward movement of the apparatus, as well as the lifting and ,lowering of the bucket frame, are effected by ordinary frictional clutches. The regula- ting levers of all the movements are brought to one point, and managed by one man. the foreman usually taking that duty upon himself. The steam 1 engine works with expansion and high steam pres- sure, and the boiler, a horizontal tubular one, is so placed that it forms an effective counterpiece to the working bucket chain. The wear dnd tear of II the working parts is nearly exclusively confined to the pitch chain, its rollers, arid the, ". polyons," which come into direct contact with gle excavated material, and these parts are, as fa' as possible, • made of castisteel and case-hardened iron—materials capable of resisting tear and wear in the highest degree. Thus the cost of wear, and the expense of repairs, are compatrativelf small considering the vast amount of work performed. These parts are also arranged so that they cdn easily be renewed. The digging buckets are made of sheet. steel, and are solidly riveted to the steel chain links. Each bucket has a capacity of 0-3 cubic yards. The axles and whee' tires are of steel, and are mounted on springs. The bucket frame is elastically bedded and supported, in order to prevent breakage and de- rangement of the working parts The excavator itself is surrounded by a sheet-iron casing in order to protect the wen. It may be further mentioned that, if foundneces- sary; these excavators can be worked night and day 'Without cessation,large paraffin torches being found sufficient to allow the men to•wcrk correctly by night. 'This has been done, amongst other places, in Brenxen, the whole work -having the character of a nightly railway working. During the .year 1884 a ,similar apparatus was used fur deepening the bed of the river Weser. It cut the new river profile ton dePth of 14 feet under the upper rail in one cut. Other machines of this type in modified form are at present in use in Hamburg, on the works for an enlargement of the Custom Rouse, and they are dredging at,a dept h of 16 feet.
I. FROM EASTRAM TO ELLESMERE PORT,
By LOOKER O.

The various plant Which has been continually arriving at Hooton Station, on the Birkenhead and Chester lines of railway, is being rapidly removed to Eastham. On Sunday ;evening a ' very large number of , workmen 'arrived at Hooton Station for the purpose of removing a powerful locomotive—the Monmouth—by it own Steam P• n ower. I order to Accomplish this limes of rlails were laid on the main road leading from Hooton Station to .Eastbani, a distance of 'about three miles, and the time it took to accomplish this was from Sunday mid-night to Wednesday morning. Large numbers of people assembled to witness the operation. , - On Thursday morning, another locomotiVe, called the Barton, was removed on a low heavy lurry by over 20 horses in about two hours, from the same place to East- him Ferry. and another in the afternoon called the Wes- ton. The Monmouth is now at work removing soil and clay in the waggons filled by one of the steam navvies. Eastham is now quite a hive of industry and the change which has taken place within the last few months is ex- tiaordinary. Near the Ferry, where the Ship Canal en- ters the estuary, a number of workmen's •cottages are erected, each containing two apartments below and above, with other places of convenience for food, fuel.: I go. There are also smiths', fitters', and joiners' shops erected, and an engine shed to hold about a dozen engines. The following locomotives are at work here, or being got ready :—The Helsby, Sutton, Barry, Hooton, Stanlow,' Eastham, Wigan, Lytham, Ellesmere, Barton, Mon. mouth, and Weston. Signal posts are put up, and lines of rails intersect each other in almost all directions. There are likewise at Work four steam navvies, which are making large and deep cuttings. The earth is taken away to form the large and wide embankment'which is required along the shore. There the groat ddcks are to be made as a refuge for the large vessels and Smaller craft which will be constantly passing up and down the canal. There are now nearly: 1,000 men employed on this section, and for their spiritual and intellectual welfare Mr. Walker, who is a strong adherent to Wesleyan Methodism, has had erected a mission-room capable of holding about 500 persons. Mr. Oak-es is the missiottry for this section, and a house, which is called by the men The .Vicarage, is being erected for him. On Sunday last over 100 of the men received his instruction. About half a mile from Eastham, on the centre line of the canal, we come through what a few months ago wai a beautiful wood skirting the shore. The scenery will now be wholly changed, for the canal goes right through it. Groups of men were to be seen enjoying their mid- day meal around fires made from underwood and branches of the oaks and other trees. A mile from East- ham the line of the canal will ,skirt the sore of the estuary and a very strong embankinent is to b,e put up as, a protection. At present there is only a temporary line of rails • and during the storm last week the ballast • was washedaway. Thi defect is now being remedied. Along this shore there are placed two water tanks that a good supply of,water can be obtained for the engines and other purposes from the high land above. . Three miles from EaStham we come, to Pool Hall mouth, where a stream of water comes from the upland. It has been bridged over, and a line of rails laid to two more steam navvies which are at work. Various sheds are being put up, and some 300 men, are at work. At Ellesmere Port the canal will run by the river for two Or three miles, and then cut through Stanlow point After crossing this strip of land it will traverse the side , , of the river for nearly two, miles, coming inland again at Ince, and crossing Frodsham marshes near to the river Mersey.' Preparations are being made both at Ellesinerel , Port and Ince for getting to work. A large number of I tip wagons, portable esiginesi arc, have arnved at Elles-
f:

• mere Port. Cottages here have been converted int(/' shops, and eiteer fresh public-houses are being opened or old ones made larger: At Ince, too a locomotive called the Grange, two portable engines, steam navvy, dredges, and other materials have arrived. It is under- stood that a: commencement will be made immedi- ately.

THE WATER FOR THE CANAL. The 'Pall Mall Gazette" says :--The sanitary condl. tion of the Irwell\ and Mershy and their tributaries is such that unless very extensive measures are adopted the Manchester Ship Canal when it is dug out will be little better than a huge sewer, and the proposed docke in Matcchester and Salford something akin to cesspools. This question of the water supply promises to be-one of tho most serious problems which the promoters of the Canal have to face. Apart from the sufficiency of the supply in the dry season, as to which grave doubts have been raised, the condition 'of the streams is ..such that navigation would be impossible unless radically im-• proved: Our authority is no less a person than the chair. mill of the company. ,At a conference held at Man- chester last week Lora Egerton said it was quite clear that there could be no successful navigation if the watc was constantly clogged up and impaired by the filth a. sewage which was. constantly thrown into it. It was necessary lib the success of the Ship Canal that the different local authorities should endeavour to carry out some distinct sewage plan, which would rssult in the waters, soon to be impounded in docks on the canal, being as pure as the necessities of the case re- quired, and such as wouldnot damage the health or give annoyance to the population residing near the decks- or the canal. Alderman Walmsley, of Salford, repeated a promise he had previously giirou to the directors of Ake canal, "that if they impounded water in their docks in the filthy, disgusting, and insanitary condition that it was in as it came down now, the Rivers Pollution Act of 1876 should be put in fore % against them as ruthlessly as against anybody else.," These are the existing condi- tions, and in view of the notoriously slow pace at which local authorithes move, the number of boards and manil- lacturers concerned, and the enormous outlay which drainage schemes entail, the directors are %affronted by -almost insuperable obstacles, apart from the en- gineering and financial difficulties of a project which will involve the expenditure of somewhere about ten inillionS sterling.

.. . . li/XTON. The steam navvy was set to, work on Monday and the engine named Irlam is very busy taking away the wagers to the tip. At present the face of the cutting is not very deep. The huge sceS flits the wagons at three lifts. Great work is expect from the navvy. As the cutting gets deeper water is encountered; 'but it is merely from drains on the land. Arrangements are Made to convey the Water into the river, so that it will prove no obstacle 'to fhe work. " On Sunday a large body of workinen, under the superintendence of Inspector Bradbury and Inspector Bate, of the Cheshire Lines Permanent Way Department, were engaged in coupling the Ship Canal CompanVs line to the east of Nam Station.- The work consisted in placing a pair of points on the down ' line, and a cross-over road. A_ cabin has been erected. The lines will, be controlled from the station box by the patent locking of the points, when other traffic is on the line.

THE FLOODING OF DUTTON-STREET, • WARRDIGTON. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Tuesda' morning, before Major Litton and Mr. R. Garnett', a case was heard in which Edward Jeffries, bricklayers labourer, .27. Dutton-street, claimed from the Corporation of Warrington, as the Urban Sanitary Authority, the sum of £5, as " eomperisa- donor damages for the flooding and spoliation of his house and property, 27, Dutton-street, Warring- ton, ind for the negligence or omission of the defen- dants under the Public Health Act, 1875." The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Wharton, barrister, instructed by Mr. II J. Longton, solicitor; and Mr. J. L. Whittle, deputy town clerk, appeared for the Cot- poration.---In opening the case for the plaintiff Mr. Wharton said that Dutton-street was off Mersey-street, and for some time the'' Corporation had allowed the water to come tip from the sewers and flood the whole of Dutton-street. The water flowed over the footpath into the houses, where it lay several inches deep, Washing the furniture about, and causing general inconvenience. It might be sugg'e.sted for the defendants that the flood was llirough the act of God, but he had to tell them that the act of God was not in law a fact which occurred every year. An unprecedented event, or one which happened\ only occasionally, was not presumed to be anticipated by a local authority, and therefore such authority could not provide • for it. They'. could not provide for an unprecedented storm, which no one expected, and which might not occur again, and it was not the duty of a Corporation to provide sewers ta carry away the water of an unprecedented storm. But if he could show that year after year the poor people in Dutton-street had been flooded out whenever there bad been anything like a heavy shower, he had no hesitation in coming to the conclusion that there must be a def on the part of the sewers in being 'unable to carry off water. If the evidence that he should call was correah it was unquestionable that there had been the graiiiiit negligence on the part of the Corporation. The storm ha regard to which the claim was made occurred on the 601 of September, 1887, when the whole of Dutton-street wail flooded. The furniture in plaintiff's house was washed about, 'his oilcloth floated on the top of the water, tbe sofa bedding was saturated, and a stench that was left in the house had caused illness to his family. In cense. quence the plaintiff asked for £5 as compensation. —The plaintiff, on being called, stated that on the 6th of last September there waa a heavy fall of raie, in conse- quence of which his house NVIS flooded. ' The water would flood his house at any time after 23 minutes' haid rain. The part of the street in which he lived had been flooded once or twice every summer. On cleaning the hbuse after the flood, material from the sewer was found ' in it. In answer to Mr. Whittle plaintiff denied that the flood from the river ever reached "Dutton-street. —Mrs Jeffries, wife of the plaintiff, gave corroborative eviaence and on this, although' he said, he had six more witnesses, Mr. Wharton rested* his case.—Addressing the Bench for the defence Mr. Whittle called attention to the sec- tion under which the claim was made which, he sqid• provided that if any person sustained damage and wag I not himself in fault; he was entitled to compensation. Bearing in mind the words "if he is not he fault" ha should call attention to the facts. The town was a low- lying one, in the valley of the Mersey, and the Corpora- tion . were not ,responsible for its position. The main sewerthroughMersey-st. was laid at the best possible gra- dient, as was also the sewer in Dutton-street. That street was actually the lowest part of, the toivii, and the plaintiff's houee -was the lowest in that particular street. if a person chose to build houses on such a level that hig ProPerty was likely be be flooded, he himself was at fault' and must take the consequences. The houses were built before the sewer was made, and before the street was a street. The owner of the property was himself in default for so constructing his pro- perty. The action was a test, one, and if it was decided against the Corporation it would mean that whenever there was a flood every tenant would come with k claim for compensation. This wee, • therefore, a serious matter to the Corporation. The sewer in Dutton-street was of a sufficient capacity to carry fifty times the usual flow of sewage, and the main sewer in Mersey-street was Capable of taking at least, twenty-four times as much sewage as usually went , through it. On the particular day in question the rain - Jail was the 'heaviest that there had been for several years, and he submitted that what had occurred wag through the act of God. He thought that Mr. +Wharton had failed to prove any negligence on the part of the Corporation. Mr.-Whittle then called witnesses in sup- liort of his defence, the evidence given by them being, of a technical chametet.—William Wood, an employe of the Corporation, and Walter Tracers,oe o the ie extraordinary i assistantin the Borough Surveyor's office, s rainfall on the 6th of last September,:and Mr. Longdin, the Borough Surveyor, deposed that the sewer was of sufficient capabilities for all practical purposes, The Corporation were not called upon to provide for abnor- mal rainfalls. Mr. William Owen, Surveyor to the Rural Sanitary Authority, gave it as his opinion that the sewer was properly. constructed, and was sufficient for any ordinary purpose.—Major Litton said that the Bench thought that there was not, the slightest grounde for an action, because the extraordinary fall of rain in so short a time fully accounted for the flooding. Again, the property was in such a low-lying part ,of the town that it had been proved to be almost impossible to get a fall to drain it. There would therefore be a verdict for the Corporation.—Mr. Whittle said that the 'action- wag ,really brought on behalf of a number of tenants, and should have been instituted by the owner of the property. Re must therefore ask for the costs.—Mr. Wharton said that the action was brought by the man himself.—The inagistriks decided to allow costi—five guineas.

Dear Fred,—YOUetfl he surprised at receiving a 'letter from me, but, thank God, I am pleased to say I am getting better every day. I shall be so glad to • breathe the fresh air again. It has seemed a dreadful long time to be in bed. You know I was' taken to the hospital last April to be treated for Bright's Disease of the kidneys. Well, on July 31 they tapped me, and took away 304 ounces of water. The same thing was done again on September 18, and 408 °nacos of water obtained. On Oct. 9 I was discharged from the hos- pital as incurable. In January this year (the 20th) was again tapped at home, and 360 ounoes of water taken away.' TT:e St. Bartholomew's Hospital in London refused me admission as a hopeless case, and fhb St. Bartholomew's Hospital,. Chatham, also refused me, as being the worst case they had seen for years, and two local doctors gave me up as hopeless. 'When I came from the hospital it took three to put me to bed. My -clothes had to be cut off. I was an object of misery and despair. After the hospitals had refused me, and doctors given me up, my wife persuaded me to try HOP BITTERS, and from the commencement have Improved daily. I have only taken them seven weeks, , . and can now get downstairs and walk about without ..even a stick. With the aid of a few more bottles of the Bitters shall be well again. The water has left my body and legs. The only• trace left is in my feet. It is a wonderful medicine. A wish I had tried it sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with -doctors' bills and other expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the hospital I had no appetite whatever, but since using the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The only difficulty is the expense, but must not mind that so long as I am getting well. ,Am -oheerful now that recovery is near, for every one Asad given me up as a had (ob.—With best wishes to—,
" Your affectionate brother, •
