div.head: PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY HUGH BETTE.
div.p: PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY HUGH BETTE.

• lII.—THIRD CLASS. The thing lies here as the man said when he burial his dog, does it pay a man to take a third class railway ticket, and be jostled about like a second-hand carpet- bag, in exchange for a peep at human nature, when he has cash enough to afford to take a first, with the result of falling into a species ef luxuriant dumps? I cer- tainly don't feel equal to settling this point myself. If a fourth class existed, I should perhaps strike a sudden base line of argument in favour of the fourth, so I cautionthe reader against accepting my opinions for more than they are worth. There are two classes of people about which we don't need to ask the question. There Is the man who goes out " smushed up" to a country party, and who might find himself sitting next to a sweep; and there is the man who makes the journey from here to Preston with steel bracelets on. If we could get the question debated pn the Market ground we might come to a wise solution. My own opinibn is thatiit depends a good deal on the good temper and nerve-pdwer of the "taker." For a start, is he prepared to stand before a third class ticket window and say, "One to Manchester, please," and hear howled at him double-fortissimo while he is picking up his change, "Now, look alive! Are you going to stand there all day ?" And, secondly, when he gets on the platforint and asks what time his train starts, to be answered "1.1 55," in a voice thokt sounds as if it had been shortened by one-half in the last railway accident? By the way, you should pass a short time before the first class booking window, and you will hear as much politeness in half an hour as would grease a dude's hair for a Month. If you ask rae if there is any "hurry up" at that 'window, you will see one of the hnest double-barrelled smiles that ever gladdened a traveller's heart. Don't get it into your head that I am blaming the man who stands thumping that stamping machine till his arm is ready to drop off; or the one who walks ever more flags in a daY than two postmen. Not a bit of it. When a man comes up to an official and asks him "What time is that nest train to Darren?" and the official replies "U 45," and the further question is put, with a look of utter amazement, "Is ther nooan afore tha d?" it is no wonder that the this-way-for-Chorley- and-Wigan (noun, third person, singular number, super- natural gender) gets his back up. I should. IWould say to that man—but never mind, the Editor doesn't allow any abusive language in these columns. Good, temper and nerve are very good things, no doubt, but they are not always to be relied upon any more than patent hair restorers or Spring chickens. There is not one man in a hundred who hasn't a fiendish desire to fight when a heavy box is dropped on Nis toe, and it is generally the good-tempered man who has to stand up in the carriage . through helping every- body else in. To get into a third-class railway' carriage you want to deceive yourself for a few seconds; you want to possess yourself of the sole idea that you are escaping from a blazing theatre, and that there is only that one narrow door between you and liberty. It is desirable, however, that you gat nod of this idea immediately you get in, or you might sit on a lady's bandbox, and have to cower under a pair of flashing eyes the rest of the journey. But there is another reason why you should be col- lected. If you want any of thatingredient known in this part of Lancashire as "gam," you are in the right place for it. As soon as the train begins to move, it seems to shake down some of those stiff partitions dividitig the reserved and the communicative sections of people, and they talk family affairs that they wouldn't talk anywhere else. • There is the labouring man absorbed in the interesting work of cutting up twist tobacco, and stuffing it into a black clay pipe. He doesn't smoke now, as ho is fixed under the eagle eye of a man in the far corner who "objects to smoking," and it is not a smoking compart- ment. Under such depressing conditions you couldn't expect the labouring man to come out of his shell in the talking line, especially as he gets out at the next station. There is no rule, however, against chewing, so he puts a big piece of the black roll in his mouth, right under the gaze of the eagle eye. Ugh! Then there is the young man Who tries to make you I believe that he is a nobleman in disguise; he doesn't say so. Not he; he wouldn't speak to you on any account. He is stiff-backed, stiff-necked, and starchy. lie seems to travel third-class as akind of philanthropist, simply to benefit you with his presence. He would sooner Elie than smile at any of the loose third-class jokes. There is nearly certain to be a woman with a baby. I don't know whether you ever noticed it or not, but wherever you go the woman with a baby is there. Is it because there is such an enormous number of women with babies, or simply that if anything of importance is going on women with babies will be there? Just notice the two that travel under one ticket—two hearts that beat as one to the company—and perhaps you will think tlAe womantolds the baby up, and turns it in different pdsitions, for the•purpose of attracting the attention of people. Upon inquiry you will find that the operation is only to keep the baby from having cramp in its legs. Then you have the individual known as " th' owd Lancashire lad." To hear this man talk you would think he never had a secret in his life. He is always ready with a story, and, his humour is very quaint. You should watch his actions as well as his words if you would have a real treat. For example, he assumes a look of sweet innocence, and asks the stiff-necked young man "if his fayther's working," and then closes one eye to the other side of the compartment with the utmost unconcern; then he stares vacantly at the lamp above him till the colour has subsided in the young man's cheeks. There is the man who reads the newspaper; he is' there to a dead certainty. He takes no interest in any- thing but, his paper, except when there is a peal of laughter, when he looks up and seems aggravated at missing the joke. ThQn you have the man who goes to sleep, and growls when he is awakened at his destination. There is the woman who always catches cold in," these beastly car- riages," no matter what weather, and who doesn't forget to tell you so. I spoke of the man with the eagle eye. This is he who nips smokers in the bud. He looks to the windows being shut, threatens the porters that he will write to , the managers, &c. Then there is the man who comes in drunk, and wants to shake hands all round; or perhaps he wants to sing, and after slurring over a few notes, the train stops, and pitches him into your arms. Now you have the interesting ceremony of examining tickets, graduated according to price, In the first class cordpartment the collector says, touching his hat, "Tickets ready, please," in a voice like a murmuring brsok. The second class he addresses with, "Tickets, please," as if it was his duty to be polite, but there had better be no fooling around him. The door of the 3rd ctass opens as if by a hurricane, and you would imagine the man had the toothache, viten he says, "All tickets

r ady." , There is more bustle and anxiety displayed in half a minute over this ticket job, than you will see at your business in a fortnight. Our friend the drunkard has lost his ticket, perhaps' at this critical time, and has to be bullied a long while before he ultimately finds it in his boots, The collector is down on the man who loses his ticket more than any other. He not only suspects him of perjury, but of the more grave offence of thinking him (the collector) a greenhorn. "Once upon a time" the members of a famous Blackburn brass band were coming home by rail, and the big drummer (no doubt because his mouth had been more at liberty during the day than the mouths of his fellows) had attained that pitch of human felicity known as being boozed. When the ticket collector came into his compartment the man of music declared, after feeling in all his pockets, that he had lost his ticket. "Lost your ticket," said the collector, "come man, you can't have lost your ticket." "Can't have lost my ticket, can't I," hiccupped the &tun pounder, "why, I've lost th' big drum." These " characters " don't often appear in the first- class carriage, where there is ordinarily about as much liveliness as in a mourning coach. Perhaps it is owing to the rsental elevation of the occupants, and only our vitiated tastes that lead us to prefer travelling third when it is not a question of s. d.

THE MAYOR AND THE PUGILISTS. " Sir.—May I, through your columns, ask His Worship the Mayor of Warrington if kis considers it consi,stent with the dignity of hishigh office, and of the town, to act as patron of a pugilistic entertainment, or boxing show, even though the first night receipts are to be devoted to that excellent institution, the Warrington Infirmary ? Yours, Sze., Warrington, Fderuary 1, 1888.
ANTI-PUGILIST.

THE CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. Sir,—l have often wondered how the Co-operative Society could pay such large dividends, but I have at last found out the secret. If shopkeepers got such large profits as they, many of them would soon be indepen- dent. Instead of the society being a benefit to tbe working-man, as we have been led to believe, it is quite the contrary. If people would only compare the prices and quality of the goods with those offered by other tradespeople, they would find that instead of having been benefitted by the society they were considerably the losers.-1 remain, yours very respectfully, LOOKER ON. Warrington, February 3rd, 1888.

, SHAM CHRISTIANITY. Sir,—There are a good many comedies played on the stage of this world, if we would only take the trouble to look at them. England prides herself upon being a Christian nation, and when some successful trader, who has.made his fortune, and perhaps after years of fraudu- lent dealings turns pious, he generally speaks of the Bible as the great secret of our commercial supremacy. The outwardprofassion of Christianity has become a busi- ness, and has produced hosts of professional theologians and sectaries, who rival each other in the production of forms of ritual and worship until an exgess in someshape or other is made which calls for the exercise of the powers of law and legislation. We are overdone ;with profes- sional pietists, who mistake a loud and noisy assertion of their views for pure religion. But of real religion we have too little; and if the great Founder were to come to seek the temple here, the operation of expelling the • money changers, and the buyers and sellers of Church benefices, would have to be repeated. Of the practical infidelity which hides itself under the garb of professional pietism, we have already had more than enough. The " Ten Commandments" are made only to apply to the offences of the poor. The world of out. great cities has, as it were,told off theclerg,y as a body of spiritualpolice con- stables, to help to keep the poor in order, to teach them to "submit-themselves to the powers that, be," kind "to walk humbly before their betters,'? i.e., themselves, the squire, and the landlord. The Church has accepted this humble commission for a consideration, and that con- sideration is to be found in the property of the Church, and in the hope of advancement. The result is that the Established Church has become, in a great measure, the tool of the opulent classes. Therefore the clergy—for the most part—whenever they touch upon social matters, instead of preaching, equality and brotherhood as pro- claimed by the Divine Founder, take an altogether op- posite course. Sitle by side with this sham profession of Christianity,we see the practice of a state of things more in accord with heathenism' than with Christianity. The great god of Mammon is enthroned on the highest pedes- tal, aud all men fall down and worship—or rather, the devotees of Mammon tread down each other in their haste to get to his shrine. Some men get there after having suffocated colliers in their coal pits, and others after having drowned sailors at sea, whilst- some rejoice that they have devoured widows houses and caused orphans to starve. The Church does not dare—with now and then a rare exception—to lift its voice against this state of thin*, yet this poor effete representation of Christianity is sup- posed by some men to be suitable for exportation to Africa, to the distant regions of British commerce ; and with it all vile practices known to commerce will follow. We send the Bible and missionaria4 to the heathen, and our commerce sends "fire water" and rifles, and idols from Birmingham, whilst no doubt the exporters of these commodities for the most part subscribe towards the British and Foreign Missionary Societies! Appeals are continually addressed to the Christian people of the coun- try to subscribe their money to these societies, as if we had no heathens at home, no misery in our streets, no ignorance to be removed, and fio humanity to be relieved. Thousands of pounds gte asked for and given to send educated gentlemen, with salaries, out to distant climes, all of whom could find exactly the same employment at home. Let us reflect that it is by the action of Christian legis- lators and magistrates, so called, the the people of Eng- land have acquired the character of being the most drunken nation in Europe. We talk of sending the gospel to Africa, but we send licenses into all our streets and villages, giving permission to trade, and make a for- tune if they can, by tempting people to drink. Nor is this all; when the secrets of trade are revealed we hear of adulteration practised, as a rule, in every department. The ruling'classes organise by law a vast system of temp- tation, and then furn round and blame the people who fall under the temptation. The great brewer makes his fortune, and perhaps builds a church or two, and such an act is accounted to him as a good deed, for which he is to find his reward hereafter. But no one thinks of th • means by which the brewer's vast fortune was acq ; In order to acquire this fortune hundreds have been in- directly slain; thousands of home S have been broken up, and the inmates for the most part become a burthen on the rates, or perhaps join the motley army of crimi- nals who exist in the streets of our large towns. But no matter; for "He hath built us a temple." Then again, we profess great solicitude concerning the spiritual condition of the half naked tribes of Africa, yet on the slightest excuse we send the Gatling olin and the Martini rifle to dispatch the poor heathens beir hundreds to "the great beyond," and our clergy w ill offer up 'pedal supplications—as in our last war with the Zulus —for the success of our arms! If the heathen takes up the gospel which we give him with one hand, whilst we have the sword in the other, he sees written within its pages "Blessed are the peacemakers." Our missionaries may well be discouraged at the slow progress they make in their efforts iti Christianizing the heathen.—l am, sir, yours, Sze., PLEBEIAN.

div.p: TILE lIANCHtSTER SHIP CANAL.
LATCHFORD.

It is expected that operations will be begun at Latchford shortly, the cricket ground haying al- ready been taken possession of, and the line of the canal marked by turning up the earth. The siding from Latchford Station to the Old Quay Canal is kept going. Large quntities of material and Ma- chinery are constantly arriving, to be despatched by water to various sections. THELWALL, &c, During this week the work of constructing the canal has been commenced in a very vigorous fashion at Tlulwall. From a point a little to the. east of Morris Brook farmhouse to the bank of the Mersey north of Thelwall village, the whole length of the canal has been invaded by navvies, there being yesterday something like 200 men en- gaged. So far, the work has been mainly of a pre- liminary nature—the cLitting down of hedges, and the removal of the surface flyer of the earth. For the most part the land on this section has been ploughed, and a large part of the soft upper por- tion of the soli has already been removed. Large piles of timber are being accumulated at various points along the line, and, in fact, there is every indication that it is intended to prosecute the work with energy. Behind Thel•ffall, as we mentioned, active operations end at Me bank of the Mersey, but there are signs that it is intended ' to begin on the other side of the river, as barrows and other plant have been deposited ix considerable quantities on the Lancashire side. In the direction of Lymm and Hollins Green work is being rapidly pushed on, a steam navvy having been got to work, rails having lapen laid, and various other additional apparatus having been got together. RUNCORN. Though somewhat impeded by the unfavourable character of the weather, the work on the Runcorn and Moore section has steadily progressed during the week, and the scene becomes more active as each day passes. In addition to the German navvy near Bob's Bridge there are three "American" nav- vies on the ground, besides steam cranes, locomo- tives, and trains of tip waggons. At a point, nearer Runcorn, the woodwork of a large viaduct crossing the canal has been erected, and already it begins to have an imposing appearance. Navvies are at work in all directions, and at a spot about a mile distant from the quay at Runcorn, three or four large wood warehouses, aswell as several smaller buildings, to be used as offices, have • been erected in readiness for the time when the operations are more advanced. Rails, planks, and other materials continue to ar- rive. CADIS READ. Operations in connection with the Ship Canal works at Irlam and Cadishead have been com- menced in Butcher's Field, situate on the north- west side of Warburton Bridge. The Irlam and Cadishead section extends about 4i miles, and about 170 men are now engaged on the various works.. The offices, stores, engine sheds, and.navvies' huts are being erected at a point known as Skeer-rock, where it is said the deepest cutting of the canal will be made, being no less than 70 feet in depth. On Thursday morning, Mr. T. A. Walker, contractor, paid a visit to the works. It is stated that the Canal Company are making satisfactory progress with the owners for the acquirement of land at Eecles and Barton.

-6 CHESHIRE v. NORTHUMBERLAND. This annual fixture was brought off on Saturday, at Jesmond, Newcastle. The Cheshire team left Liverpoor on Friday night at five o'clock, arriving at Newcastle at 11-30 p.m., after a tedious journey,, where they found some few inches of snow, fol 4 lowed by a keen frost. On Saturday an official examination was made of the ground, and some diversity of opinion existed as to the advisability of playing under the circum-tances, a few inches of snow covering the hard ground. It was, however, decided to play the match. It was 3-15 when the teams appeared, Cheshire being represented by .1 Tomlinson (Sale), back; T H Davies. H C Speakman, and W H Cawley (Runcorn), three-quarter backs; II Hughes, captain (Runcorn), S M Holden (Birkenhead Park), half backs; W Hughes, W Faulkner, J Clarke, G T Wainwright (Runcorn). A G Wood, J Cowan, P H Lockwood (Birkenhead Park), T Lings (Sale), and J H Giffard (New Brighton), forwards. Northum- berland—H Haslam (North Elswick), back; B Sutherland and T Coulson (Percy Park), and Rev A S Carr (Northumberland), three-quarters; T Hoyle (Northern) and H Douglas (Percy Park), half bachs; T Elliott (Tynedale), j Livingstone (Percy Park), F Manford and H Angus (Northern), T Gee and A Gee (Percy Park), C W Harrison (Tynedalel, J W Groenwell (Tynemouth), arwl G Mole (North Els- wick), forwards. W. Cail, umpire; C. H. Sample, referee. Cheshire lost.the toss, and W. Hughes kicked off up hill, and against a sharp cutting wind, to which Carr replied, when a series of very smart exchanges were effected by Speakman. Davies, and Cawley, who ran and kicked into the north quarter, Ches- hire forwards forcing their way nearer the line, 'Lee and Haslam got the ball awity, but only mo- mentarily, as&eakman saved and IL Hughes ran across the ground, and throwing •to Davies, who sprinted off, and' kicking on, but Haslam was smart with his return, and Speakman came along the cen- tre, but Carr was safe,!collaring being his forte. From the scrimmage, which Cheshire easily carried, some passing ensued. Davies snapped up the ball, a g plendid pick up, and dashed off along touch, and, thinking he was across the line, grounded, but a deep rut had deceived him (thanks to the snow). and Carr immediately touched down. Shotton dropped out, Tomlinson being slow, got his kick charged, but Speakman, being handy, saved cleverly. Following upon the drop out, Clarke, Lings, and Holden took on the ball; Cheshire backs got on

passing, Davies being checked in a good atteinpt to score. Sutherland relieved the pressure, getting the ball to the quarter flag, from which A. G. Wood came from the scrimmage with the ball, dribbled on to Haslam, who picked up the ball from Woods' feet, and checked the movement. From here the North men came on into the Cheshire half, Lings saving. Coulson then clairded a mark in front of the Cheshire goal. Gee took the place. but failed, greatly to the relief of Cheshire. W. ,Hughes and Lockwood got the ball away. Holden getting on a bit further, when the whistle announced change of ends. At the commencement of the second half' the wind moderated. Gee restarted, and Davies, who tried to get off, was brought down by Manford. Faulkner and Lings came on from the pack, being quickly joined by their colleagues, and for a time the Northumberland backs had a warm time of it, Davies running grandly and forcing Haslam to save. Speakman following suit, struggled near the line, Carr and Sutherland having to check Hughes, who immediately after dropped at goal—a near thing, the ball just falling short of its mark. During this fast raid on the Northumberland goal, Carr and Has- lam shone at the defence. Speakman herosfliouts had a good chance to drop outAint he hesitated, and Carr and Haslam brought him dßwn under the posts. The bome•forwards got tho ball out of danger to centre from which Wainwright sprinted back, Douglass and Sutherland stopping the movement. Cawley now had very little if any work to do, shot at goal, a dead ball only resulting. Following the drop out. Douglass pulsed to Sutherland, the only i pass n the game for the North team. This attempt lost them ground, as Holdden gave Davies the ball,. the latter getting to the home quarters. W. Hughes and Wood getting nearer the line, Baskin got clear of his charge when a general rush back of the Che- shire forwards, Wainwright, Faulkner, and Lings being joined by Giffard, who unfortunately knocked on, a grand opportunity for scoring being lost. Che- shire still pressed hard, but the defence was equally fine. In the last minute of the game, Gee got i.way clear, but Tomlinson kept cool, and brought him down on the line. No side being then announced, the game ending in a draw—Cheshire, 3 minors; , Northumberland, I. - On the Cheshire side, Tomlinson, of Sale, appeared for the first time in the county team, and did fairly well. Speakman played well in taking the passes and running well. Davies was in excellent form. running and kicking smartly. Cawley had very little work to do, but what came in his way he did well, getting in his kicks very timely. Hughes and Holden were fairly in the thick of the struggle, Hughes' drop nearly winning. In the forward ranks Clarke and Wainwright appeared for the first time, and right well they played, assisting in sus- taining the packs against their heavy opponents. Hughes, Wood, Lings, Faulkner, and Lockwood were in excellent form, their dribbling and collaring be- ing of the highest order. The state of the ground ' spoiled the play. On the Northumberland side Has- lam, the back, played a fine game. Carr and Suther- land were the only other backs who were prominent. Forward, flaslam, Gee, Harrison, and Manifold were , best of a sturdy lot. OLD QUAY (RUNCORN) Ir. WIDNES ALKALL—OR Thursday afternoon a football match was played on the ground of the Runcorn club, in aid of the fund for providing a treat to the aged persons of the town. There was a good attendance of spectators, and the match was between the Old Quay Works and the Widnes.alkali Work teams. The following composed the home team :—Back, IJ. Brazendale ; three-quarter backs, W. 11, Cawley, T. H. Davies. and G. T. Wainwright; half backs, W: Moores and J. Gayter; forwards, J. Gatley (captain). W. Stubbs, W. H. Broady, T. Cox, G. Page,- J. Hoffland, W. Cox, T. Dugdale, and A. Hampson. The Widnes team were—Back, T. Wailing; three-quarter backs, E. Farrell (captain), H. C. Speakman and M. Ryan; half-backs, J. Donough and E. Beesley; forwards, T: Hughes, J. Gandy, E. Gordon, TIP Gregory. T. Davenport, W. Wright, R. Roberts, R. Carroll. and J. Trumbleton. The game was very evenly contested throu,hout, but the state of the ground was against a good exhibition of football. The result was two minors each.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, tEBRUARY 4, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, tEBRUARY 4, 1888.
WFSTON SONS OF TEMPtRA.NCE.

On Wednesday evening the Weston Sans of Tem- perance celebrated their seventh anniterstiry 'in the Weston Wesleyan schoolroom. An excellent teit was provided, to which about 150 members and friends did ample justice. The tables were pre- sided over by Mrs. Ed. Aaron, Mrs. D. Kirkham, Mrs. Moores, Mrs. Davies, Miss Armstrong, Miss Hughes, anftiss Dunbebin, assisted by Mrs. Cottrell, Mrs. Dodd, Mrs. Breese, Mrs. Cooper, and Mrs. Daviston. After tea an entertainment was held. Mr. 4J. W. Kirkham. presided, and in an earnest and practical address he spoke of the benefits of total abstinence, and urged upon the young men prekent if they wanted to succeed in life, the necessity of keeping clear of the public-house. Mr. Thottas Cooke, of Runcorn, Vie secretary for the district, was present, and, in t excellen,t speech, spoke of the society's progress during Me past year. He stated that 13 new lodges had been instituted, and 22 juvenile branches, over 3,000 members initiated, and over .-54.000 of an increase in the funds of the society. He also stated that during the past year the society had paid away in sick claims over £16,000, and in death claims £3,000, and given away to de- serving members in distress over .E.lOO. Mr. Thomas Heesom, of Runcorn, also addressed the meeting on the advantages of young men connecting themselves with an Order like the Sons of Temperance. No young man who joined the Order would ever regret it. He himself had been copnected with the Order about 20 years, and was more than pleased that he lutd joined the Order when he did. The following programme was then /one through :—Recitations by Miss Hulse, Mr. A. Flulse, Mr. Jones, Mr. Knap- ham, Mr. Hazlehurst, and Mr. J. Coltrell ; songs by Miss Hibbert,efiss Steward, and Mr. H. Dixon; humorous dialogue by Messrs. Cooper, Dunbabin, Hazlehurst, Owen, and Brown; cornet solo, Mr. J. Ward; cornet duet, Messrs. J. Ford and J. Smith. During the evening selections of music were ren- dered by the Weston Wesleyan Brass Band, under the ilk conductorship of Mr. J. Ford. A vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Mr. W. Dun- babin, seconded by Mr. T. Cottrell, and supported by Mr. T. lisvenscroft, brought what had been a most enjoyabfb evening to a close.

MASONIC INSTALLATION AT WIDNES. The members of the "Equity" Lodge of Free- masons, No. 1,384, celebrated the festival of St. John on Thursday, at the Masonic Rooms, Central Hotel, Widnes, Bro. John Patten,W.M., in the chair, when Bro. Dr. Cooper was duly installed the W.M. :or the ensuing twelve months, according to ancient custom. The installation ceremony was performed by ,Bro. James White, P.M. There was a good attendance of brethren. Amongst the visitors were the following:—Bros. W. Barnes, S. 941; W. Taylor, P.M. 1250; S. H. Hartley, P.M. 86, P.G.S.;" J. Leatherbarrow, W.M. 86. 897; A. Johnstone, 897: ,T. H. Hitchen, W.M. 1.908; C. H. Lewin, S.W. , 1,908; G. H. Denby, P.G.S.D. Chester;' J. W. White, J.D. 1,908; J. Dobson. 1,259. The newly-installed W.M. appointed the follow- ing .brethren as his officers' for the ensuing twelve months ;—Bros. John Patten, I.P.M. ; T. Williams, S.W.; George Claye, J.W.; A. G. Kyle, treasurer; John (WE, secretary; W. White, S.D. ; W. Walker, J.D. ; Shepherd. I.G. •, Sayce, steward; Hnit, tyler ; James White P.M.D.C. The ceremony being over, the brethren dined together at the house of Brother Parks, \ under the presidency of the newly-installed W.M. The usual loyal and masonic toasts were duly given and responded to, During the evening a P.M.S. jewel was presented to Bro. John Patten from the brethren of the lodge, in ap- preciation of his services as W.M. Brother Patten suitably responded, thanking the brethren for their kindness. A special Jubilee jewel, subscribed by members of the lodge, was presonted to Brother James White, P.M, for his services to the lodge during the last 15 years. Brother White thanked the brethren for so marked an appreciation of his services. Much as he prized the P. 31.5. jewel, he valued much more the one presented to him by the Initiates during his year of office as W.M., but. both had been.eclipsed by the beautiful jewel now pre- sented to him. He felt how little he deserved it, • but hoped to merit i by future services to his lodge.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIAN. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present: Mr. J. Fisher (chairman), the Rev. T. Chambers, Rev. Dean Finegan, and Messrs. Y. Burchall, J. Musson,W. Middle- hurst, J. Buckley, W. G. Ashton, J. Lowe, E. Syder, C. B. Johnson, J. Whalley, J. Ranson, T. F. Hill, J. KenwriFht, J. Griffiths, B. A. Graves, J. Leatherbar- row, P. B. Longton, and H. S. Hartley (clerk). • e. THE DEATH OF Ma. P. Mtemenunsr.—The Chairman raid he was sure they would all deeply regret the death of one If their members, Mr. Peter Middlehurst, of Rain- ford, whose genial behaviour and conduct had made him dear to them all. He had been a useful member' and his generosity was unbounded, as they would know froth his and his wife's noble gift to the Providence Hospital at St. Hclens.-•—The Rev. Dean Finegan moved that a lctter of condolence be sent to Mrs. Middlehurst, and said that the Board had lost a good member, the district. had lost a benefactor, and charity had lost at. good friend.—The Rev. T. Chambers seconded the motion, which was passed. WORKHOUSE IN3Qams.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 534 inmates in the house this week, 543 last week, and 497 in the corresponding week last year. Ix7CTIOUS DISEASES.—The Clerk said the Medical Offie r had reported that a case had been received into the hospital which he was afraid would develope into typhoid fever. If that was so, some accommodation should be made to isolate the case.—lt was decided that the Medical Officer be instructed to make the.necessary arrangements lor isolating the ease if necessary.—Mr. Burchall asked if any agreement had been arrived at about sending fever case! the St -Helens Infectious Hospital P—The Chairman said nothing had yet been done.—The Rev. T. Chambers asked when the Wiriston Hospital would be fit for use P—Mr. Leatherbarrow said the Whiston Hcspital belonged to the Rural Sanitary Authority, and arrangements would have to be mae with alai body before any could be admitted.—Mr. Lowe Sr lcl thematter abaut thiSt. Helens Hospital was only a question as to how much should be paid for each patient. That Was the difference between the Guardians and the St Helens Carporation.—The Rev. Dean Fineglia said the Widnes authorities were willing to make arrange- ments for the admission of patients into the Widnes Hospital, and if the same offer was made to them as had been made to St. Helens he thought it would be accep- ted. Smallpox was spreading in the country, and they ought not to wait until an epidemic broke out in their midst before they had prepared for it -- Mr. Lowe moved that a deputation be appointed to wait on the St. Helens Corporation and the Widnes Local Board in reference to the terms upon which patients suf- fering from infectious disease could be received into the hospitals.—Mr. Buckley seconded the motion, which was passed .—The deputation was elected as follOws : The Chai- rman (Mr. Fisher), Mr. Lowe, Mr. Wareing, Mr. Leather- barrow, and Mr. Burchall, with the Clerk.—Mr. Johnson afterwards stated that a case of fever had broken out at Prescot, and it was asked if the case could be admitted to the hospitaL—The Board decided that as it was not a pauper case they.could not entertain the proposal.— The Clerk remarked that it was the duty of the local health authorities to take steps to protect the public health. It was no part of the duty of the Board of Guar- dians to prevent the spreading of infectious disease.—The subject then dropped. DETENTION OF CASUAL PAIIPERS.—The Clerk read •a letter from the Local Government Board suggesting,that the Guardians should exercise their discretion in permit- ting casual paupers to leaye the casual wards before the time fixed by Act of Parliament. The Clerk observed that had been done for some years in that workhouse, and the Board decided that the practice should be con- tinued.

TnE Woincitousn ALTERATIONSPLA letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the plans of the proposed alterations to the Workhouse premises, and asking to be informed of the estimated cost of the works, and how the Guardians proposed to repay it. The Clerk said the letter had been before the Building ConiJ mittee, who had directed the akhiteet to prepare a specification and submit an estimate of the cost. The committee also desired to have the sanction of the Board to advertise for tenders and to do any other 'natters necessary to the time of receiving tenders.—The minutes were adopted. EU:MEM—The Clerk submitted an elaborate return showing the number of eases admitted into tht Work, house from each relievint officer's district week!' during the 12 months ending 18th January last. The totals were as follow :—Mr. Stuart (Windle) 162, Mr. Barton (Eecleston) 286, Mr. Pennington (Sutton) 134, Mr. Bul- lock (Prescot and Wootton) 111, Mr. Treacey (Widnes) 587. total 1,280. The Clerk also stated that he had re- ceived a letter from Mr. Wareing, a member of the Board, regretting his inability to attend the meeting, and asking for a copy of the return to be sent to him. It was for the Boara to consider'whether it should be printed, as it was useful as showing the ebbing and flowing of pau- perism.—Mr. Flill moved that the return be printed and a copy sent topach member, and Mr.Kenwright seconded the motion, which was passed.—Mr. Leatherbarrow ob' served that Mr. Treacey was sending nearly as manycases as the other officers combined, and the Rev. Dean Fine- gan said he thought that showed that a workhouse was wanted at Widnes.--After some conversation the matter dropped. -

THE VACANCY AT RAINFORD.—The Clerk was instruc- ted to take the necessary steps for the election of a guardian for Rainford to fill the vacancy caused by the death of the late Mr. P. Middlehurst. This concluded the business.
CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT RUNCORN.

A public meeting under the auspices of the North- wieli Division Conserv,ative Associa,tion, was held in? RuncOrn Public Hall. on Monday-evening. At half- past seven, the time announced for the commence- •ment of the proceedings, the audience did not *num- ber more than a score, and when a start was made a quarter of an hour later, there would be about afty persons present. • As the meeting progressed people "dropped in" in twos and threes, but at no time did the number of those present exceed 250. Dr. , Steele took the chair, and on the platform weire Col. ' Eyre, M.P. for Gainsborough, the Rev. W. Wonbing-b ton (of Bromborough), tne Rev. W. Preston, Messrs. T. Fielding (Manchester), W. . Whittaker, F. A. Lake, G. Simmerfield, H. Coke, J. Meadowcroft, W. Hankinson, J. E. Meredith, IL White, and J. W. Lightburn (agent.) *Letters of apology for non-attendance 'were read from Sir Richard Brooke, Mr. T. B. Royden, M.P., Mr. Mattinson, candidate for Walton Division, Mr. W. J. Stewart, the Rev. J. Lockwood, and Major Hazlehurst; while a telegram had been received from Mr. W. H. Verdin, who is at Hastings, to the same effect. The Chairman, after expressing his sorrow that so few people were pre- sent called upon Colonel Eyre, who said when he saw such weather, he was in doubt whether they would have any meeting at all. After alluding to the acts passed by the Government last session, the speaker re- ferred to the proposed Local Government Bill. Mr. Ritchie had told him the other day that it would be the biggest bill that was ever brought forward. He (Colonel Eyre) was not in the secret, but he believed it would De a beneficial bill. One great change would be that instead of county matters being managed by ex-officios, in future the business would-be carried on by popularly elected members. Speaking for himself he did not see if the electors could be trusted to send members to Parliament, why they could not be trusted to elect members to a county Board. (Ap- plause.) As to the land question, all classes were deeply interested in land. The insurance offices had not less than fifty per cent of their capital invested in land, and the Oddfellows and other friendly societies nearly in the same proportion. As the working-men-were great sup- porters of these organisations, and in any deprecia- tion qf land value they must suffer. One of the great injuffe.s of land, it was said, were the high rents, and landloreg were told they must lower their rents. But the landlord did not fix his rents ; the law of supply and demand fixed the rent. The spending power of the land- Io xis was something like 40 millions a pox less than it used 'to be. Who was the richer for this fall of rents? He maintained that a great many were poorer. As rents 'had fallen wages had fallen too. It was evident that the poverty of the land did not make anybody richer. (Ap- plause.) He should like to know the direction in which the land laws had to be altered. Under the Present system we produced more corn per acre than any other country in the whole world, even in an adverse climate and a worn out soil, and we produced the finest flocks, the finest herds, and the finest horses. This was easily proved, because the American agriculturists came to buy from us, and he did not suppose they did so from love of England, but because we had the finest breeds. He ad- vised the electors to be careful how they touched laws which had induced 400 millions of capital to be invested in land on mortgage, and in addition had produced such satisfactory results. He challenged any man to name a single system of land tenure, which did riot exist in Eng- land, and which• had more prosperous results. (Ap- plause.) Alluding to Ireland, Colonel Eyre contended that the Irish people had many advantages over the Eng- lish. Scotch, and Welsh people, but they had been pre- vented from securing the benefits of many acts passed for them through the power of the National League, which Mr. Balfour was now endeavouring to break the back of. (Applause.) He was happy to say that , the other day he had a letter from Mr. Balfour—(applause) who informed him that during the past. year there had been a considerable advance in the business connected ith Lord Ashbourrie's Act for allowing tenants to pur- chase their holdings with money lent by the British tax- payer. He thought therswas not a Conservative nor a Liberal who world not hail that as a s'gn of the coming quiet in Ireland. (Applause.) At any rate it was a sign that as soon as they knew that the Quein's writ was more Powerful than the National League tile, people of Ireland would ta*e advantage of the mOny benacial acts passed for their benefit. (Applause.) On the motion of the Rev. W. Worthington, seconded by Mr. W. T. Fielding, and supported by Mr. H. Coke, a vote of thanks was accorded to Colonel Eyre, and a similar compliment was paid to the chairman, on the proposition of the Rev. W. Preston, seconded by Mr. F. A. Lake.

They affirmed that the Bible was not intended to teach us our religion, and that the church was not the church of the Bible. They were also endeavouring to bring into use le Ilayer Bopk'of 1549, in which the Roman Catho- lie doctrines of the Mass, elevation, reservation, the seven sacraments, and nb cup to-the laity were taught. Tha Irtualists enjoined fasting, which waa, a vractic con- trary te§'criptUre, a fact which was ',loved by the omiss- fon of the word " fasting " in au fewer than four placas in the 'R'evised Version of the New Testament. The Church had been deceived for centuries by monkish im- position. Mr. Foulkes condemned the practice of con- fessing to a priest, saying that there was but one priest —Jesus Christ, and touching upon the question of eau- dies, said they were not legal in churches except. when used for the purpose of giving light ; and he quoted from an old writer, who said: 'The two unlit on the re- table, or super-altar, are symbolic of empty noddles without light or learning." As to crosses and crucifixes, he said the cross as an instrumentum was unlawful in the service. It was not lawfel to place the cross on the Communion table. It was exchfded from the Book of Common Prayer. The lecturer concluded by a reference to his resignation of the office of • gunday teacher,' and read seieral letters on the Abject.

WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY _ AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of thisi Authority was held at the Workhouse yesterday morning'. There Were present Messrs. Darhyshire (in the chair), W. Long, Owen, Pennington, J. Houghton, W. Houghton, Grange, Swinton, Z. Armitage; S. Sutton, (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. 0 wen (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (inspector).
THE- ALLOTMENT ACT.

A letter was read from Mr. Henley, Local Government Board Inspector for the District, asking as to the work- ing of did Allotments ,Act in the Authority's district. The questions he asked wore, first, the number of cases in whink application had been made to the Rural Sani- tary Authority under the Act; second, the action the Authority might have taken in 'regard to the applica- tions.—The CLERK said he•ad written to Mr. Henley to say that there had been no applications made to the Authority, and that it was not considered probable that there would be any at present at any rate. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. SEPIITON reported that the births were, males 20, females 15; deaths, males 14, females 8. The death rate from all causes was equal to 19 per 1,000, against 17 the corresponding month of last year. There were several Cases of measles and whooping cough, and three cases of scarlet fever in the Liverpool-road and Lovely-lane dis- tricts. With respect to the smallpox cases at Sankey Bridges, the patients were all convalescent, and he had not heard of any further outbreak. He had had the houses disinfected and the beds and bedding burnt, and he wished the Authority to allow compensation for the articles he,hactcondemned. Reportag on the outbreak of dithena in The superintendent's house at Padgate dustrial Schools, the medical offieet said he WI ex- amined the premises along pith Mr. Owen, their sur- veyor an he had no doubt but the disease had been pro- duced' by sewer gas finding its way into the house through the down spouts, which were connected ditectly with the sewer, without any traps or gullies, and through these spouts into the cavity walls, and then into the rooms. There was also a want of ventilation throughout the house, especially over the stairs. He recommended that the spouts be disconnected from the sewer, and the drains trapped and a ventilator placed in the ceiling over the staircase. He had also to report a case of typhoid

fevek at the Boat House, Thelwall, and a. case Of scarb fever at Croft.—This report wag adopted. It was agreeu that as compensation 'for the arttples 'Ordered to be des- troyed in connection with the smiPlipox cases at Sankey Bridges, £8 18s should be allowed.—ln answer to the chairman, Dr. SEPRTON said he thought the river big been the cause of the case of typhoid fever at Thelwall. SURVEYOR'S REPORT. 4471'he SURVEYOR (Mr. V.T. Owen) repotted-that pis.. .had been Submitted by Mr. J. B. Aldred for 12 houses Knutsford-road, Grappenhall,.which might be approved. but he had shown two streets running at right angles ' the highroad, to be 30 feet wide, sand which in 1881 we passed by this Authority as being 38 feet wide. 7 I streets had not been-made, but any alteration from. feet in width would require the sanction ofthat Autho) ity. As one of the streets in question waS 170 yard long and the,other 130 yards long, he (Mr. Owen) &Ili) that unless the houses on either side were set back they would not sanction. the 30 feet width. The owner sub- mittte the streets with the building line set back nine feet on ea.Oh side, giving ; clear width of 48 feet betweer the buildings, and in that case, if it had tile approval ( the Authority, he saw no objection to the streets bell 30 feet wide. With regard to the. Manchester Canal, the contractor had sent him a sketch plan f( fonr cottages to be erected of wood at Rixtotrvard,fitt( with earth closets, drained to the river, and suppli, with drinking water by carts. Although the bye-lal required dwellings to be brick built and slated, Ihe sa no reapn why the houses should not be erected .for tl purpose for which they were intended; there was Hal likelihood of any nuisance arising, and with periodical visits of their , inspector the general cleanliness of tt premises would be ensured. With regard to the di theria at Padgate Schools, Mr. Owen reported that 4 had asked Mr. Mines, the superintendent, to cut off th, connection of the two downpipes of his house with tr sewer, and to procure gullies fx them to empty This report was adopted, and Mr. Owen was requested) to inspect Padgate Schools and report to the Board Guardians as to their sanitary condition. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
[FROX 0.011 OWN CORRESPONDENT.I - 23, Old Broad-street. E.C.

The tentative state of the stock markets during the past week is characteristic of the uncertainty which pre- vails in all matters relating to the Stock Exchange. A change may take place very shortly, and one thing is certain that the public ure.taking much more interest in the reafket than they used to do. The outside atten- dance in the street is significantly large. Formerly three or four visitors would be considered a large crowd, but now they may be seen by twenties and thirties, and at the present most of them are dabbling in copper or diamonds.

Copper maintains ita firmness, Aio Tintos, Masori and Barry, and Namaquas being in active demand. Atten- tion was called in these columns to the latter company when the shares were quoted at a little over 5 premium. It Was pointed out that there was every probability of their reaching 10 premiuth. They are within half a point below this figure, and those investors who acted on this advice have secured a good profit. Nevertheless, now that the French syndicate has got ,thisc,company under its control, in addition to other companies, its future be- comes so much a suLject for mere market rigging that it would be absurd to attempt to advise as to its future course. The copper market is entirely in the hands of a group of French financiers, who can do what they like ith it.

Diamond sha-es are beginning to claim •considerable at- tention. De Beers have been in active demand, and are fully one better on the week. It is, however, in the lower- priced shares of mining companies at the public can only make money; but unfortunatellithey too often wait until the market has got to its height before• coming in. Few companies present a more favourable opportunity far a sharp speculative rise than the St. Augustine Ittatriond Minifig C 9., which at present can be bought for less than lOs for £1 fully paid up shares. • Home Rails continue to be very dull and inactive. If a slight rise occurs in the morning in these stocks, by the afternoon it is entirely lost, and so the market see- saws with the whole benefit to the dealers. In. spite of the large increase- in traffic in several of the leading Northern lines, ko flat is the market that it has had scarce'y a perceptible influence upon prices. North British, Midland, North "astern have ,shown unusatal large increase in the takings for the past week, which at any other time would have been sufficient to send up the market. In American Rails the market is almost dead, and if a, fractional rise takes placeon this side, New York imme- diately responds by sending it down a fraction under the original lance. There is, however,'undoubtedly a large field open to the speculator in some of the leading stocks inAmericans for a gc4cl rise, which we venture•to think cannot long be delayed. In miscellaneous securities there is little interest. The PavilioriMusic Hall Company has aaracted considerable attentiori in London, and the general consensus of opinion, in view of the balance sheet just published, is teat these shares have been immensely iaflated, and it may be fully expected to see them at par befole long. ,
LATEST NEWS.
Mr. Balfour arrived in London from Dublin on Friday morning to attend the Cabinet Council.

Dr. Obonnell, Prefect of Maynooth—College, has been , appointed Roman Catholic Bishop qf Raphoe. Three thousand hands have been locked out of the slibe factories at Cincinnati owing to differences with their employers.

'three buildings, occupied as tinplate andlitincase 4orks, at Bermondsey, were burped down on Friday morning. The darnage is considerable. At-Edinburgh, on Friday, twelve Aignish crofters were sentenced to terms of imprisonment varying from fifteen to nine months each ; one Clashmore crofter to twelve months; and two others to six months. A .settlement has been effected between Colonel O'Callaghan and his Boclyke. tenantry, the latter paying one thousand pounds, receiving a clear receipt up to March last, and the reinstatement of evicted tenants.

INPENDING MINERS'.STRIKE.—The majority of the Fife miners have given notice that they intend ceasing work on Saturday week if the proposed 10 per cent, reduction in wages is not withdrawn. The men have asked for a conference with the employers. The Clackmannan miners are also striking. ELEcTiox INTELLIGENCE.—Mr. H. F. Beaumont, M.P., has declined to resign his seat for the Colne Valley Divi- sion. Mr. Dodgson H. Madden, Conservative, was on Friday returned unopposed foq Dublin University, on his appointment as Solicitor-Genefal for Ireland. Mr. M. W. Mattinson, Conservative, was, on Friday, elected with- out opposition for the Walton Division of Liverpool, In the room of Mr. Gibson, the new Irish judge. ' SENTENCE ON TNE DYNANITARDS.—At the London Old Bailey, on Friday, in the trial of the alleged dynamiters Callan and Harkins, the Attorry-General replied on be- half of the Wown, pointing out that the accused had I done no businets in England, and had given no account of themselves. The jury found both prisoners guilty, and the Judge sentenced them to fifteen years' penal ser- vitude each.

THE RIPON-MORLEY VISIT.—Lord Ripon and Mr. Mor- ley were presented, in the Mansion Heuse, Dublin, by deputations, with the freedom of Limerick, and with addresses from the Corporations of Cork, Waterford, Clonmel, Sligo, Drogheda, Cashel, and Kilkenny, from the Town Commissioners of many other places, from the Royal University, the Gaelic Athletic Association, National League: branches, the Protestant Homekßule Association, and the Dublin Trades Council. " LORD SALISBURY AND THE IRISH LANDLORDS.—A depu- tation of •Irish landlords, introduced by the Duke of Abercorn, waited on Lord Salisbury (with whom was Mr. Balfour) on Friday afternoon, and urged reasons why Irish landlords should receive some compensation for past losses, inasmuch as legislation had converted them frOm owners of soil ,to simple owners of rent charge. Various suggestions as to form of relief or com- pensation were made by the niembers of the deputation, and in reply Lord Salisbury said he thought Irish land- lords were wise in seekinif compensation in an indirect form by the mitigation and improvement of existing laws. The Government would therefore earnestly con- sider any propositions placed before them. THE SALFORD GASWORKS: ARREST OF HUNTER.—TiIe late manager of the Salford Gasworks, Mr. Samuel Hunter, who was dismissed by the committee for receiv- ing bribes, as the outcome of the libel case of Hunter v. Lever, was placed in the dock at the Salford Police Court, on Friday morning, on a charge of forgery. The particular charge brought against him is that he forged the name of the Chairman of the Gas Committee to satisfy a contractor who refused to pay Hunter any fur- ther commission on coal contracts unless he knew that _ . _

the commmittee were aware of what was being done. He received a letter stating that the committee were aware of the practice, and purporting to be signed by Alderman Sharp, but which Mr. Sharp declares js a forgery, Prisoner was remanded in custody, bail being refused. COUNTY GOVERNMENT AND THE LICENSING QUESTION. —A depitation of about 100 persons, representing the licensed victualler of the United. Kingdom, waited upon Mr. Ritchie, as President of the Local Government Board, on Friday afternoon, with reference to the County Boards Bill. The deputation was introduced by Mr Ernest W. Norfolk. secretary.of the Licensed Victuallers' Protection Society, who stated that the trade viewed the proposals to transfer the control of the grant and refusal of licences from the present justices to an elec- tive body with alarm. If not too late, the deputation urged the Gsvernment to leave the subject of the licen- sing system out of the contemplated Bill.—Mr. Ritchie, replying to the depittation, said the Government did not intend to introduce Any general legislation on the licen- sing question. The provisions of the County Govern- ment Bill affecting licensing wotld in no sense be con- fiscatory. He was sure the reasonable members of the trade would have no ground for complaint when the bill was introduced. • .
SHOCKING TRAGEDY IN SALFORD.-AN ENTIRE FAMILY MURDERED.

One of the most awful tragedies which has over oc- curred in this district was discovered in Salford on Fri- day. It appears that a man named DerbY, a chemist and herbalist, having a shop on Regent-road, Salford, resided in Garfield-street, off Regent-road, with his wife and six children, the eldest of whom was aged about fif- teen years, and the youngest, a baby, aged a 'little more than a year. For some time past Derby has been suffer- ing from an abscess in the head, and his behaviour has been somewhat strange in consequence, though no actual traces of any aberration of mind have shown them- selves. The house next his was .unoccupied, but the next but one is occupied by a tradesman, and tkisr man states that on Sunday night he heard sounds of scuffling in Derby's House. However this may be, nothing whatever was seen' or heard of any of the family on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, and no signs of life were seen about the house. This fact aroused the suspicions of the residents of the shop, and they decided on Friday morning to en- deavour to satisfy their minds that all was right. They accordingly proceeded to. Derby's house and sought ad- Mission by knocking. No answer being forthcoming the door was broken open, and a terrible and horrifying spectacle presented itself. On the sofa in the parlour was found the body of Derby, and on proceeding upstairs they found in . one bedroom four of the children quite dead, and in another bed waiMri. Derby, and the other two children, also dead. All had the appearance of hav- ing died asleep, and it is thought that Derby, either in conducting some experiment, or wilfully, caused his wife and childten to inhale poisonous gas' which suffocated them. From an interview with the father of the deceased man, also a chemist, it is assumed that the latter construction is placed upon the affair. It is said that though business has not latterly been very success- ful with the dead man he had just come into a small for- tune, the papers relating to which were found upon his body. None of the- bodies show any, signs a violence, all looking as though death had overtaken them in sleep. The affair has caused intense excitelment. A late telegram says indications point to the cmclusion that Derby and his wife first poisoned their children and then committed suicide together. Amongst fle letters found in the house were several addressed by s Derby to relatives, expvtssing hi intention of commit- ting suicide owing to difficulties connected with the settlement of a dispute about property. In a letter ad- dressed to his sister at Eccles he wrote : "I cannot leave my darling wife and children behind; in fact Annie often said she did not want to leave them after I went; and when I told her, a few days ago, that I could not . stand this any longer she said she was quite ready to go. I wish our bodies to be sent to Owen's College for diseec- tion, etc., or, if they are buried, let tlie funeral be con- ducted in the quietest way possible, and at the least possible expense." Derby was thirty-three years of age, his wife was thirty-eight, and the children were—Gladys three years, Florence Helena five, Clara Elizabeth seven, Frederick Cecil nine,, Harold Percy eleven, and Earnest Llewellyn thirteen. Derby was a sober man and had been in a comfortable position.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

- The monthly meeting of this Committee was held at the Workhouse yesterday morning. There were present Messrs Derbyshire (in the chair)„W. Long, Z. Armitage, Blackhurst, Balharry, Ratcliffe, J. Houghton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and W. Owen (valuer). A COMBINATION OF SMELLS.—COLIBCiIIOr 3: Pierpoint appealed against the assessment of his house at Bewsey, which stood at £6O gross and £5l rateable. The reason for the appeal was that the house was not worth the amount it was assessed at, and Mr. Pierpoint remarked that he would be glad if any one would find him, a ten- ant at £5O a year. The reason why the property had been reduced in value was that when the east wind blew it got the smoke from Dallam forge, with the north-east wind they got the stench from the Longford depot, which bad been fixed there since the house was built, and when the wind was in the north-west they got the very offensive odour of Sankey brook, so that he was pretty well surrounded.—The Chairman: It does not Matter which way the wind blows then? (Laughter.)— Mr. Jolla Houghton: It has always been that way.—Mr. Pierpoint said they had not always had the depot, and when he went into the house Dallam forge was only about a tenth of what it now is.—Mr. Blackhurst said there vas no doubt that property in thdt neighbourhood had been depreciated.—Mr. Pennington moved, the Chairman seconded, ' and it was agreed to, that the ‘ssessment be reduced to £5O gross. „ Sr. PETER'S SOROOLS.—The Rev. G. D..Wray appealed against the assessment of St. Peter's ScAl, John-street, which stands at £6 lOs gross, $25 lOs rateable. The g2ound of the appeal was that the school was appropria- t3d to relikious worship, and ought therefore to be ex- empted.—ln answer to the Clerk, Mr. Wray stated that the school,-besides besides being used for religious wor- ship, were also used as day schools, at which the scholars were charged so much per week'.—lt wa4 there- fore held that they were liable to assessment As —Mr. Pennington said Orford school was in a similar was in a similar position.—The Clerk: There are several schools on the ' same, tooting.—The Chairman thought thatunder the circumstances they could not reduce the assessment. . This was all the business of public interest. •

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

FRODSHAM AND FRODSHAM LORDSHIP PAROCHIAL COM- MITTEES.—At the Monthly meeting, of these 'Committees, the Inspector reported that he had conferred with the Law Clerk in reference to certain plans of a proposed new street, proposed to be laid oUt on land belonging to Mr. Wm. Collier, of Delsby, situate off Main-street, Frodsham, and the decision arrived at was that such plans were not'in Accordance with the bye-laws, and such being the case, they were not approved. KINGSLEY PARISH CHURCH.—The annual Parochial tea meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon in the girls schoolroom. Among those who sat (3.9wn to tea, were the Vicar (Rev. A. P. Reynolds), and the churchwardens Dr. Steel and Mr. E. J. Steward. In the evening a childrens' concert was held in the larger schoolroom, which was well filled. Tha programme was rendered in a satisfactory manner, and reflected great credit on the conductor, Mr. T. G. Cole. The chief accompanist was Mr. A. P. Reynolds. LECTURE ON ENTOMOLOGY.—At the weekly meeting of the Frodsham Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Class, Mr. T. Sant, of Frod.sham, delivered a lecture on the above subject. He held quite a contrary view to those who stated that a hard nter was destructive to insect life, and so beneficial to the farmers, his reason for that be- ing because a hard winter often destroyed the birds in large numbers, which were naturally the enemies of the insetts. A hearty vote of thanks was 'accorded to Mr. Sant foil his very able lecture, and the meeting ter- minated.

---ASSAULT AT NORLET.—On Monday at the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, GoOrge Watson was summoned for assaulting Joseph Chrimes, at Norley, on the 27th Janu- ary.—Complainant said the defendant struck him half a dozen times, and knocked him in the ditch. Defendant had had a grudge against him because at the last elec- tion complainant had shouted " Tollemache for ever," whereupon the defendant threw him down And acted as 'if he was going to strangle him.—Defendant said the oompiginant began the row, and had been spreading some scandal about him.—Defendant was bound over to !rep the peace. GAME TP-ESPASS.—At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Frederick Woodcock, Edward Booth, Joseph Birchhood, and Isaac Jenkins were charged with being in the unlawful pursuit of game at Alvanley, on the 7th January.—Robert Thompson, keeper to Mr. John Brun- drit, said on the afternoon of the date in question he saw the four defendants ferreting, and they had a lurcher dog with them. He got within 50 yards of the defend- ants when they ran away. Ite iaentified all of them except Woodcock, as he *knew them by sight. He ran after Woodcock, and on catching him took two rabbits from him and a net.—Each defendant was.fined 20s and costs.

" RITUALISM ; OR, THE ROAD TO SOME." On Monday evening, at the Town Hall, FrodOiam, a lecture was given by Mr. Robert Foulkes, before a small audience, upon the above subject. The lecturer began by giving a description of the English Church Union, which he said was composed of 17 bishops, about 2,600 clergy, and over 20,000 of the laity, their object being to bnng the Church of England back to Rornanism.

Mr. Gibbs has erected hot water circulation both in the Church of St. Mary, Drogheda, and in the Convent of Mercy, tif same parish, and I feel great pleasure in bearing willing testimony to the satisfactory manner in which he has com- pleted both contracts. The members of Mercy Community, the priests of the parish, and the congregation testify to the complete success of his method of llating by small bore pipes. When freezing outside, we have a temperature inside of close on 60 degrees. The cost of coke is small, we have no leakages, little trouble, and no filth. • (Signed) THOMAS ALLEN, P.P., St. Mary's, Drogheda.
